findings.title: Failing or missing clean filter in the daemon's environment commits the plaintext value and pushes it to refs/cowork
findings.scenario: The team's clean/smudge filter is defined in .git/config or ~/.gitconfig and calls a tool (sed, python, a script). The detached daemon runs `git add -A` into its private index. Case 1: the tool is not on the daemon's PATH, or the script fails. Case 2: the driver is defined only in a global config that the daemon's HOME/env does not see. Neither case sets filter.<name>.required.
findings.consequence: git prints an error but `git add -A` exits 0 (case 1) or says nothing (case 2), and the blob holds the raw smudged content (the real value). The next push publishes it on refs/cowork/<b>/code to every collaborator's clone. Resetting the live ref at save does not remove it from GitHub, which keeps force-push residue as cruft for an unknown time. The daemon reports success, so nobody notices.
findings.evidence_detail: sweep/e1: filter.tok.clean='nonexistent_tool_xyz' -> 'error: external filter ... failed', add -A exit=0, `git cat-file -p :cfg.txt` = 'key=REAL_VALUE'. Driver unset -> silent passthrough, same blob. With `-c filter.tok.required=true` -> 'fatal: cfg.txt: clean filter 'tok' failed', exit 128, index unchanged. Retention of overwritten data: https://github.blog/engineering/architecture-optimization/scaling-gits-garbage-collection/
findings.mitigation: 1) At start, list every filter=<name> in use (`git ls-files | git check-attr --stdin filter`). Pass `-c filter.<name>.required=true` on every daemon git invocation, so a failing or undefined filter aborts the snapshot. 2) Preflight in `/cowork doctor` and at start: for each filtered path, check that clean(working file) equals the HEAD blob, and that clean(smudge(blob)) equals the blob, run in the daemon's own process environment. 3) Never push a snapshot whose filtered paths' blobs differ from base while no hook-observed edit touched them. 4) If a check fails, sync stays stopped and the hooks tell Claude and the user why.
findings.test: Integration test with a file:// remote: configure a token filter, then break it (rename the tool and unset the driver). Assert that the daemon makes no push, `git ls-remote` shows the live ref unchanged, the blob in any local snapshot never contains the plain token, and doctor reports FAIL. Repeat with the filter working and assert that sync resumes.

findings.title: Committing the raw snapshot 'on top' of the fetched tip after a failed or skipped apply reverts every peer's work
findings.scenario: The loop fetches tip R2, but applying it to disk fails: a Windows-invalid path (see poison-path), a locked file, 'not uptodate' after the retry cap, or the user's git operation in progress. The loop then continues to 'commit local changes on top': commit-tree with tree=SNAPSHOT (the worktree, which still reflects R1) and parent=R2, pushed with lease R2. A variant: after a CAS reject, the daemon uses its own unpushed commit P as the merge base for the new tip R3. P is not an ancestor of R3, so diff(P->R3) contains 'remove my local edits'.
findings.consequence: The CAS succeeds because the lease matches R2. The new commit's diff against its parent is the inverse of every change between R1 and R2, and every peer applies it. Teammates' work disappears from their disks and the live ref, and the chain records it as this user's edit. In the base=P variant, the user's own unpushed edits are silently reverted on their disk.
findings.evidence_detail: Follows from 3-way merge semantics and the approved loop order. The trigger conditions (apply failures) are VERIFIED in poison-path, partial-apply-on-lock and locked-file-stalls-snapshot.
findings.mitigation: Hard invariants, asserted in code before every push: (a) pushed tree = `merge-tree --write-tree --merge-base=LAST_APPLIED SNAPSHOT TIP` where TIP is exactly the lease value; the raw snapshot tree is pushable only when TIP == LAST_APPLIED. (b) LAST_APPLIED is the last remote commit whose tree was fully on disk, stored in a ref (refs/cowork-local/<b>/applied, in the daemon's private GIT_DIR) and updated only after a fully successful apply. Before every merge, `git merge-base --is-ancestor LAST_APPLIED TIP` must hold; if not, run the join procedure (see join-or-restart-seeds-revert). (c) While any incoming change is unapplied on disk, publish only paths whose incoming version is already on disk. (d) Sanity check: the paths in diff(TIP, pushed) must be a subset of the paths in diff(LAST_APPLIED, SNAPSHOT).
findings.test: Property test with a file:// remote and 2-3 simulated daemons. Randomly inject apply failures (a locked file through a held handle, an invalid path, CAS rejects). For every pushed commit P with parent R, assert that no path's content in R that came from another peer is changed in P unless the local session edited that path. Explicit regression: an apply that fails with a locked file must not lead to a push that reverts the other files.

findings.title: stash, checkout, bisect, /rewind, a stale editor buffer or Bash rewriters change the worktree back, and the daemon publishes it as a teammate-wide revert
findings.scenario: Any operation that rewrites the worktree to older content without leaving the markers the design watches (index.lock, MERGE_HEAD, REBASE_HEAD): `git stash -u` (for example, to get past the blocked pull after a save), `git checkout <branch>`, `git checkout <old-sha>`, `git bisect` (only BISECT_LOG exists), `git reset --hard`, `git checkout -- .`, Claude Code's checkpoint /rewind (restores whole files as they were before teammates' changes arrived), an IDE saving a buffer loaded before the daemon applied a peer change, or a Bash-run formatter, codegen or `sed -i` doing read-modify-write across a daemon apply. None of these go through the Edit/Write file fence.
findings.consequence: The next snapshot shows 'files reverted / new files deleted'. The daemon commits it as this user's edit and pushes it. Every peer's daemon applies the revert to disk. With a branch switch, the whole other branch's diff is broadcast onto main's live ref. Nothing errors, so the revert is noticed only when someone looks for lost code.
findings.evidence_detail: sweep/e17: during bisect only BISECT_LOG exists, HEAD is detached and f.txt is at the old version. After stash there are no markers and the worktree is reverted. sweep/e10: `git stash -u` restored f.py=v1 and removed new.py. Broadcasting it follows from the loop (REASONED). /rewind restores file content: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/checkpointing (URL not fetched in this sweep).
findings.mitigation: 1) Bind the daemon to (symbolic HEAD, HEAD oid) read each loop. On any change, freeze snapshots and applies immediately and require `/cowork resume`, which runs the join merge. 2) Extend pause markers to CHERRY_PICK_HEAD, REVERT_HEAD, BISECT_LOG, rebase-merge/, rebase-apply/, sequencer/ and AUTO_MERGE. 3) Revert detector: before pushing, for each hunk in diff(LAST_APPLIED, SNAPSHOT), check whether the new content equals the pre-image of a hunk applied from a peer in the last N minutes. If so, hold the hunk as a 'suspected revert', ask the owning Claude or user, and do not push it. 4) Mass-change breaker: more than 20 files or more than 30% of a file's lines changed in one snapshot without matching Edit/Write/Bash hook events: hold and ask. 5) While a Bash tool call runs in a cowork session (PreToolUse(Bash) to PostToolUse), defer applies to that worktree, with a cap such as 120 s.
findings.test: Scripted scenarios against a 2-peer file:// setup: (a) B runs `git stash -u` after receiving A's changes; (b) B runs `git checkout other-branch`; (c) B runs `git bisect start`; (d) a file is rewritten with its pre-peer content. In every case, assert that refs/cowork/<b>/code receives no commit that removes A's content, and that B's status shows 'held: suspected revert' or 'frozen: HEAD moved'.

findings.title: Joining or restarting with LAST_APPLIED set to the live tip makes the joiner's worktree look like edits that undo the live session
findings.scenario: Peer C joins a session whose live ref is based on B0 with 40 live edits, but C's HEAD is B1 (it pulled a newer main) or C has uncommitted work. Or a daemon crashes or the PC sleeps, its state file is lost or stale, and it restarts. If the daemon seeds LAST_APPLIED = live tip and snapshots the worktree, diff(live tip -> worktree) = 'remove the 40 live edits + add C's local state'.
findings.consequence: C's first push reverts the whole session for everyone, and the board attributes it to C. With 'commit on top' semantics this is one CAS push and needs no conflict to happen.
findings.evidence_detail: Follows from 3-way merge semantics when the wrong base is chosen. merge-tree takes exactly one --merge-base (https://git-scm.com/docs/git-merge-tree).
findings.mitigation: Join and restart procedure: ours = snapshot of the worktree; theirs = live tip; base = `git merge-base HEAD <live base commit>` (normally HEAD itself when C is on B0). Show a preview (N files will change on disk, M local files will be published) and require confirmation if M > 0. Do not push anything until the first apply has fully succeeded. Persist LAST_APPLIED as a ref and update it atomically after each successful apply. A state file is never the source of truth.
findings.test: Peer C starts with HEAD=B1 (one extra commit) plus a dirty file, while the live ref holds edits from A and B. Assert that after joining, C's disk = B1 + dirty file + A and B edits, the live ref contains all three, and no commit drops A's or B's hunks. Kill the daemon at random points during apply and restart it: same assertion.

findings.title: `read-tree -m -u` is not all-or-nothing when a write fails: other files land, deletions happen, and the private index is not updated
findings.scenario: A file the merge changes is open in a process that denies write or delete: Excel on a tracked .xlsx/.csv, a running dev server holding a log or SQLite file, a Visual Studio build, or AV. The daemon runs `read-tree -m -u S M` with its private index.
findings.consequence: Exit 128 with 'unable to unlink old 'b.txt': Invalid argument'. Every other changed file was already written and the deleted file was removed, but the private index still says S. A loop that assumes 'exit 128 = not uptodate, nothing written' re-snapshots and records the peer's changes as this user's local edits (wrong attribution, false claims and handoffs, possible revert through pushed-tree-must-be-merge-result). It retries forever while Excel stays open.
findings.evidence_detail: sweep/e2: b.txt held with [IO.File]::Open(p,'Open','Read','Read') in another PowerShell process. M changed a, b and z and deleted d. Result: exit=128, a.txt and z.txt = v2 CRLF on disk, d.txt <missing>, b.txt = v1, and `ls-files -s` on the private index unchanged (S). This settles the UNK in git-transport.md section 8.
findings.mitigation: 1) Classify stderr: 'not uptodate' / 'would be overwritten' means retry after re-snapshot; 'unable to unlink' / 'Permission denied' / 'Invalid argument' / 'invalid path' means a materialization failure. 2) After any non-zero exit, rehash every path in diff(S,M). Paths whose disk content equals M are applied, so record them, never as local edits. The remaining paths are pending. 3) Tree surgery: M' = M with pending paths taken from S. Run `read-tree -m S M'` (no -u) to sync the private index, and record pending paths with the reason (e.g. 'locked by EXCEL.EXE'). 4) Retry pending paths with backoff, show them in /cowork status and the hook context, and never block other paths' sync.
findings.test: Hold b.txt (FileShare.Read) and apply a merge that changes a, b and z and deletes d. Assert: state records a, z and d as applied and b as pending; the next push contains no a/z/d hunks attributed to this user; status shows the lock; after the handle closes, b is applied within one loop and the live ref is unchanged by the episode.

findings.title: One unreadable file makes `git add -A` fatal, so this PC publishes and receives nothing while Excel has a workbook open
findings.scenario: A user opens a workbook in the repo. Excel creates the owner file `~$book.xlsx` (untracked, held exclusively) and holds the workbook. Alternatively, any exclusively locked untracked or tracked file (DB, log). The daemon's snapshot runs `git add -A`. Related case: Excel or atomic-save editors save by writing a temp file, deleting the original, then renaming. A snapshot taken in that window sees the .xlsx deleted and a temp file added.
findings.consequence: `git add -A` fails ('error: open("~$book.xlsx"): Permission denied ... fatal: adding files failed', exit 128) and the index is untouched. No snapshot means no push of local edits, and the apply needs a fresh snapshot, so no incoming changes either. Sync stops silently for as long as the file is open. In the atomic-save case, peers receive a deletion of the workbook (and a partial apply where they also have it open), then a re-add.
findings.evidence_detail: sweep/e2: '~$book.xlsx' held FileShare.None -> add -A exit=128, private index unchanged; `git add -A --ignore-errors` -> exit 1 with the other changes captured. The Excel save sequence is REASONED (not reproduced with real Excel).
findings.mitigation:
1) Snapshot with `git add -A --ignore-errors` and parse 'unable to index file

' lines. Those paths keep their previous index entry and are listed as unreadable in status. 2) Built-in ignore list for lock and temp files: `~$*`, `~WRL*.tmp`, 8-hex temp names next to Office files, `.~lock.*#`, `*.swp`, `*.swx`, `4913`, `*.crswap`, `*.tmp`. 3) Deletion debounce: publish a delete only if the path is still absent in two snapshots at least 1.5 s apart, or a hook (Bash rm, Write) explains it.
findings.test: Hold '~$book.xlsx' exclusively and edit a.txt: assert a.txt reaches the remote within one push window. Simulate the atomic save (write temp, delete original, rename) with a snapshot forced in the window: assert no deletion is ever pushed.

findings.title: A path that cannot exist on Windows (or a case collision) blocks every later apply on Windows peers
findings.scenario: A macOS or Linux teammate's Claude creates `aux.py`, `con.py`, `notes:old.md`, `What?.md`, `dir.` (trailing dot or space), a path over 260 characters, or `readme.md` next to `README.md`. Their daemon publishes it.
findings.consequence: On Windows, `read-tree -m -u` rejects the whole merge ('error: invalid path', exit 128) and writes nothing, not even unrelated files. Every later live tip still contains the path, so the Windows peer never applies again: it is permanently out of sync, and the rule 'retry on failure' spins. Combined with pushed-tree-must-be-merge-result, its next push can revert everyone. Case collision: the apply 'succeeds', the disk keeps one file, `readme.md`, with the Linux content, the Windows user's later edits land in `readme.md`, and `README.md` can no longer be seen or edited on Windows.
findings.evidence_detail: sweep/e4: trees built with `git mktree` containing con.py / a:b.txt / 'trail.' / 'q?.md' plus a valid x.txt change -> exit 128 'invalid path', x.txt not updated. sweep/e9: README.md + readme.md -> exit 0, only 'readme.md' on disk, and a human edit is recorded under readme.md. A case-only rename Utils.py->utils.py applied correctly (negative result).
findings.mitigation: 1) Portability gate at snapshot time on every OS: refuse to publish new paths with Windows-reserved names (CON, PRN, AUX, NUL, COM1-9, LPT1-9 with any extension), characters <>:"|?* or control characters, trailing dot or space, a case-fold or NFC collision with an existing path, or a repo-relative length over 200. The file stays local and the creating Claude is told why through the PostToolUse context. 2) Receiving side: if M contains a path this OS cannot materialize, use tree surgery (keep it in the tree, mark it skip-worktree or pending), apply the rest, and report. Never fail the whole apply.
findings.test: A Linux-simulated peer (mktree) publishes con.py plus an edit to x.txt. Assert the Windows daemon applies x.txt, lists con.py as unmaterializable, and keeps applying later changes. Assert the Linux-side gate refuses to publish con.py when the gate runs on Linux.

findings.title: An incoming new path overwrites a peer's locally ignored file without warning (and leaks the sender's copy)
findings.scenario: Ignore rules differ between PCs: .git/info/exclude, global core.excludesFile, or a .gitignore edit not yet received. A's `.env`, `settings.local.json` or `.claude/settings.local.json` is not ignored on A, so `git add -A` publishes it. B has the same path ignored with its own private content.
findings.consequence: A's file is pushed to GitHub (leak). On B, `read-tree -m -u` exits 0 and replaces B's ignored file with A's content. B's local credentials or settings (possibly its Claude permission settings) are destroyed with no backup and no message. An unignored untracked collision is refused instead (exit 128), so only ignored files are at risk, which is where private files live.
findings.evidence_detail: sweep/e14: B's '.env' ignored through .git/info/exclude and 'secret_local.json' ignored through .gitignore; incoming tree adds both -> read-tree -m -u exit=0 and B's files replaced with A's content. A non-ignored untracked file in the same situation -> 'Untracked working tree file ... would be overwritten', exit 128.
findings.mitigation: 1) Before every apply, for each path that M adds and S lacks, lstat the disk. If a file exists (necessarily ignored or created after the snapshot), do not apply that path: tree surgery, mark it as a conflict, and copy the local file to .git/cowork/backup/ in any case. 2) Do not auto-publish new untracked files (see untracked-sweep). 3) Record each peer's effective ignore fingerprint (hash of `git status --ignored --porcelain` restricted to known-sensitive patterns) on the board and warn on mismatch.
findings.test: B has .env ignored (info/exclude) with content X; A publishes .env=Y. Assert B's .env is still X, a backup exists, and the board shows a conflict for .env. Assert A's daemon would not have published .env unless it was explicitly added.

findings.title: `git add -A` publishes scratch files, environments, nested repos and huge files, and one bad object can block pushes for good
findings.scenario: Untracked, non-ignored files appear in the repo: Claude's `_tmp_debug.py`, test_runs/ outputs, a venv or node_modules in a folder without ignore rules, a 150 MB CSV or dump, a nested clone, or Claude Code worktrees under `.claude/worktrees/<name>` (directories with a .git file). The daemon snapshots them all.
findings.consequence: Peers get platform-specific binaries (a Windows venv on macOS) and someone's scratch files, and save commits them. Nested repos and worktrees become 160000 gitlinks to commits that exist only on one PC, so a save puts broken gitlinks into main. A file over 100 MiB, or a value caught by GitHub push protection or a push ruleset, makes the push fail. If the daemon builds a chain of local commits, each retry pushes the same bad object again, so this PC can never push until the chain is rewritten. Large sweeps also use up the shared 6-pushes-per-minute budget.
findings.evidence_detail: sweep/e12: `git worktree add .claude/worktrees/agent-1` + a nested clone -> add -A records '160000 2b0bea... .claude/worktrees/agent-1' and '160000 d887c5... tools/bundled' (local-only commits). 100 MiB block: https://docs.github.com/en/repositories/working-with-files/managing-large-files/about-large-files-on-github ; push protection: https://docs.github.com/en/code-security/secret-scanning/introduction/about-push-protection ; push rulesets apply to all pushes (git-transport.md section 1). Whether Claude Code auto-ignores .claude/worktrees is UNKNOWN.
findings.mitigation: 1) Sync scope = paths tracked in the live base, plus new files created through Write/NotebookEdit hooks in a cowork session or added explicitly with `/cowork add <path>`. Other untracked files stay local and are listed in status. 2) Never add or change a 160000 entry (force gitlinks to the base value). 3) Cap new or changed files at 5 MB each (configurable) and 200 files per snapshot; anything over the cap is held and the user is asked. 4) Each push attempt is one fresh commit (parent = remote tip, tree = merge result) built from the current state, never a stack of earlier local commits, so a removed file stops blocking the push at once. 5) Handle 'GH001' / 'GH013' / 'pre-receive hook declined' rejections as 'path X blocked by host', drop X from the scope, and report.
findings.test: Create .claude/worktrees/w1 (a git worktree), a 120 MB untracked file and tmp.py: assert none of them is published and status lists them. Use a pre-receive hook on the file:// remote that rejects blobs over 1 MB: create one, then delete it, and assert the next push succeeds without manual repair.

findings.title: EOL normalization with no edit behind it (and EOL/BOM flips from Write or peer config) creates whole-file conflicts that no claim covered
findings.scenario: (a) A path carries an explicit `text` or `eol=crlf` attribute while its committed blob still has CRLF (it was committed before the attribute was added). In a long-lived repo the user's stat-cached index can hide this. The daemon's private index, seeded from the tree, rehashes the file and stores an LF blob, a whole-file change nobody made. (In the fresh fixture the user's `git status` also flagged it; with a warm stat cache in a long-lived repo it does not.) (b) A peer runs a different core.autocrlf/eol (Windows autocrlf=false, macOS input). (c) A Claude Write drops the BOM, which changes line 1. Or, where the blob holds CRLF or a peer runs autocrlf=false, the Write flips the EOL. With the team's autocrlf=true and LF blobs, an on-disk CRLF->LF flip alone does not change the blob. Meanwhile another peer, holding a valid function claim, edits one line of the same file.
findings.consequence: merge-tree reports CONFLICT (content) on the whole file (exit 1), even though the claim system, which normalizes BOM and CRLF before mapping symbols (region-detect.md), saw no overlap. The legitimate edit becomes a 'conflict' with no causer, or if the daemon resolves blindly the 1.3 MB file flips line endings for everyone. Merging with -X renormalize avoids it.
findings.evidence_detail: sweep/e6: CRLF blob, then `*.py text` (or `text eol=crlf`) added -> tree-seeded add -A gives a renormalized blob (35+/35-) with no edit; text=auto and plain autocrlf are protected by git's CRLF-in-index check. A peer's one-line edit merged against it -> 'CONFLICT (content): Merge conflict in big.py', exit 1; `merge-tree --write-tree -X renormalize` -> exit 0 with the peer's edit. Note: on Git 2.55 merge-tree accepts -X.
findings.mitigation: 1) Always run `git merge-tree --write-tree -X renormalize`. 2) At start, snapshot HEAD into a scratch index. If any blob changes without an edit, refuse to start and name the files: the team commits a renormalization first, or those paths are excluded. 3) EOL/BOM guard in the snapshot: if a modified file's BOM presence or dominant EOL differs from its base blob, restore the base style in the blob (rewrite through `hash-object --stdin` before update-index) and notify, or deny the Write in PreToolUse. 4) Publish each peer's core.autocrlf, core.eol, core.safecrlf and the .gitattributes hash on the board, and refuse to join on mismatch.
findings.test: Fixture repo from sweep/e6 (CRLF blob + `*.py text`): assert the daemon refuses to start and names big.py. Second fixture: peer A writes the file without its BOM and LF-only while peer B edits one function; assert the merge is clean and the result keeps the BOM and the base EOL.

findings.title: On merge-tree exit 1 the result tree contains conflict markers, and the obvious auto-resolutions silently corrupt or drop code
findings.scenario: A window race the claims cannot stop: two Claudes both append a new function at the end of the same file (both claim '<toplevel after=last>' within the propagation window), or both add an import. merge-tree exits 1. The design does not say what happens next.
findings.consequence: Applying the result tree writes '<<<<<<< / ======= / >>>>>>>' into the file and pushes it to everyone, and Claudes then 'fix' the markers in different ways. Automatic strategies are worse because they are silent: `merge-file --union` produced `def g_from_A():` directly followed by `def h_from_B():` and one shared `pass` (broken code, exit 0); `-X ours`/`-X theirs` drops one teammate's function with exit 0.
findings.evidence_detail: sweep/e5: the EOF-append race -> exit 1, `cat-file -p <tree>:m.py` shows the markers. `git merge-file --union --object-id` on the stages -> broken interleaving. `merge-tree -X ours` -> exit 0 (the other side is dropped). Edits on either side of one blank line between functions merged cleanly.
findings.mitigation: Conflict policy: 1) Never write a tree from an exit-1 merge-tree, and never use union, ours or theirs. 2) For each conflicted path, the version already published (incoming) goes on disk. The local version (the stage-2 blob) is kept under refs/cowork-local/<b>/conflicts/<id> and recorded on the board as a handoff entry with a patch against the incoming version, so the 'conflict causer' Claude re-applies its change on top, as a person would. 3) Conflicted paths are reported in the next hook context of both sessions. 4) Clean paths in the same merge are still applied, using tree surgery. 5) Binary conflicts (for example an .xlsx edited by two peers) always cover the whole file and follow the same rule: the published version goes on disk and the local blob is kept and handed off.
findings.test: Two daemons each append a different function at EOF within the same push window. Assert that no file anywhere contains conflict markers, the earlier-published function is on every disk, the later one is in the causer's handoff queue with a patch that applies cleanly on top, and after the causer re-applies it both functions are present and the file parses.

findings.title: After a save, teammates' HEAD and index still point at the old base, so `git pull` refuses and the usual fix (stash) causes a revert
findings.scenario: A runs /cowork save: the shared tree is committed as C on main and pushed, and the live ref is reset onto C. B's worktree already equals C (the daemon applied it), but B's HEAD and index are still B0 because the daemon never touches them. B runs `git pull`.
findings.consequence: Pull and `merge --ff-only` refuse ('untracked working tree files would be overwritten' / 'Please commit your changes or stash them'). The natural next step, `git stash -u` + pull + pop (or the IDE's 'stash and pull'), reverts the worktree to B0, and the daemon publishes the revert (user-git-ops-broadcast-as-revert). Until then, B's `git diff` and IDE show the whole session's work as B's uncommitted changes, which invites `git checkout -- .` 'cleanups' by B or B's Claude.
findings.evidence_detail: sweep/e10: bob with HEAD=B0 and worktree == C -> `git pull --ff-only` and `git merge --ff-only origin/main` exit 1 with 'would be overwritten'. `git stash -u` -> f.py back to v1 and new.py removed. The broadcast half is REASONED.
findings.mitigation: Design change: when a save lands, each peer's daemon (with HEAD = the recorded live base, on the saved branch, and with its worktree equal to C's tree for the saved paths) moves the user's branch ref and index to C without touching files (the equivalent of `git reset --mixed C`: `update-ref` with the old-value check, then `read-tree C` into the real index under index.lock, with retry). If any condition fails, show the exact one-line command and freeze publishing until it is run. Update the board with 'base=C'.
findings.test: Two peers; A saves. Assert B's HEAD becomes C within one loop, `git status` on B is clean except for B's own unsaved edits, `git pull` is a no-op, and no file on B changed during the switch (compare mtimes).

findings.title: Submodule pointer changes bounce between peers forever and use up the push budget
findings.scenario: A checks out a newer commit in submodule lib/. A's snapshot records the new gitlink and pushes it. B's apply updates the gitlink in B's private index (read-tree does not recurse), but B's lib/ checkout stays on the old commit. B's next `git add -A` records lib/ at B's checked-out commit.
findings.consequence: B publishes a gitlink revert, A publishes it forward again, and so on. Every round uses up the team's 6 pushes per minute. Which pointer ends up in a save depends on timing.
findings.evidence_detail: sweep/e13 (file:// submodule): A's snapshot lib=e9b175. B applies it (exit 0) but `git -C lib rev-parse HEAD` stays b40e24. B's next snapshot, with a persistent or reseeded index, records b40e24 again: 'DIFFERS: B would push gitlink revert'.
findings.mitigation: Live sync never carries gitlinks. In every snapshot, force each 160000 entry to its value in the live base (`update-index --cacheinfo 160000,<base oid>,<path>`). A submodule pointer changes only through /cowork save, with an explicit note, or a dedicated `/cowork submodule <path>` command that peers apply with `git submodule update`.
findings.test: Fixture with a submodule. A moves lib/. Assert no live push contains a gitlink change, the pointer stays at the base value on the live ref for 5 minutes of looping, and the push count stays at zero.

findings.title: A 'move' done in two steps (Write new, rm old) defeats rename detection, so a teammate's concurrent edit to the old path ends in a modify/delete conflict
findings.scenario: Claude moves helper.py to util/helper.py by Write-ing the new file, which is snapshotted and pushed, and later running `rm helper.py` in Bash, which goes into a later snapshot. Peer B applied the copy commit, then B's Claude edited helper.py (B's claim covers the function in helper.py). B merges with base = its last applied commit (the copy).
findings.consequence: With that base, A's side is a pure delete, so the result is CONFLICT (modify/delete) and old.py is left in the tree. B's edit never follows the file. Depending on conflict handling, either the deleted file comes back for everyone or B's edit goes to the handoff queue for no real reason.
findings.evidence_detail: sweep/e16: base=C1 -> 'CONFLICT (modify/delete): old.py deleted ... Version ... of old.py left in tree', exit 1. The same merge with --merge-base=C0 (before the copy) -> exit 0, and B's edited line 10 is in new.py.
findings.mitigation: On a modify/delete conflict, before the conflict policy runs, retry merge-tree with the base walked back along the live chain (up to 20 commits or 10 minutes) to the newest commit where the deleted path existed and the added similar file did not. Accept the retry only if it exits 0. Also record Write-then-rm pairs from hooks as an intended rename on the board.
findings.test: Replay sweep/e16 through the daemon: assert B's edit ends up in util/helper.py on every peer, helper.py is gone everywhere, and no conflict record is created.

findings.title: The real branch moves during the session (PR merge, bot commit), so save is non-fast-forward and peers drift onto different bases
findings.scenario: While the team is live on main (base B0), a PR is merged on GitHub (main = B1). Some peers `git pull`: it succeeds when the PR touched only files that are not live, and is refused otherwise. Later someone runs /cowork save.
findings.consequence: Peers whose pull succeeded see the PR content as new local changes, and their daemons publish it as their own edits (wrong attribution, and conflicts with peers that also pulled). The save commit (parent B0) is rejected as non-fast-forward. If the save path falls back to --force or to a lease that someone refreshed by fetching, the PR merge on main is erased.
findings.evidence_detail: Follows from the save design (commit the shared tree with parent = live base). That a ff pull succeeds or fails per file follows from the read-tree two-way rules (https://git-scm.com/docs/git-read-tree); the refusal case is VERIFIED in sweep/e10.
findings.mitigation: 1) The daemon tracks origin/<branch>. When it moves past the live base, one daemon (elected by CAS on the board) publishes a 'rebase' live commit: merge-tree -X renormalize with --merge-base=<live base>, ours = live tip, theirs = origin tip. The board records the new live base, and every daemon then runs the post-save-head-drift HEAD/index move. On a conflict, save is blocked and the conflict is reported. 2) Save pushes the branch with `--force-with-lease=refs/heads/<b>:<origin tip it merged>`, never plain --force, atomically with the live-ref reset where supported.
findings.test: Live session on main; push an outside commit to main touching one live file and one non-live file. Assert that within one poll the live ref contains the outside commit's changes exactly once, every peer's base becomes B1, save fast-forwards, and git log on main still has the outside commit.

findings.title: Objects reachable only from the private index or unpushed snapshots are pruned by the user's gc, and snapshots bloat the user's object store
findings.scenario: The user, or a GUI's 'cleanup', runs `git gc --prune=now` or `git prune` while the daemon holds snapshot blobs referenced only by its GIT_INDEX_FILE or by an unpushed commit with no ref. Separately, the daemon's `git fetch` every 2-3 s runs `git maintenance run --auto` in the user's repo by default, and each snapshot of the 1.3 MB file adds a new object.
findings.consequence: write-tree fails ('invalid object ... error building trees', exit 128), so the daemon is stuck until its index is rebuilt, and an unpushed local commit can lose its objects. Auto-gc and cruft packing can start inside the user's repo at random times. Each snapshot of a one-line edit added about 112 KB (synthetic 1.8 MB file); real code compresses less.
findings.evidence_detail: sweep/e8: blob only in the private index -> after `git prune --expire=now` `cat-file -e` fails and write-tree exits 128. Protected once the blob is reachable from refs/cowork-local/... sweep/e11: 5 snapshots grew .git/objects by 564 KB. fetch runs maintenance by default: https://git-scm.com/docs/git-fetch (--[no-]auto-maintenance).
findings.mitigation: Design change: the daemon works in its own GIT_DIR (a bare repo under .git/cowork/repo.git with objects/info/alternates pointing at the user's .git/objects, its own refs and its own private index, and core.autocrlf, filter.* and attributes mirrored from the user's config), with GIT_WORK_TREE = the user's worktree. Every object it needs is reachable from its own refs (applied, pending, conflicts). It fetches with --no-auto-maintenance and runs its own `git gc --cruft --prune=2.days` when idle. The user's `git log --all`, gc and IDE never see daemon refs.
findings.test: While the daemon runs, run `git gc --prune=now` in the user's repo between a snapshot and its push: assert the push still succeeds. After 1,000 loops with edits, assert the user's .git/objects did not grow from snapshots and `git for-each-ref` in the user's repo shows no cowork refs.

findings.title: On Windows with core.symlinks=false, editing a symlink's placeholder file publishes a symlink whose target is the file's contents
findings.scenario: A macOS teammate's repo has `current.yaml -> config.yaml`. On Windows it is a plain file containing the text 'config.yaml'. A Windows Claude or user 'edits the config' by writing YAML into current.yaml.
findings.consequence: The private index (seeded from the tree) keeps mode 120000, so the snapshot publishes a symlink whose target is 'mode: prod\nretries: 3\n'. macOS and Linux peers get a dangling symlink in place of their config. The intended change never reaches config.yaml.
findings.evidence_detail: sweep/e15: after the edit, `ls-tree` shows '120000 blob 52c71c... current.yaml', and `cat-file -p` gives the YAML text as the link target.
findings.mitigation: On a peer with core.symlinks=false, PreToolUse denies Edit and Write on paths whose base mode is 120000 ('this is a symlink to config.yaml; edit that file'). The snapshot keeps 120000 entries at their base value unless the new content is a single line with no newline that resolves to an existing repo path.
findings.test: Windows peer writes YAML into a symlink placeholder: assert the Write is denied with the target named, and that writing directly to the placeholder file outside Claude publishes nothing for that path.

findings.title: Tracked generated files (such as the 2.6 MB docs regenerated on each PC) conflict, bounce between peers and use up the push budget
findings.scenario: Two PCs each run the doc or spec generator. The output contains PC-specific bytes (absolute paths like C:\Users\<name>, timestamps, unstable ordering). Each daemon snapshots its own 2.6 MB version.
findings.consequence: merge-tree conflicts in many hunks, or the versions overwrite each other back and forth. Each round is a full-size snapshot plus a push from the shared 6-per-minute budget, so real edits wait tens of seconds longer. The saved commit gets whichever version came last.
findings.evidence_detail: Both sides changed the same file differently from the base, so a 3-way merge conflict follows (merge behaviour as in sweep/e5). Per-snapshot object cost is measured in sweep/e11.
findings.mitigation: Per-path live-sync policy: paths with `linguist-generated` or a `cowork-sync=off` attribute, or listed in .cowork/config, are never live-synced and are regenerated or committed only by /cowork save on the saver's PC. Auto-detect: if a path over 1 MB changes in 3 consecutive snapshots without any Edit or Write hook touching it, pause that path and ask.
findings.test: Two daemons each write a different 2.6 MB docs file every 10 s: assert zero pushes caused by that path, no conflict records, and that save includes the saver's regenerated version.

findings.title: Live pushes run the repo's pre-push hooks: skipping them breaks LFS, running them stalls every sync, and LFS storage is never reclaimed
findings.scenario: The repo uses git-lfs, or a husky or pre-commit pre-push hook (tests, lint). The daemon pushes refs/cowork/* every few seconds to tens of seconds.
findings.consequence: With hooks: every live push waits for the test suite or fails on lint, so sync effectively stops. With --no-verify: LFS pointers are pushed without their objects, peers' smudge fails ('Smudge error'), and their apply fails for good on that path. Either way, every live version of an LFS binary that does upload stays in GitHub LFS storage until the repository is deleted.
findings.evidence_detail: The daemon's push runs pre-push hooks (git-transport.md section 8). GitHub LFS objects are removed only by deleting the repo: https://docs.github.com/en/repositories/working-with-files/managing-large-files/removing-files-from-git-large-file-storage
findings.mitigation: Live pushes use --no-verify. LFS-tracked paths (filter=lfs) are out of live scope (they change only at save, which runs normal hooks). The daemon checks this at start with `git check-attr filter` and states it in status. If the team insists on LFS live sync, run `git lfs pre-push` explicitly, only for those paths.
findings.test: Fixture with a pre-push hook that sleeps 60 s and a filter=lfs path: assert live pushes finish in under 5 s, the LFS path change is reported as 'save-only', and no pointer without its object is ever pushed.

design_changes: Run the daemon in a private GIT_DIR (bare repo under .git/cowork/ with alternates pointing at the user's objects, its own refs, private index and gc), with GIT_WORK_TREE = the user's worktree. Reasons: objects referenced only by the daemon are prunable today (objects-only-in-private-index); the 2-3 s fetch triggers auto-maintenance in the user's repo; and daemon refs would clutter `git log --all`, IDE branch lists and `push --mirror`.

Make the apply tolerant per path instead of all-or-nothing. Pending paths are handled by tree surgery (M' = M with unmaterializable, locked, fenced or colliding paths taken from S) plus `read-tree -m` to sync the private index. Reason: read-tree -m -u is not atomic when a write fails (partial-apply-on-lock), and an all-or-nothing failure on one path stops a peer for good (poison-path).

Keep a persistent private index (keep stat info) and reseed from a tree only on join or recovery, not every loop. Reasons: reseeding re-runs clean filters and EOL conversion on every file each loop (eol-renormalization), and costs about 3x (204 ms vs 68 ms on 3,000 files).

Push invariants: each push is one freshly built commit with parent = the exact lease tip and tree = merge-tree(--merge-base=LAST_APPLIED, snapshot, tip), never the raw snapshot and never a stack of local commits. LAST_APPLIED is a ref updated only after a fully successful apply. Reason: pushed-tree-must-be-merge-result and untracked-sweep (an unpushable object must not block pushes permanently).

Specify the conflict policy (currently undefined): on merge-tree exit 1, never apply the result tree and never use union, ours or theirs. The published version goes on disk, the local stage-2 blob is kept in a ref and recorded as a handoff with a patch, and modify/delete conflicts are retried first with a walked-back base.

Set the sync scope by allow-list rather than `git add -A`: tracked paths of the live base, plus new files created through Claude Write/NotebookEdit hooks or `/cowork add`. Exclude gitlinks, LFS paths, generated paths and files over 5 MB. Run a portability gate (reserved names, invalid characters, case and NFC collisions, length) on publish.

Bind the daemon to HEAD (symbolic ref + oid) and freeze publishing on any change. Add a revert detector and a mass-change breaker before every push. Defer applies while a Bash tool call runs in that worktree.

At save, move every peer's branch ref and index to the saved commit without touching files (equivalent to `git reset --mixed C` under index.lock). This is a narrow exception to 'never touch the user's index or HEAD', needed because otherwise pull is blocked and stash causes a revert (post-save-head-drift). When the real branch moves, publish a live 'rebase' commit; save always uses a lease, never force.

Fixed flags on every daemon git call: `-c filter.<name>.required=true` for each filter in use; `merge-tree --write-tree -X renormalize`; `fetch --no-auto-maintenance`; `push --no-verify` (with LFS paths out of live scope); `add -A --ignore-errors`, parsing 'unable to index file'.
open_questions: What are the team repo's actual .gitattributes, and what does `git ls-files --eol` show for the 1.3 MB BOM+CRLF Python file (i/lf or i/crlf)? This decides whether eol-renormalization fires on day one. It can be checked read-only without touching the working tree.

Where is the clean/smudge filter defined (repo .git/config or global), what does it execute, and does a detached Node daemon started from a SessionStart hook see the same PATH, HOME and environment? If the filter is sed run through git-bash it also strips CR on checkout (sweep/e11), so the filtered file lands LF after every apply.

Does Claude Code's Write tool keep an existing file's BOM and CRLF? (region-detect confirms only Edit.) Does Claude Code auto-ignore .claude/worktrees/ and .claude/settings.local.json, and through which mechanism (repo .gitignore, info/exclude or global)?

Will the user accept the narrow exception that, at save, the daemon moves each peer's branch ref and index to the saved commit? Without it, every save leaves teammates unable to pull, and the usual workaround (stash) reverts everyone's work.

Should new untracked files sync live at all? The proposal is an allow-list (only files created by Claude Write in a cowork session or added with /cowork add); auto-sync of all non-ignored files is the source of untracked-sweep and ignored-file-overwrite.

How long does GitHub keep objects pushed to a custom ref after the ref is force-reset? This matters for how long a leaked value stays retrievable (filter-passthrough-leak). Is push protection or secret scanning enabled on the team's private repo plan?

Real Excel behaviour on these PCs: does saving a tracked .xlsx go through temp-file, delete, then rename, and which share mode does it hold on the workbook and on ~$ owner files? Only simulated with .NET handles here.
Is core.longpaths enabled on every Windows PC? Without it, any repo-relative path over about 200 characters from a macOS or Linux peer becomes a poison path.

findings.title: read-tree -m -u silently overwrites a save (human or Claude Edit) that lands during the apply, with exit 0
findings.scenario: Bob's peer change touches many files (a rename across modules, a formatter run, or a reset after 'save'), so Alice's daemon runs a 3,001-file `read-tree -m -u BASE MERGED`, which takes about 1 s. git checks that every path is up to date first, then writes the files one by one. 50-1000 ms in, Alice presses Ctrl+S in VS Code on zzz_human.py, or her Claude's Edit writes it. The file passed its check before the save, so git then unlinks it and writes the peer version.
findings.consequence: Alice's keystrokes or Claude's edit vanish from disk. read-tree exits 0, so the daemon advances. The next snapshot sees nothing local to publish, so the edit is lost everywhere. VS Code then auto-reloads the now-clean buffer, so the text disappears from the editor too. Claude's PostToolUse reported success. Nobody is told.
findings.evidence_detail: Harness <scratchpad>/sweep/ed/e3/lost.js (Windows 11, git 2.55.0.windows.3, autocrlf=true, 3,000 files + zzz_human.py, apply ~1,045 ms). A write 0 ms after start was rejected with 'not uptodate' (exit 128). Writes at 50, 100, 200, 400, 700 and 1000 ms all ended with final content = peer version and exit 0 (6/6 LOST). A write at 1500 ms (after the apply) survived. This also refutes decision 4's stated property that the apply is all-or-nothing and only fails with 'not uptodate'.
findings.test: Rerun lost.js against the new applier at delays 0-1500 ms, 50 trials each. Assert zero cases where the writer's bytes are missing from both the final file and the published tree. Each trial must end either with the human's content kept, or with a clean merge that contains both changes.

findings.title: Saving a dirty editor buffer opened before the daemon's write publishes a revert of the teammate's change
findings.scenario:
1. Alice has hub.py open in VS Code with unsaved typing in f7.
2. Bob's Claude's change to f2 arrives, and the daemon rewrites the file (V0->V1). VS Code does not reload dirty buffers.
3. On save, VS Code reports that the file on disk is newer ("The content of the file is newer") and offers Compare/Overwrite. Alice clicks Overwrite.
Same outcome in other editors:
- Visual Studio: Alice answers No to 'reload?', and 'save all before build' later writes the stale buffer.
- JetBrains: 'Keep Memory Changes'.
- vim: `:w!` after the 'file changed since reading' warning.
- VS Code hot exit restores yesterday's dirty buffer, which is later saved.
The disk now holds V0 plus Alice's hunk. The snapshot diff against last-applied V1 contains Alice's hunk and the inverse of Bob's hunk.
findings.consequence: Bob's change is reverted on every PC, attributed to Alice, with no conflict raised. Bob's Claude still holds the f2 claim. It sees its work disappear and redoes it, or wrongly decides the work is done. The hot 26k-line file, rewritten on every incoming change, is where this happens most.
findings.evidence_detail:
Git-level reproduction: <scratchpad>/sweep/ed/e7/stale.js. The diff of SAVED against V1 shows '-return 2 # peer change' plus the human hunk, which is a revert. `git merge-file -p SAVED V0 V1` exits 0 and keeps both changes.
Editor behaviour, documented:
- VS Code files.saveConflictResolution askUser|overwriteFileOnDisk (https://code.visualstudio.com/updates/v1_42). overwriteFileOnDisk offers Overwrite directly; it does not overwrite silently.
- Visual Studio 'Detect when file is changed outside the environment' / 'Reload modified files unless there are unsaved changes' (https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/previous-versions/visualstudio/visual-studio-2015/ide/reference/documents-environment-options-dialog-box).
JetBrains 'Keep Memory Changes' comes only from community support posts (https://intellij-support.jetbrains.com/hc/en-us/community/posts/208238045). The hot-exit variant is REASONED.
findings.mitigation:
Keep a per-path write ring of (pre-write blob, post-write blob, time) for every daemon write. Persist it in .git/cowork and keep entries for at least 14 days (hot exit). When a path changes, choose base B from {last applied, ring pre-write blobs} as the one that minimises the diff to the new working blob W.
- If B is not last-applied, the save is stale-based. Publish `merge-file(ours=W, base=B, theirs=last-applied)` instead of W, and write the merged bytes back through the verifying writer.
- If that merge conflicts, publish nothing for P and keep W on disk. Post a conflict record and notify Alice and the symbol holder.
Separate rule: a hunk whose new text equals the pre-write text of a daemon write still in the ring is classified revert-of-others. It is never auto-published; publishing it needs explicit `/cowork accept-revert`.
findings.test: Fixture: the daemon writes V1 over V0, then the harness writes V0 plus its own hunk. Assert the published blob contains both changes and the disk converges to it. Variants: the save happens 3 days later (ring persisted across a daemon restart), and a deliberate manual revert is held until accept-revert.

findings.title: A file held open by Excel or the running app makes the apply half-write the tree; advancing the base then publishes a revert
findings.scenario:
Bob's change touches a.txt, b.txt and c.txt. On Alice's PC, b.txt is open in a process that allows reads but denies write and delete: Excel holding a tracked .xlsx, the app under development holding a tracked file, or Defender scanning it. git writes a.txt and c.txt, fails to unlink b.txt, and exits 128.
If the daemon treats the run as applied, or commits the raw snapshot on top of the remote head, the next snapshot contains b's old content as a local change.
With a deny-all lock (.NET File.Open defaults to FileShare.None), the apply is refused, and `git add -A` also aborts with 'unable to index file'. Outbound sync stops for every file while that one is open.
findings.consequence: Option 1: Bob's change to b is silently reverted for the whole team. Option 2: Alice's PC stops publishing anything while Excel is open. In both cases the working tree mixes new a/c with old b, so related changes are half-present (ImportError, mismatched callers), and nothing is shown to the user.
findings.evidence_detail:
Experiment in <scratchpad>/sweep/ed/e1. A background PowerShell process held [IO.File]::Open(b.txt,'Open','Read',<share>).
- share=Read: "error: unable to unlink old 'b.txt': Invalid argument", exit 128. a.txt=a2 and c.txt=c2 were written, b.txt stayed b1, and the temp index was unchanged. A snapshot seeded from MERGED then diffs '-b2 +b1'. A raw snapshot committed on the remote head reverts b. merge-tree(base=old applied, ours=snapshot, theirs=remote) == MERGED, which is safe.
- share=None: apply exit 128 'not uptodate', all-or-nothing. `git add -A` failed with 'open("b.txt"): Permission denied … fatal: updating files failed'.
findings.mitigation:
Keep last-applied as a per-path map, not one tree. A path counts as applied only when the verifying writer confirmed it. Build the outgoing commit tree as merge-tree(base=last-applied tree, ours=snapshot, theirs=remote head), never from the raw snapshot.
Defer locked paths one at a time, retrying with backoff (100 ms to 30 s). Show them in /cowork status, and post a board note naming the holder process when a lock lasts more than 60 s.
In the snapshot, an unreadable path keeps its previous blob and does not abort the cycle.
Spawn git with stdin set to 'ignore', so the Git for Windows prompt 'Unlink of file … Should I try again? (y/n)' can never block the daemon (REASONED from Git for Windows source).

findings.title: Branch switch, stash, 'Discard Changes' or reset in one working tree is published to everyone as a mass edit or revert
findings.consequence: After a branch switch, refs/cowork/main/code receives feature's content, and every peer's main working tree is rewritten. After a stash or discard, all peers' work in those files is reverted on every PC. It is recoverable only from live-ref history, which nobody knows to look at.
findings.evidence_detail:
Run in <scratchpad>/sweep/ed/e13.
- After `git checkout feature`, the next snapshot seeded from the last-applied tree would publish 300 changed files ('-v1 main +v1 FEATURE').
- After `git stash`, the snapshot publishes '-v1 main + peer edit +v1 main'.
findings.mitigation:
Each cycle, read HEAD (symbolic ref and oid), refs/stash, ORIG_HEAD and the tracked-path count before snapshotting. On any change, freeze outbound at once (publish nothing) and enter a 'resolve' state shown in status and sent to the local Claude.
Resume only through `/cowork resume`, which re-bases on the new HEAD or tells the user to switch back or `stash pop`.
Apply the revert-of-others rule from the stale-buffer finding.
Mass-change gate: a snapshot touching more than 50 paths or more than 20% of tracked paths without matching Claude hooks is held for explicit confirmation.
Cap any index.lock pause at 30 s, then report a stale lock loudly instead of pausing forever.
findings.test: Use the e13 fixture with checkout, stash, `checkout -- f` and `reset --hard`. In each case assert zero pushes and that the live ref still contains the peer change. After `git checkout main` or `stash pop` and resume, assert no work is lost.

findings.title: If the clean filter can't run in the detached daemon's environment, git add stores the real secret with exit 0
findings.scenario:
Alice's .git/config defines the secret filter, and the command works from her interactive shell. The daemon is spawned detached with a different PATH or environment, so it cannot find the filter tool (or the filter needs an environment variable only the login shell sets). The filter is not marked required.
A second case: a new teammate never set up the filter, so his checkout has no smudged secret, and he pastes the real key into the file to make the app run.
findings.consequence: The plaintext secret is committed to refs/cowork/<b>/code and pushed to every collaborator. Resetting the ref later does not purge it: unreachable objects stay on the host (cruft packs, per the git-transport report).
findings.evidence_detail:
Run in <scratchpad>/sweep/ed/e6.
- clean='secret-clean-tool' (not on PATH): 'cannot spawn secret-clean-tool … external filter failed', add exit=0, and the stored blob is 'API_KEY = "REAL_SECRET_123"'.
- Same with `-c filter.secret.required=true`: exit 128.
- Driver not configured at all: blob is plaintext; with `-c filter.secret.required=true`: exit 128.
findings.mitigation:
Discover every filter driver named by attributes (`git check-attr filter` over tracked paths). Pass `-c filter.<d>.required=true` on every daemon git invocation that cleans or smudges, so a missing or failed filter aborts the cycle and is reported.
At `/cowork start` and every 10 minutes, run a canary: `hash-object --path=<filtered file>` must equal the HEAD blob when the content is unchanged.
Record a secret canary pattern at setup, and refuse to push any blob that matches it.
Capture the user's shell PATH and environment at start, rather than inheriting a minimal detached environment.
findings.test: Remove the filter tool from the daemon's PATH and edit the filtered file. Assert no push, a red status 'filter failed', and that no object containing the canary exists in the pushed pack (inspect with `git verify-pack` on a file:// remote).

findings.title: Every apply leaves a window in which the file is missing or zero bytes; Claude Read, dev-server reloaders and tests read it
findings.scenario: git's checkout unlinks the old file and then creates and writes the new one. A process reading that path during the apply gets ENOENT, an empty file, or EPERM. The readers that matter react to the same change event: uvicorn, watchfiles, nodemon and dotnet watch reload the app; Claude's Read or Edit on hub.py; test runners; VS Code marking the tab '(deleted)'.
findings.consequence:
- The dev server imports an empty module (routes missing) or crashes.
- Claude gets 'file does not exist' and may re-create the file with Write from memory, a full-file overwrite of the peer's version, or treat the file as broken and 'repair' it.
- Edit fails with 'old_string not found' on a 0-byte file.
findings.evidence_detail: Harness <scratchpad>/sweep/ed/e4/harness.js: a 2 MB BOM+CRLF file alternated between two trees by read-tree -m -u (609 applies in 15 s), with a tight-loop reader in a separate process. The reader observed ENOENT, 0-byte reads (33) and EPERM (5) over the run, so applies routinely expose a missing or empty-file window. The raw ENOENT ratio is an artifact of back-to-back applies and is not a real-world rate.
findings.mitigation:
Use the verifying per-path writer from 'apply-clobbers-concurrent-save', with temp and backup files under .git/cowork/tmp so watchers never see them. The new file appears in one step (link or rename), never as a partial write.
PreToolUse on Read, Edit, Write, MultiEdit and NotebookEdit for path P waits (at most 2 s) for any in-flight write of P to finish.
findings.test: Rerun harness.js against the new writer. Assert 0 zero-byte or partial reads, and ENOENT only within the rename-to-link gap (at most a handful per 600 applies; 0 with the rename-over fallback).

findings.title: The snapshot can capture a half-written file, and git reading the file makes editor saves fail with UNKNOWN
findings.scenario: Many editors save in place (truncate, then write). If the daemon's `git add -A` reads hub.py while VS Code is writing it, the snapshot stores a truncated blob. Separately, while git is hashing the file, a truncating open by the editor fails.
findings.consequence:
- A truncated copy of the 26k-line file (0 bytes or the first 0.5 MB) is published. Peers merge against it, delete-style conflicts appear, and peer Claudes 'restore' the missing code.
- VS Code shows 'Failed to save … UNKNOWN'. Claude's Edit fails with an I/O error, and the model may fall back to writing through Bash (python or sed), which bypasses the hooks and the fence.
findings.evidence_detail:
Harness <scratchpad>/sweep/ed/e5/partial.js. An in-place writer saved 1.67 MB in 64 KB chunks with small pauses, against back-to-back temp-index `git add -A` snapshots (an exaggerated duty cycle).
- Result: 145 of 252 snapshots stored truncated blobs (0 or 515,931 bytes), and 37 of 181 save attempts failed with UNKNOWN (-4094).
- A separate test held a memory-mapped section on a file; a truncating open then failed with UNKNOWN -4094. That suggests git maps files while hashing, but this is an inference about git internals.
- partial2.js (daemon reads the bytes with Node, then hashes them with git): 0 save failures. Adding a 50 ms quiet period plus a stat-before/after check: 0 partial blobs.
- CAUTION, verified in e14: `git hash-object --stdin --path` converts a CRLF-stored blob (i/crlf) to LF under autocrlf=true (500/500 lines), even with GIT_INDEX_FILE set. `git add` keeps CRLF (1/1). With `-c core.autocrlf=false` it gives 1/1, and the clean filter still runs.
findings.mitigation:
The snapshotter reads changed paths itself with Node (no memory mapping). It accepts a read only if:
- size and mtime are unchanged across the read;
- mtime is at least 300 ms old.
It then hashes with `git hash-object -w --stdin --path=P`, choosing the eol settings per path that reproduce the base blob's stored form (see 'eol-bom-stored-form-flip'). If the stored-form check fails, it falls back to `git add -- P` on the private index.
Shrink and parse guard: if a non-Claude change shrinks a blob by more than 50%, or a file that parsed before no longer parses, hold that path for one more stable cycle.
findings.test: Run partial.js against the new snapshotter. Assert 0 partial blobs published, 0 writer open failures, and the e14 CRLF fixture diffing 1/1.

findings.title: A line-ending or BOM change by one peer or tool becomes a whole-file diff, conflicting with every concurrent edit
findings.scenario:
Ways the stored form flips:
- A peer with core.autocrlf=false, or a macOS/Linux peer, has an editor that writes CRLF over an LF-stored file (Visual Studio does this for .cs).
- A file stored CRLF (i/crlf) gets rewritten with LF by Claude's Write, Bash sed or python, or a macOS peer's editor. Even with autocrlf=true, git keeps the new LF.
- A tool drops or adds the BOM.
The snapshot then stores a different EOL form for every line.
findings.consequence:
- The 1-line edit becomes a 280/280 (or 500/500) diff and conflicts with an unrelated edit 27 functions away.
- A Write-based claim becomes a whole-file claim and blocks the team.
- 'save' destroys blame for the 26k-line file and credits one person with every symbol.
- Removing the BOM changes how PowerShell 5.1 decodes Korean strings in .ps1 files (REASONED).
findings.evidence_detail:
Both runs under <scratchpad>/sweep/ed.
- e7 (gen.js): a peer with autocrlf=false saves CRLF over an LF blob with one line changed, giving a numstat of 280 280. merge-tree with an unrelated edit exits 1. The same edit with EOL preserved is 1 1, and the merge exits 0.
- e14: a blob stored i/crlf, rewritten with LF and one line changed, then `git add` under autocrlf=true, gives 500 500.
findings.mitigation:
Treat the stored form as a property of each path. Record the base blob's EOL style (lf, crlf or mixed) and BOM presence.
Before hashing a changed path, choose the conversion that reproduces that form:
- CRLF-stored blob: `-c core.autocrlf=false`;
- LF-stored blob: `true` or `input`.
After hashing, verify the result has the same EOL style and BOM; if not, normalise the new content to the base form.
EOL or BOM changes happen only through an explicit `/cowork eol` command.
Run all daemon plumbing with team-pinned `-c core.autocrlf`/`core.eol` stored on the board, not each peer's local config.
findings.test: In the e7 fixture, the autocrlf=false peer's CRLF save must publish a 1-line diff, and merging it with an unrelated edit must be clean. In the e14 fixture, an LF rewrite of an i/crlf blob must publish 1/1. A BOM-stripped save must keep the BOM in the published blob.

findings.title: A snapshot taken mid-way through an editor's atomic save records the file as deleted or renamed
findings.scenario: JetBrains safe write (write Foo.py___jb_tmp___, rename Foo.py to ___jb_old___, rename tmp to Foo.py, delete old), vim with backupcopy=no, and Sublime's atomic_save all leave a moment where Foo.py does not exist. A snapshot in that moment stages Foo.py as removed or renamed, and adds the temp file.
findings.consequence: Peers' daemons delete Foo.py from their disks. Their editors show it as deleted, and a peer Claude editing it gets 'file not found' and may Write it from memory. A peer with local changes to Foo.py gets a modify/delete conflict. The file comes back on the next cycle, so the change history churns.
findings.evidence_detail: Run in <scratchpad>/sweep/ed/e15: a snapshot frozen between safe-write steps 2 and 3 gives 'R100 Foo.py -> Foo.py___jb_old___' plus 'A Foo.py___jb_tmp___'.
findings.mitigation:
Publish a disappearance only if the path is still absent after a confirmation cycle (2 s or more) and no create or rename-to event for it followed. Treat a delete as user intent mainly when it comes from a Claude hook or an explicit git rm.
Never treat editor temp or backup patterns as new paths: *___jb_tmp___, *___jb_old___, .*.swp, 4913, *~, #*#, .#*, ~$*, *.orig, .sublime temp files.
Apply the mass-deletion gate as in 'git-ops-publish-team-revert'.
findings.test: Freeze-step harness for each editor's save sequence (as in e15). Assert the snapshot published during the window has no D or R for Foo.py and no temp paths, and that the content change is published after the rename completes.

findings.title: 'git add -A' pulls swap, backup, owner-lock, .env and runtime-generated files into the shared tree
findings.consequence:
- The .env key is pushed to all collaborators and persists on the host.
- A peer's vim opens foo.py and hits E325 'ATTENTION … Recover?' from Alice's swap file. Recovering it applies her unsaved buffer.
- A peer's Excel sees ~$report.xlsx and may treat the workbook as locked by Alice.
- Files that change every second create a new tree every cycle and use up the shared 6-pushes/min budget, so real edits wait (REASONED).
findings.evidence_detail: Run in <scratchpad>/sweep/ed/e12: the snapshot added '#foo.py#', .env, .foo.py.swp, .vs/state.json, 4913, foo.py.orig, foo.py___jb_tmp___, foo.py~ and ~$report.xlsx (hidden). The e1 run also swept an untracked ids.txt. Cross-peer effects are REASONED.
findings.mitigation:
Snapshot only tracked paths plus paths explicitly introduced: a Claude Write or Edit hook on a new path, or `/cowork track <path>`.
Apply a built-in deny list of editor and OS temp patterns even to introduced paths.
New binary files or files over 1 MB need explicit track.
Churn quarantine: a path that changes in 5 or more consecutive snapshots with no Claude hook and no human-save cadence is marked machine-generated and excluded until confirmed.
findings.test: Drop the e12 file set, a 50 MB file and a log appended every 500 ms into the tree. Assert that over 5 minutes no push contains them and the push count stays 0.

findings.title: A path that is legal on macOS/Linux but not Windows blocks a Windows peer, or half-applies and then publishes a deletion
findings.consequence:
- Long path: the apply exits 128 after writing some files. If the base is advanced, the next snapshot publishes deletion of the long-path file and reverts other incoming files.
- Reserved or trailing-dot name: the whole apply is refused every cycle, so the Windows peer silently gets no further changes from anyone.
- NFD versus NFC: two paths for one Korean filename (REASONED).
findings.evidence_detail:
Run in <scratchpad>/sweep/ed/e11.
- Long path: 'fatal: cannot create directory', exit 128. a.txt=a2 was written, z.txt stayed z1. A snapshot seeded from the merged tree shows 'D <longpath>' and 'M z.txt'.
- 'aux.js' and 'notes.': "error: invalid path", exit 128, nothing written.
- A case-only rename Foo.cs->foo.cs applied correctly (git 2.55), so it is not a finding.
findings.mitigation:
Publish side: a portable-path validator covering the union of the platforms of peers registered on the board. It rejects:
- relative paths over 200 characters (configurable);
- Windows reserved names, a trailing dot or space, and the characters :*?"<>|\;
- paths that collide when case-folded or NFC-normalised.
NFC-normalise paths. Tell the creating Claude or human instead of publishing.
Receive side: the per-path applier quarantines an unwritable path on its own, without blocking others or marking it applied, and posts a board note.
`/cowork start` sets and verifies core.longpaths=true on Windows.
findings.test: Using the e11 fixtures pushed by a 'Linux' peer: the Windows receiver applies every other path, never publishes a deletion, lists the quarantined path in status, and the publisher's validator rejects the path before pushing.

findings.title: Humans have no hooks, so they edit symbols Claudes hold, and Claudes edit code humans are typing in
findings.scenario:
Case 1: Bob's Claude holds Pricing.compute and is between Edits. Alice, a human in VS Code, fixes a line in the same function and saves. Nothing denies her, and her daemon publishes it. On Bob's side:
- if the lines overlap, merge-tree conflicts, and the design has no live-conflict policy (markers in a file Claude is editing get 'fixed' by deleting Alice's side);
- if they don't overlap, Claude's next Edit still applies, because Edit doesn't refuse stale reads, onto code it never saw.
Case 2: Alice is typing in g with an unsaved buffer. Humans hold no claims, so Bob's Claude edits g freely, and Alice's save then reverts it (see the stale-buffer finding).
findings.consequence: A semantically broken function attributed to Bob; Alice's fix deleted by a Claude cleaning conflict markers; or Claude's edit reverted by a human save. Claude-to-Claude enforcement gives no protection whenever a human is involved.
findings.evidence_detail: Follows from decision 5 (Edit applies to the current content, no stale-read refusal), decision 6 (claims are taken only in PreToolUse) and decision 2 (human edits sync).
findings.mitigation:
(a) Human soft claims: a change with no local Claude PreToolUse/PostToolUse for that path within the fence window is attributed to '<user> (human)'. It claims the touched symbols, with a TTL of 10 minutes after the last save, published like other claims, so other Claudes are denied. Accepted consequence: Claude's Bash edits will also be classed as human, which is the safe direction.
(b) Breach stamp on the holder's side: when incoming content changes a symbol a local session holds, that session's next Edit or Write on the symbol is denied once, with the incoming diff and author in the reason, until the session Reads the file. The stamp is also delivered through the inbox.
(c) Never write conflict markers into a working file. On a textual conflict, keep the local bytes, save the incoming version to .git/cowork/conflicts/<path>@<peer>, post a board conflict record, and pause publishing that path until it is resolved.

findings.title: Format-on-save, Claude's format hooks and formatter version differences rewrite symbols other people hold, without any claim
findings.scenario:
Three ways it happens:
(1) Claude Code PostToolUse format hooks (prettier, black, csharpier) or VS Code formatOnSave or organizeImports reformat the whole file after a 1-line Edit. The claim comes only from the Edit's old_string, so formatting changes in other people's symbols are published unclaimed.
(2) Alice has black 24 and Bob has black 23, or different configs, so every save reformats the file back and forth.
(3) A human runs a formatter once on the never-formatted 26k-line file.
findings.consequence:
- Merge conflicts with the holders' concurrent edits, and <imports> reorders on every save.
- Each flip is a whole-file diff that spends the team's 6/min push budget.
- A giant diff crosses the Write threshold and becomes a whole-file claim that blocks the team.
- Claudes see their symbols change cosmetically and re-edit them.
findings.evidence_detail: Consequence of decision 6 (claims come only from the tool input) and decision 3 (push budget). The whole-file conflict mechanics are the same as the verified EOL flip (e7).
findings.mitigation:
At snapshot time, classify each changed hunk per symbol as semantic or format-only: the tree-sitter token stream, ignoring whitespace and trivia, is unchanged.
- Format-only hunks in symbols claimed by other sessions are not published, and are restored on disk to the shared version through the verifying writer.
- Other format-only changes are published only if the peer's formatter fingerprint (tool, version, config hash, recorded on the board by `/cowork doctor`) equals the team-pinned one.
- Import-block reorders are published only if the set of imports changed.
findings.test: Two peers with different formatter configs and a PostToolUse format hook each edit different functions for 5 minutes. Assert zero whole-file diffs published, zero merge conflicts, and a push count roughly equal to the number of semantic edits.

findings.title: The file fence is checked too late for an apply already in progress, and it never clears if PostToolUse doesn't fire
findings.scenario:
Case A: a 1 s multi-file apply is running. Claude's PreToolUse for hub.py arrives 100 ms in. The daemon sets the fence and allows the edit, but the running read-tree still writes that path afterwards.
Case B: PreToolUse sets the fence, then the user presses Esc, the tool errors (PostToolUseFailure rather than PostToolUse), the hook times out, or the session crashes. The fence is never cleared.
findings.consequence: In case A, Claude's edit is overwritten (the same mechanism as the lost-save finding) while the transcript says it succeeded. In case B, that file silently stops receiving incoming changes, drifts, and later produces a large conflict.
findings.evidence_detail: Case A is the same mechanism as e3/lost.js (<scratchpad>/sweep/ed/e3/lost.js): any write landing during an in-flight apply is clobbered with exit 0. Case B is REASONED from the hook lifecycle (PostToolUseFailure is a separate event).
findings.mitigation:
Make the fence a per-path mutex shared with the applier:
- PreToolUse acquires it and waits up to 2 s for any in-flight write of that path;
- the applier skips fenced paths individually.
Release it on PostToolUse, PostToolUseFailure, Stop or SubagentStop, MCP server disconnect, or a 60 s TTL. Fences older than the TTL are shown in status and logged.
findings.test: Start a slow apply and fire PreToolUse plus a write mid-apply: assert the write survives. Fire PreToolUse with no PostToolUse: assert incoming writes to that path resume after the TTL and status shows the expired fence.

findings.title: Any daemon code that round-trips file bytes through JavaScript strings corrupts cp949 text and strips BOMs
findings.scenario: The daemon's own file-level merge, stored-form normaliser, format classifier or restore step reads a file as a JS string (fs.readFile 'utf8' or TextDecoder) and writes the result back. Affected files include the pilot team's cp949 legacy files (.bas, .bat, .csv, .txt with Korean) and the 1.3 MB UTF-8 BOM file.
findings.consequence:
- Korean text in cp949 files is silently replaced on every peer: U+FFFD, plus different valid characters where byte pairs happen to form valid UTF-8.
- The default TextDecoder drops the BOM, which changes the first line of BOM files on every write and adds attribution noise.
findings.test: cp949 and UTF-16LE (working-tree-encoding) fixtures with concurrent edits through two daemons, including the merge, normalise and restore paths. Assert byte-identical results against the expected git merge, with the BOM preserved.

findings.title: One file that keeps changing (or only gets touched) blocks the all-or-nothing apply for every other file
findings.scenario: Alice types in hub.py with VS Code autosave afterDelay (1 s), or her Claude makes back-to-back Edits, or a tool touches the file's mtime without changing it. Each cycle the whole-tree read-tree finds that file 'not uptodate' and refuses all paths; the design re-snapshots and retries, and the file changes again.
findings.consequence: Alice receives none of her peers' changes, in any file, while she keeps working: a livelock. Her Claude works on a stale tree, then a large batch lands at once and causes more conflicts. Combined with the file fence (decision 5), every Claude edit stalls all incoming sync for that PC.
findings.evidence_detail:
Two runs under <scratchpad>/sweep/ed:
- e10: an mtime-only `touch` (identical bytes) on a target file gave "Entry 'a.txt' not uptodate", exit 128.
- e1, deny-all lock: one non-uptodate file blocked the other two changed files.
The livelock under continuous autosave is REASONED.
findings.mitigation:
Apply each path separately with the verifying writer. A path with local unsnapshotted changes gets a 3-way merge into the working file through git; other paths are never held back by it.
Before declaring a path dirty, compare content hashes, so an mtime-only change counts as clean.
The fence blocks only its own path.
findings.test: An autosave simulator rewrites one file every 800 ms while peers push changes to 20 other files. Assert all 20 land within one cycle and the hot file's incoming change merges within 3 cycles.

findings.title: Re-seeding the private index from a tree every cycle makes git re-read and re-hash every tracked file every 2-3 s
findings.scenario: Decision 4 seeds a fresh temp index from the last applied tree each cycle. The entries have no stat data, so `git add -A` must read every tracked file, run the filters, and hash it.
findings.consequence: Constant CPU and disk load: about 0.75 s per cycle on a 3,000-file repo, more on the real one. Every file, including the 1.3 MB one, is opened every cycle, which raises the chance of the editor-save failures in 'snapshot-captures-half-written-file' (an inference). Battery drain and fan noise make users switch the daemon off.
findings.evidence_detail: Run in <scratchpad>/sweep/ed/e3, with 3,004 files including a 2 MB file. Re-seeded `read-tree <tree>; add -A; write-tree` took 729, 768 and 754 ms. A persistent stat-fresh private index took 54, 54 and 52 ms. The added save-failure exposure is inferred.
findings.mitigation: Keep one long-lived private index. The per-path applier updates it with fresh stat data (update-index --cacheinfo plus refresh). Enable core.fsmonitor=true and core.untrackedCache for it; git's fsmonitor daemon handles watcher overflow by forcing a rescan, and fs.watch is only a hint. Re-seed only for recovery, and run a full verification every 10 minutes.
findings.test: On a 5,000-file fixture, a no-change cycle must take under 100 ms, and GIT_TRACE2_PERF must show 0 files hashed. After an apply, the next cycle must hash only the paths that actually changed.

findings.title: Autosave publishes half-typed human code, and peer Claudes 'fix' someone else's work in progress
findings.consequence: Peer Claudes repair code they don't own (prior-art failure #4). Alice's next save then conflicts with, or reverts, their 'fix'. Tests fail team-wide in the meantime, and agents waste turns.
findings.evidence_detail: Combines documented editor autosave modes, decision 2 (human edits sync), and prior-art finding #4 (agents repair unexpected changes).
findings.mitigation:
Parse gate for changes not made by Claude: if a changed symbol parsed at base and now contains ERROR or MISSING nodes, hold that one path until it parses or has been idle for 60 s.
If it is published while broken, mark the symbol on the board as 'in progress by <user> (human)'. This uses the soft claim, so other Claudes are denied, and the inbox note says not to fix it.
findings.test: Write a save with a syntax error. Assert it is not published for 60 s, is then published with the in-progress marker, and a peer Claude's Edit on that symbol is denied with the reason.

findings.title: A repo inside OneDrive, Dropbox or iCloud gets a second sync engine that locks, rewrites and duplicates files
findings.consequence:
- Locks trigger the partial-apply and starvation failures.
- Conflict copies are untracked files that get swept and published.
- Opening placeholder files triggers downloads and stalls snapshots.
- Two engines fighting over the tree can revert each other's writes.
findings.evidence_detail: Combines the verified lock behaviour (e1) and untracked sweep (e12) with how cloud-sync clients work. Not reproduced here.
findings.mitigation: `/cowork start` refuses to run, with a clear message, when the repo path is under %OneDrive%, %OneDriveCommercial%, a Dropbox or Google Drive root, or ~/Library/Mobile Documents.
