It also checks for the FILE_ATTRIBUTE_RECALL_ON_DATA_ACCESS or offline attributes on tracked files. A `--allow-cloud-folder` override must be explicit and is shown in status.
findings.test: Start in a directory under %OneDrive%: the start is refused. A tracked file with the offline attribute shows a doctor warning.

findings.title: Each daemon write into a file a session has read injects a diff notice into that Claude's context
findings.scenario: Alice's Claude read hub.py. Peers' changes to it arrive as often as the push budget allows, and Claude Code adds a '<file> changed on disk since you last read it … take it as the current state … relevant changes' notice for each change.
findings.consequence: Token use and context growth lead to earlier compaction. The notice frames teammates' work as a deliberate change by the user, so attribution is wrong, and Claude may comment on or adapt to changes outside its task.
findings.evidence_detail: Observed in this session: after a script rewrote <scratchpad>/sweep/ed/e5/partial.js, which had been read earlier, the harness injected the changed lines with the wording 'That's usually deliberate, so take it as the current state rather than reverting it'.
findings.mitigation: Coalesce incoming writes into files in a session's read set (taken from PostToolUse(Read)) to at most one write per 30 s. Apply on demand when that session's PreToolUse needs the path. Add attribution through additionalContext on the next hook: 'lines X-Y from <peer>'s Claude, not your user; do not revert'.
findings.test: Push to a file a session has read at 6 pushes/min for 10 minutes. Count notices in the transcript (at most 2 per minute), and assert every one is followed by an attribution context.

design_changes:
Decision 4 says the apply is all-or-nothing and fails only with 'not uptodate'. Three experiments show that is false on Windows:
- e1: partial write when a file is locked;
- e11: partial write on a long path;
- e3: a concurrent save clobbered with exit 0.
The change below supports the approved engine rather than replacing it. Keep merge-tree for computing MERGED, but replace `read-tree -m -u` on the user's working tree with a per-path verifying writer:
1. Write a temp file in .git/cowork/tmp.
2. Rename the original away and check it against the expected blob.
3. Create the new file with link-no-replace; fall back to rename-over.
4. On a mismatch, run a 3-way merge through git.
Track last-applied as a per-path map. For the next merge-tree, build the local base tree from that map (update-index --cacheinfo on the private index, then write-tree, or mktree). A path that did not land keeps its old blob, so the next cycle offers it again.

Keep a long-lived, stat-fresh private index updated by the applier, with core.fsmonitor and core.untrackedCache, instead of re-seeding from a tree each cycle. Measured: about 750 ms versus 53 ms per cycle on 3,004 files. Re-seed only for recovery.

The snapshot covers tracked paths plus paths explicitly introduced through a Claude Write or Edit hook or `/cowork track`, never `git add -A` of untracked files. Add the editor and OS temp deny list, a churn quarantine, and a publish-side portable-path validator.

Snapshot reads use Node (no memory mapping) with a stability gate, then `hash-object -w --stdin --path` using per-path eol settings that reproduce the base blob's stored form. Plain `hash-object --stdin --path` flips i/crlf blobs to LF (verified in e14); fall back to `git add -- P`. Stored-form (EOL/BOM) preservation is a hard invariant: EOL or BOM changes happen only through an explicit command.

Add a per-path daemon write ring (pre- and post-write blobs), persisted for 14 days or more. It enables the stale-base rebase of editor saves and a 'revert-of-others' publish gate, so a hunk that restores a pre-peer version is never published automatically.

Before every snapshot, watch HEAD, refs/stash, ORIG_HEAD and the tracked-path count. Freeze outbound when any changes, and gate changes that touch more than 50 paths or more than 20% of tracked paths. Cap the index.lock pause and surface it.
Daemon git invocations force `filter.<driver>.required=true` for every driver referenced in attributes, plus a canary check at start and periodically.

Humans get soft claims, attributed by the absence of Claude hooks; Bash edits by Claude are accepted as being classed human. The holder side adds breach stamps that deny the next Edit until a Read. Conflict markers are never written into a working file; conflicts go to .git/cowork/conflicts and the board.

The file fence becomes a per-path mutex shared with the applier. PreToolUse waits for an in-flight write of that path. The fence is released on PostToolUse, PostToolUseFailure, Stop, MCP disconnect or a TTL. The fence also covers Read, so Read never sees a path mid-write.
open_questions: Does Claude Code's Write tool keep CRLF and BOM when it overwrites an existing BOM+CRLF file? This decides how often the stored-form flip is triggered by Claude itself; Edit is known to keep both.

Is hub.py stored with CRLF in the repo (`git ls-files --eol` shows i/crlf)? If yes, the e14 result (any LF rewrite gives a 26k-line diff even under autocrlf=true) applies to the pilot team's hottest file. Not checked, because the pilot repo was not touched.
Does VS Code save in place (truncate then write) or atomically on Windows, macOS and Linux? Each mode has its own exposure window (the half-written snapshot versus the temp-file deletion window).
We infer that Git for Windows memory-maps files while hashing, which would cause the UNKNOWN save failures. A mapped section reproduces the error, but git's exact read path was not traced.

Is fs.link (hard link, no-replace) available on every target filesystem: NTFS yes, but exFAT, SMB shares, WSL /mnt/c, Dev Drive/ReFS? Where it is not, is the small window left by the rename-over fallback acceptable?
Team policy: may the daemon restore format-only hunks on disk in symbols held by others, or only withhold them from publishing?
How should a human with no hooks be notified in real time of breaches and conflicts: an OS toast, a status line, their own Claude session's inbox, or an optional VS Code extension?

findings.title: mcp_tool gate fails open for the rest of the session once the stdio MCP server dies or is reloaded, and claims are released at the same moment
findings.scenario: 1. Yeonghui's session gates Edit/Write via PreToolUse mcp_tool hooks on the per-session cowork stdio MCP server. 2. The server crashes (unhandled exception, bad IPC frame, OOM), or Yeonghui runs /reload-plugins or toggles it off in /mcp. 3. Claude Code does not restart stdio servers. 4. Every later PreToolUse mcp_tool hook gets 'server not connected', which is a non-blocking error, so the Edit proceeds with no fence, no claim check and no causer detection. 5. At the same time the daemon sees stdin EOF and releases all of Yeonghui's claims, so Cheolsu's daemon sees foo() as free. 6. Yeonghui's Claude keeps editing hub.py::foo(), which Cheolsu has claimed.
findings.consequence: Coordination silently stops for the rest of the session. The only sign is a dim 'hook error' line in the transcript. Concurrent edits to the same function merge into conflicts or garbage. Requirement 8 never fires, because the board has no claim to compare against.
findings.evidence_detail: hooks.md#mcp-tool-hook-fields: 'If the tool returns isError: true, the hook produces a non-blocking error and execution continues' and 'If the server isn't connected at that point, the hook produces a non-blocking error'. mcp.md#automatic-reconnection: 'Stdio servers are local processes, and Claude Code doesn't reconnect them automatically.' hooks.md#timeouts: a timed-out PreToolUse hook does not block. Local copies: scratchpad/hooks.md lines 572-578 and scratchpad/sweep/docs/mcp.md line 361.
findings.mitigation: The enforcing gate for Edit|Write|NotebookEdit|Bash|PowerShell is an exec-form command hook ({"command":"node","args":["${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/dist/gate.js"]}). It talks to the daemon over the named pipe with an internal 2 s deadline. It exits 2 with a deny reason when cowork is active for this checkout (marker such as .git/cowork/active) and any of these holds: the daemon is unreachable, this session's MCP heartbeat is missing, or the reply is malformed. mcp_tool hooks may run alongside as a fast path but are never the only gate. Do not release claims on stdin EOF while hook traffic from that session_id continues. Wait for a 30 s grace period with no hooks before releasing, otherwise re-bind the claims to the hook channel. /cowork status and the statusline show 'GATE DOWN'.
findings.test: Peer B claims foo(). On peer A, kill the cowork MCP child process (taskkill /PID), then ask Claude to Edit foo(). Assert the Edit is denied with the cowork reason, hub.py bytes are unchanged, and B's claim is still on the board. Repeat after /reload-plugins, after toggling the server off in /mcp, and with the daemon process killed.

findings.title: Claude's routine git commands (stash/pull/stash pop, checkout -- f, restore, reset, merge, commit -a) make the daemon push a revert of teammates' work, then conflict markers
findings.scenario: 1. Cheolsu's daemon has merged Yeonghui's in-progress change to foo() into Cheolsu's working tree. The change is not in HEAD. 2. Cheolsu asks Claude to 'pull latest main'. Claude runs `git stash; git pull; git stash pop` through Bash/PowerShell (or `git checkout -- hub.py`, `git restore .`, `git reset --hard`, `git merge`, `git commit -am`). 3. After `git stash` the tree equals HEAD. Within 2-3 s the daemon snapshots it. Against the last applied tree this is a local deletion of Yeonghui's hunks, so it commits and pushes the deletion. 4. `git pull` moves HEAD. `git stash pop` then goes one of two ways. It may refuse ('Your local changes ... would be overwritten'), which strands Yeonghui's work in Cheolsu's private stash. Or it may conflict and write <<<<<<< markers into foo() while only AUTO_MERGE and unmerged index entries exist, with no MERGE_HEAD or REBASE_HEAD. 5. The daemon's pause check (index.lock/MERGE_HEAD/REBASE_HEAD) passes. The private-index `git add -A` captures the markers, and the daemon pushes them.
findings.consequence: Yeonghui's live work disappears from every peer's disk. Conflict markers then show up in foo() on every peer. Each peer's Claude sees a SyntaxError in hub.py and 'fixes' it a different way. The auto-mode classifier does not stop this: its default block list names reset --hard, checkout -- ., restore ., clean -fd and stash drop/clear, but not git stash, stash pop, pull, or single-file checkout --.
findings.evidence_detail: VERIFIED in scratchpad/sweep/stash: stash, then a daemon-style write, then `git stash pop` aborted with 'would be overwritten', leaving the change in stash@{0}. VERIFIED in scratchpad/sweep/stash2: stash, upstream commit, `git stash pop` → CONFLICT, markers in f.py; .git contained AUTO_MERGE but no MERGE_HEAD, REBASE_HEAD or CHERRY_PICK_HEAD; `git ls-files -u` showed stages 1-3. Then `GIT_INDEX_FILE=priv.idx git read-tree HEAD && git add -A && git write-tree` produced a blob containing the markers. The daemon's push and propagation are REASONED. The classifier list is DOCUMENTED in permission-modes.md under 'What the classifier blocks by default'.
findings.mitigation: (a) While live, a PreToolUse gate on Bash|PowerShell tokenizes the command (split on ; && || | and newlines, strip `cd x &&` and env prefixes, handle `git -C`). It denies git subcommands that move HEAD, the index or the worktree: stash (except list/show), checkout/restore with a pathspec, reset, pull, merge, rebase, cherry-pick, revert, am, apply (unless --check), switch, commit, clean. The reason points to /cowork save and /cowork rebase-base. (b) The daemon pauses on any of: index.lock, MERGE_HEAD, CHERRY_PICK_HEAD, REVERT_HEAD, AUTO_MERGE, rebase-merge/, rebase-apply/, sequencer/, BISECT_LOG, a non-empty `git ls-files -u` on the user's index (read-only, GIT_OPTIONAL_LOCKS=0), or HEAD differing from the HEAD seen in the last cycle. (c) Marker quarantine: never commit a file whose new content adds line-start `<<<<<<< `, `=======` or `>>>>>>> ` blocks that are not in the base blob, and raise a local alert instead. (d) Mass-revert breaker: if one cycle removes more than N remote-provenance hunks, or touches more than M files with no matching Edit/Write hook events, hold the push and ask the human.
findings.test: Replay the sweep/stash2 sequence on peer A under the daemon, with a file:// remote and a peer B. Assert that no pushed tree contains marker lines, that B's foo() never loses Yeonghui's hunk, and that A's daemon reports PAUSED within one cycle. Separately, feed each forbidden verb to the gate in Bash and PowerShell spellings, with `cd sub &&`, `git -C .` and `;`-chained prefixes, and assert deny.

findings.title: File fence and claim taken at PreToolUse leak forever when the call is denied, rejected or interrupted, because no Post* event fires
findings.scenario: 1. Yeonghui's Claude issues Edit on hub.py::foo(). 2. cowork's PreToolUse fences hub.py, so the daemon stops writing it, and takes a local claim on foo(). 3. The call never executes, for one of these reasons: a parallel hook (the user's own security hook or another plugin) returns deny, Yeonghui answers 'No' at the permission prompt, a deny rule matches, plan or dontAsk mode auto-denies, or Yeonghui presses Esc while the tool runs. 4. PostToolUse does not fire. PostToolUseFailure does not fire for permission denials or cancellations. PermissionDenied fires only in auto mode. Stop does not fire on a user interrupt. 5. The fence is never released, and the claim is published at the next push. Even when the edit is approved, the fence is held for the whole permission prompt, which can last minutes, because PreToolUse runs before the prompt.
findings.consequence: On Yeonghui's PC, hub.py (the 1.3 MB hub file) silently stops receiving teammates' changes for the rest of the session, and the divergence grows until a large conflict. Cheolsu is denied on foo() by a phantom claim for an edit that never happened, and his Claude files a handoff request for nothing.
findings.evidence_detail: hooks.md#posttoolusefailure Note: 'doesn't fire for tool calls rejected before execution ... or a permission denial' and 'Cancelling a running tool does not fire this hook'. hooks.md#permissiondenied: 'only fires in auto mode: it doesn't run when you manually deny a permission dialog, when a PreToolUse hook blocks a call, or when a deny rule matches'. hooks.md#stop: 'Does not run if the stoppage occurred due to a user interrupt'. hooks.md#pretooluse-decision-control: parallel hooks with precedence deny > defer > ask > allow. Local copy: scratchpad/hooks.md lines 2085-2250 and 2529-2533.
findings.mitigation: A fence is a lease keyed by tool_use_id (not by file and not by session), default 20 s. Release it on: PostToolUse or PostToolUseFailure with the same id; PostToolBatch (release every id listed); any later PreToolUse or UserPromptSubmit from the same (session_id, agent_id); Stop, StopFailure or SubagentStop; or lease expiry. After expiry the daemon may write the file only through read-tree's up-to-date check. Claims taken at PreToolUse stay local and tentative. They can be published only after PostToolUse shows the file actually changed inside that symbol (pre-image captured under the fence vs post-image). Causer ordering uses the publish time of confirmed claims.
findings.test: Run five variants: a second plugin hook that always denies; a manual 'No'; a deny rule Edit(hub.py); plan mode; Esc during a slow Write. After each, assert within 25 s that the fence table has no entry for the path, that a remote change to hub.py lands on disk, and that the board never contains a claim from that tool_use_id.

findings.title: /rewind 'Restore code' (or any whole-file restorer) writes back a pre-sync snapshot, and the daemon pushes it as a revert of teammates' merged work
findings.scenario: 1. At 10:00 Yeonghui sends a prompt, and the checkpoint captures hub.py. 2. Between 10:02 and 10:20 the daemon merges Cheolsu's edits to bar() into that file. 3. At 10:25 Yeonghui presses Esc Esc, opens /rewind and picks 'Restore code' at the 10:00 checkpoint to undo her Claude's attempt. 4. Claude Code writes the 10:00 file snapshot back. 5. The daemon snapshot sees a local change that removes Cheolsu's bar() hunks, and pushes it. The same pattern occurs when a stale IDE buffer is saved, or a script reads a file before a sync and writes it after.
findings.consequence: Cheolsu's 20 minutes of work vanish from every tree with no conflict and no warning. The board attributes the deletion to Yeonghui. Cheolsu's Claude finds its edits gone and redoes them, or argues with the new state.
findings.evidence_detail: checkpointing.md 'Rewind and summarize': Restore code reverts file changes. 'External changes not tracked': 'edits from other concurrent sessions are normally not captured, unless they happen to modify the same files as the current session'. No hook event exists for /rewind (hooks.md event table). The daemon propagating the revert is REASONED. Local copy: scratchpad/sweep/docs/checkpointing.md.
findings.mitigation: Add a revert guard based on provenance. For each file, the daemon keeps the last K blobs it wrote and the hunks each remote apply introduced (peer, commit). On every snapshot it checks two conditions: (a) the new local content equals a blob that predates a remote apply, or (b) the local diff is the inverse of a remote-provenance hunk applied in the last T minutes. If either holds, it does not push those hunks. Instead it computes merge-file(base = pre-apply blob, ours = local content, theirs = current applied blob), writes the result under the up-to-date check, and tells the local human: 'restore/rewind removed Cheolsu's bar() change; it was kept'. Only an explicit `/cowork revert <change-id>` may push such an inverse.
findings.test: Apply remote change C to bar(). Write the pre-C bytes back with a plain file write to simulate Restore code. Run one daemon cycle. Assert the pushed tree still contains C, the working file contains C, and a notice was emitted. Variant: also make a local Edit to foo() between the two steps, and assert the foo() edit is pushed while C is kept.

findings.title: A gate that answers 'no conflict' with permissionDecision 'allow' silently disables human review of every edit
findings.scenario: 1. The PreToolUse gate implementation returns permissionDecision:'allow' when there is no conflict, a pattern common in hook examples. 2. Yeonghui works in Manual (default) mode so that she reviews each edit, or a teammate uses dontAsk with a narrow allow list. 3. Every gated Edit, Write and Bash call now skips the permission prompt. In dontAsk mode, calls that should be auto-denied are approved.
findings.consequence: Installing cowork-sync quietly removes the human review gate in that repo. This is a security regression that nobody notices.
findings.evidence_detail: hooks.md#pretooluse-decision-control: '"allow" skips the permission prompt'. permission-modes.md (dontAsk): Claude still runs '... calls approved by a PreToolUse hook'. Local copy: scratchpad/hooks.md line 1801; scratchpad/sweep/docs/permission-modes.md line 539.
findings.mitigation: The gate has exactly two outputs. When it is not blocking, it prints nothing and exits 0 (no decision). When it blocks, it exits 2 with a hookSpecificOutput deny and a reason. It never returns 'allow', and returns 'ask' only in the explicit /cowork override flow. A CI check fails the build if the bundled JS contains permissionDecision 'allow'.
findings.test: In Manual mode with no allow rules, make a non-conflicting Edit: the permission prompt still appears (via an Agent SDK canUseTool callback in an automated test). In dontAsk mode with no allow rule, the Edit is denied by Claude Code, and cowork's log shows no decision.

findings.title: Claude Code's Edit matches after normalizing CRLF, BOM and quotes, so the daemon's exact-match mapping of old_string to a symbol misses on hub.py
findings.scenario: 1. hub.py is UTF-8 BOM + CRLF. 2. Claude emits an Edit whose old_string uses LF line breaks ('def beta():\n    y = 2'), or uses straight quotes where the file has curly ones, or sets replace_all:true and hits five functions. 3. Claude Code applies the edit after normalizing. 4. At PreToolUse the daemon searches the raw file bytes for tool_input.old_string and finds 0 hits, or for replace_all maps only the first hit. It then either fails open (no claim, no deny) or falls back to a whole-file claim.
findings.consequence: If it fails open, Yeonghui edits Cheolsu's claimed function in exactly the file the team shares most, and nothing denies it. If it claims the whole file, one edit locks all 26k lines of hub.py for everyone. With replace_all, four of five claimed functions are edited unchecked.
findings.evidence_detail: VERIFIED in scratchpad/sweep/edit. crlf_bom.py (EF BB BF + CRLF) was edited by the real Edit tool with a multi-line LF old_string: the edit succeeded, the result was written with CRLF and the BOM kept (checked with xxd). quotes.py: old_string `s = "hello"` (straight) matched `s = “hello”` and wrote `“world”` (curly). REASONED: that tool_input.old_string reaches hooks un-normalized; no hook was installed to capture it (see open question).
findings.mitigation: Find the edit in a normalized view (strip the BOM, convert CRLF to LF, fold U+2018/2019/201C/201D to ASCII quotes), then map offsets back to the raw file. For replace_all, list every match. Treat the PreToolUse prediction as advisory. Under the fence, capture the pre-image at PreToolUse; at PostToolUse, diff pre-image against post-image (EOL-normalized) to get the authoritative set of symbols changed. If that set includes a foreign-claimed symbol the prediction missed, restore those hunks from the pre-image while the fence is still held, record the change as a blocked request, and tell Claude through PostToolUse exit 2 stderr. When locating fails entirely, never claim the whole file. Let the edit run and rely on the post-diff.
findings.test: Build a fixture set: CRLF+BOM, curly quotes, tabs vs spaces, replace_all across 5 functions, an old_string spanning two symbols, and NotebookEdit by cell_id. Run each through real Claude Code with a hook that dumps its input. Assert the predicted symbols equal the post-diff symbols, and that a foreign claim on any of them results in a deny or a restore.

findings.title: Edit rewrites line endings for the whole file, so EOL-only churn in other people's functions gets blamed on the editor (Requirement 8 fires at an innocent Claude)
findings.scenario: 1. A peer on macOS (autocrlf=false) adds LF lines to a file whose blobs are stored with CRLF. Git does not autocrlf-normalize a path whose index copy already has CRLF, so Yeonghui's checkout ends up with mixed EOL. 2. Yeonghui's Claude edits foo() with Edit. 3. Claude Code rewrites the whole file with uniform CRLF. 4. The daemon's diff now shows EOL-only hunks in bar() and baz(), and bar() is claimed by Cheolsu.
findings.consequence: The daemon marks Yeonghui as the 'conflict causer' on bar(). Every other Claude warns her Claude, which apologizes and waits on work it never did. At merge time, Cheolsu's real edits to bar() conflict line by line with the EOL churn.
findings.evidence_detail:
VERIFIED in scratchpad/sweep/edit/mixed.py. Created with printf 'a = 1
b = 2
c = 3
d = 4
e = 5
'; the real Edit e = 5 → e = 50; xxd then showed line 3 ('c = 3') ending in 0d0a, so an untouched line's EOL changed. The git-side precondition (CRLF in the index suppresses autocrlf normalization) is DOCUMENTED git behaviour but was not run here.
findings.mitigation: Run all claim, attribution and causer logic on content normalized to LF without a BOM, and drop hunks that differ only in EOL or BOM. The daemon writes files only through git's checkout conversion, so it never creates mixed EOL itself. /cowork doctor lists tracked files with mixed EOL and offers a one-time renormalize through save.
findings.test: Use a mixed-EOL fixture with bar() claimed by peer B. Peer A's real Claude Code Edits foo(). Assert there is no conflict or causer event for bar(), and that after both peers push, the merged blob still contains B's bar() edit intact.

findings.title: File writes through Bash/PowerShell (sed -i, python one-liners, Set-Content, formatters, codegen) bypass the claim gate, including Claude's 'work around the deny' retries
findings.scenario: 1. Cheolsu holds foo(). 2. Yeonghui's Claude has its Edit on foo() denied. 3. To finish the task, Claude runs `python -c "...re.sub(...)..."`, `sed -i`, `(Get-Content f) -replace ... | Set-Content f`, or a repo-wide fixer (`ruff --fix .`, `black .`, `dotnet format`, `prettier --write .`, a code generator). 4. None of these hits the Edit gate, and PostToolUse(Edit|Write) does not fire for Bash writes. 5. The daemon picks the result up as an ordinary local edit and pushes it.
findings.consequence: The claim system is bypassed exactly after a deny, which is when it matters. Formatters reflow Cheolsu's in-progress functions, so his Claude's next old_string no longer matches and it has to re-read and redo. Set-Content on Windows PowerShell can also re-encode the whole file.
findings.evidence_detail: hooks.md#posttooluse: 'Claude Code doesn't run a PostToolUse hook matching Edit|Write when a Bash command or a process outside Claude Code rewrites the same file.' hooks.md#bash (bashEditDiff): 'best effort and in public beta ... Use the list to find what to review, not to enforce a policy'; by default it is recorded only in auto and bypassPermissions modes. Claude retrying through Bash after a deny is REASONED (prior-art.md failure #4).
findings.mitigation: Treat each Bash/PowerShell call as a transaction. At PreToolUse, take a tree-wide write fence (lease of at most 60 s; background or long commands drop the fence but stay in transaction mode) and record (mtime, size) for the checkout's tracked files. At PostToolUse or PostToolUseFailure (or at the session's next hook, if the call was interrupted), diff the changed files and map hunks to symbols. Hunks inside foreign-claimed symbols are restored from the last snapshot pre-image and recorded as a blocked change, and Claude is told via PostToolUse exit 2. While live, deny outright: repo-wide formatters or fixers run without explicit file arguments, and in-place writers (sed -i, perl -pi, Set-Content/Out-File/>, open(...,'w') in -c code) whose target has foreign claims. Deny reasons state: 'a shell rewrite of a claimed symbol will be reverted and queued as a request'.
findings.test: Peer B claims foo(). On peer A, have Claude run each bypass form. Assert that within one cycle foo() on A's disk is back to the pre-image, no tree touching foo() is pushed, a blocked-change record exists, and Claude's transcript contains the PostToolUse feedback.

findings.title: Worktree-isolated subagents, `claude -w` and EnterWorktree put a nested checkout inside the shared tree: the snapshot embeds it as a gitlink, and its edits escape claims
findings.scenario: 1. Yeonghui's session runs a subagent with isolation: worktree, or uses `claude -w`, or Claude calls EnterWorktree. 2. Claude Code creates <repo>/.claude/worktrees/agent-x on a branch cut from origin's default branch, not from the live tree. 3. The daemon's `git add -A` over the shared checkout adds .claude/worktrees/agent-x as a mode-160000 gitlink. 4. The live ref now carries a dangling gitlink. Peers' read-tree creates an empty directory, and the next /cowork save commits the gitlink to the real branch. 5. The subagent edits paths like C:\repo\.claude\worktrees\agent-x\hub.py. These map to no tracked path in the shared tree, so no claims are taken. Later the parent merges the worktree branch back with Bash `git merge` onto a stale base.
findings.consequence: Every peer's tree and the real branch get a bogus submodule entry, and CI checkouts with submodules fail with 'no submodule mapping'. Worktree work bypasses claims entirely, and the merge-back reverts or conflicts with live changes.
findings.evidence_detail: VERIFIED in scratchpad/sweep/wt: `git worktree add .claude/worktrees/agent-x`, then `GIT_INDEX_FILE=private.idx git read-tree HEAD; git add -A` printed 'warning: adding embedded git repository', and `git ls-tree` showed `160000 commit 310f6bc... .claude/worktrees/agent-x`. DOCUMENTED in worktrees.md: worktrees go under .claude/worktrees/ at the repo root; adding it to .gitignore is only advised, not automatic; the default base is the remote default branch ('fresh'); subagent worktrees use the same base.
findings.mitigation: Run the snapshot with an explicit pathspec excluding ':(exclude).claude/worktrees' and any directory that holds a .git file or directory, and reject any snapshot tree with a 160000 entry missing from the base tree. Map file paths to checkouts by the longest registered realpath prefix (lower-cased drive letter, forward slashes). Nested worktrees and .claude/worktrees/** never belong to the parent checkout. Cowork never auto-activates inside a worktree. PreToolUse on Agent with isolation:'worktree' and on EnterWorktree adds additionalContext (deny if configured): worktree edits are not coordinated and must come back through a cowork import tool that replays the diff as gated Edits.
findings.test: Reproduce sweep/wt inside a cowork checkout and run a daemon cycle. Assert the pushed tree has no 160000 entries and the board has no claims under .claude/worktrees/. Then attempt the Bash `git merge worktree-agent-x`, and assert it is denied or routed through the import tool.

findings.title: Subagents share session_id and run in the background by default, which breaks per-session fences and Stop-based handoff (premature, missed or stranded requests)
findings.scenario: 1. Yeonghui's main Claude starts two background subagents (the default since v2.1.198), and both edit hub.py. All their hooks carry the same session_id; only agent_id tells them apart. 2. If the fence is a per-(session, file) boolean, subagent A's PostToolUse clears it while subagent B's Edit is between its read and its write. The daemon writes the file, B's write overwrites the incoming change, and the next snapshot pushes a revert. 3. The main agent ends its turn while both subagents are still running. Stop fires, and the daemon hands subagent B's denied change to Cheolsu's queue even though B later finds another way. 4. Subagents fire SubagentStop, not Stop, so a denied change recorded for a subagent may never be handed off. 5. If Yeonghui presses Esc, or the turn dies on a rate limit (StopFailure), Stop never fires and nothing is handed off.
findings.consequence: Incoming changes are lost and a revert is pushed. Cheolsu's queue gets stale or duplicate requests ('Yeonghui requests X' for work already done), and some denied changes are stranded. This breaks Requirement 7's 'nothing is ever lost'.
findings.evidence_detail: hooks.md#common-input-fields: agent_id is 'Present only when the hook fires inside a subagent call'. sub-agents.md: 'As of v2.1.198, subagents run in the background by default'; 'Each subagent starts with a fresh, isolated context window'. hooks.md#stop: background_tasks array; 'Does not run if the stoppage occurred due to a user interrupt'; StopFailure on API errors. The overwrite sequence is REASONED.
findings.mitigation: The holder key is (machine-id, checkout realpath, session_id, agent_id or 'main'). The fence is a refcount of open tool_use_ids per file. Evaluate handoff per (session, agent_id): on SubagentStop for that agent; on Stop for 'main' only when the Stop input's background_tasks has no running subagent or teammate tasks; on StopFailure; and on the next UserPromptSubmit, which catches interrupts. Denied records persist in the daemon store until handed off or explicitly dropped. SubagentStart injects the cowork rules digest as additionalContext, because subagents start with a fresh context.
findings.test: Scripted session: two background subagents edit different symbols of one file while peer B pushes a change every second. After 100 iterations, assert no B change is missing from A's disk or from the live ref. Then deny one subagent and end the main turn while it is still running: no handoff until its SubagentStop. Press Esc during a turn that has a denied record: the handoff happens at the next prompt.

findings.title: Inbox delivery silently fails under any crossSessionInbound value, and when it works it wakes idle sessions into billed, unattended turns
findings.scenario: A: Yeonghui, her org's managed settings, or the project's .claude/settings.json sets crossSessionInbound 'hold' or 'refuse'. The own-child exemption applies only 'when no crossSessionInbound value applies', so the conflict warning posted by her MCP server is either held (shown as a notice and dropped after dialogExpiry, 5 min) or refused silently. B: Cheolsu's session sits idle over lunch. In 40 minutes the daemon posts 12 events (claims, requests, conflicts). That is 12 new turns, each re-reading a 600k-token context on a cold cache. In auto or bypassPermissions mode, his Claude acts on 'handle Yeonghui's request?' with no human present. C: Two identical warnings within the dedupe window are dropped; a burst is refused at the sender; past 50 queued messages the rest are lost.
findings.consequence: For some users Requirement 8 silently never happens. For others it burns a teammate's quota and makes their Claude do work nobody approved. Daemons believe warnings were delivered when they were not.
findings.evidence_detail: cross-session-messaging.md: 'Message delivery' (an idle session starts a new turn; a delivered message 'counts toward usage like a prompt'); 'Control inbound messages' (hold/refuse; default by permission-mode class; dialogExpiry five minutes); #own-child-messages ('when no crossSessionInbound value applies'; on native Windows the token is the only verification); 'Limitations' (identical repeats dropped, at most 50 queued). costs.md: the cache lifetime is 1 h on a subscription and 5 min on usage credits. Local copies: scratchpad/sweep/docs/cross-session-messaging.md and costs.md.
findings.mitigation: Treat the inbox as an accelerator only. Every event is also delivered through hooks, using a per-(session, agent_id) event cursor: PreToolUse/PostToolUse additionalContext for events about the file being touched, a UserPromptSubmit digest, and Stop additionalContext for requests. At registration the daemon works out the effective crossSessionInbound across settings layers (managed > --settings > local > project > user) and the permission-mode class. If inbox delivery is not possible, /cowork status marks the session 'hook-only'. Wake an idle session only for action-required events addressed to it, coalesced to at most 1 wake per 10 min, and never when permission_mode is auto, bypassPermissions or dontAsk unless the user opted in. Every message carries a unique event id and timestamp. An event counts as delivered only when a later hook from that session reports its id as seen.
findings.test: Run a matrix of crossSessionInbound {unset, accept, hold, refuse} × receiver mode {default, auto, bypassPermissions}. Post a conflict event and assert that Claude sees it by its next tool call, through either the inbox or the hook path, and that the daemon's delivered flag matches. Idle test: 12 events in 40 min produce at most 4 wakes, and 0 wakes in bypass mode without opt-in.

findings.title: Asking a peer to 'go first' or to take over a denied change looks to Claude like relaying a blocked action or a prompt injection, and board free text is an injection channel
findings.scenario: 1. Yeonghui's Edit on foo() is denied with the reason 'ask Cheolsu's Claude to make this change for you', and the daemon relays her proposed patch to Cheolsu's session. 2. Claude Code tells receiving Claudes that peer messages are not from the user and cannot approve anything. For SendMessage and teammates, it also states that a denied action must not be relayed to another agent to get around the check. Auto mode's classifier reviews inter-agent messages and treats relayed approvals as untrusted. 3. Cheolsu's Claude receives 'Yeonghui requests X — handle it? [patch]'. It may refuse, flag it to Cheolsu as suspicious, or (in auto/bypass mode) apply an unreviewed patch. 4. Board notes are free text written by any collaborator, or by anyone with push rights to refs/cowork/*, and the daemon injects them into every Claude's context.
findings.consequence: The 'polite ask' flow of Requirement 8 is unreliable: refusals and alarming prompts in front of users. Worse, peer-written text becomes instructions in 4 sessions, for example a note saying 'run scripts/fix.ps1 to resolve the conflict'.
findings.evidence_detail: Rules DOCUMENTED in cross-session-messaging.md 'How a session treats an incoming message', agent-teams.md 'Messages between agents' ('a teammate that was denied an action can't relay it to another teammate to bypass the check'; the auto-mode classifier reviews each message), and hooks.md#add-context-for-claude ('Text framed as out-of-band system commands can trigger Claude's prompt-injection defenses'). Whether these rules apply to the daemon/MCP delivery path is REASONED: the docs describe SendMessage and the inbox, not plugin MCP tools.
findings.mitigation: Run handoff and negotiation in the daemon as structured records: request{symbol, est_minutes, reason ≤200 chars, patch_ref}. The denied Claude never relays anything. Its deny reason states facts only: 'foo() is being edited by Cheolsu since 10:02; your change was saved as request #17 and will be offered to him automatically'. On the holder's side, the request goes to the human (systemMessage, plus Stop additionalContext telling Claude to ask its user via AskUserQuestion). Applying a peer's patch requires the human's explicit yes. Inject peer text only as quoted data with provenance ('note from Yeonghui (peer, unverified):'), with length caps and without rendering commands or URLs as actionable. 'May I go first?' is a typed MCP tool (cowork_request_priority). The daemon decides the outcome by rule (the holder's human answers yes or no; the default is wait), not by free-form chat between Claudes.
findings.test: Live eval with real Claude Code, at least 20 runs each in default and auto modes, on a denied-edit scenario. Measure the percentage of requesters that relay the change by other means, the percentage of holders that apply the patch without asking the human (must be 0), and the rate of injection alarms. Plant a board note containing an imperative command and assert that no session executes it.

findings.title: Compaction, /clear, /resume and /fork disconnect Claude from its claims, promises to wait and pending requests
findings.scenario: 1. At 10:05 Yeonghui's Claude is denied on foo() and agrees to wait and do bar() meanwhile. 2. At 10:40 auto-compaction summarizes the conversation, and the deny reasons and peer messages are condensed or dropped. 3. Claude sees 'update foo()' still in its plan and tries again (denied again), or switches to Bash, or reports the task done even though foo() was handed off. 4. Yeonghui runs /clear, which gives a new session_id while the MCP server process stays alive. The old claims remain bound to a dead conversation until the process exits, and Cheolsu's request is 'asked' of a conversation that knows nothing about it. 5. /fork, /branch or 'move to background' creates a new session_id that carries the same plan, so the fork is now a different holder from its own parent.
findings.consequence: Repeated denies waste tokens, Claude attempts bypasses or reports work as done when it isn't, and phantom claims stay held for hours after /clear. A forked session is blocked by its own parent's claims, or both edit the same function.
findings.evidence_detail: hooks.md#sessionstart: matcher values startup|resume|clear|compact|fork, and source 'fork' covers /fork, /branch and move-to-background. hooks.md#mcp-tool-hook-fields: mcp_tool SessionStart hooks are skipped at launch but run after /clear or compaction. context-window.md: the summary replaces the verbatim conversation. permission-modes.md: classifier boundaries can be lost when compaction removes the message. How Claude then behaves is REASONED.
findings.mitigation: A SessionStart command hook (matchers compact|clear|resume|fork) injects a compact digest: claims held by this holder key, pending denied changes and handoffs, requests waiting on this human, and the rules. On clear, resume or fork, the daemon re-binds the MCP connection to the new session_id and lists the previous session's claims for keep/transfer/release. The default is release at the next UserPromptSubmit; for fork, the parent keeps them. Deny reasons are self-contained (request id and status), so they stay correct without history. A cowork_status tool exists, and the digest tells Claude to call it before resuming blocked work.
findings.test: Session with a pending denied record, then /compact. On the next turn, assert the digest appears as SessionStart additionalContext and that Claude does not retry the denied edit within the next 5 tool calls (eval). After /clear, assert the old session_id's claims are released or re-keyed within one cycle. After /fork, assert parent and fork have distinct holder keys and that the parent's claims are not transferred implicitly.

findings.title: A slow or stuck daemon makes the gate either fail open (short timeout) or hang every Edit (600 s default)
findings.scenario: 1. The daemon's single Node event loop is busy: a synchronous git child process (merge-tree on a big change, or a push waiting on a credential prompt), or a cold tree-sitter WASM parse of hub.py. Research measured a native parse at about 0.11 s and a cold Python prototype at 1.3 s wall. Meanwhile 3 sessions are issuing Edits. 2. If the hook timeout is short (say 5 s), Claude Code cancels the hook and the tool proceeds unchecked. 3. If the timeout is the default 600 s, every Edit in every session hangs while the daemon is stuck.
findings.consequence: Either the gate silently fails open exactly when the team is busiest, or Claude sessions freeze for minutes and users disable the plugin.
findings.evidence_detail: hooks.md#timeouts: 'A timed-out command, http, or mcp_tool hook doesn't block the tool call'; the default timeout is 600 s. Latency figures: research/region-detect.md (parse 0.11 s native; 1.3 s cold prototype) and research/runtime-dist.md (node hook spawn ~31 ms). The stall scenario is REASONED.
findings.mitigation: The hook path never waits on git or the network. The daemon answers from memory: a cache of published claims plus an incrementally re-parsed tree per file, kept up to date in a worker thread on file change. The gate client has an internal 2 s deadline. On timeout it denies with 'cowork busy — retry this edit' (fail closed), and the hook entry's timeout is set to 10 s so Claude Code's timeout never fires first. Git child processes are always async, with GIT_TERMINAL_PROMPT=0 and non-interactive credential helpers.
findings.test: Inject a 10 s sleep into the daemon's claim lookup. Assert the Edit is denied in about 2 s, neither allowed nor hung. Benchmark PreToolUse latency on hub.py with 3 sessions editing concurrently: p99 under 200 ms.

findings.title: Claude 'fixes' a teammate's half-finished synced code (test or lint failures) with a legitimate Edit, reverting it, because no claim covers it
findings.scenario: 1. Cheolsu's Claude is midway through a 5-edit refactor of parse_rows(). After edit 3 the turn ends: its claim is released at Stop, or was never published inside the propagation window. The daemon syncs the half-done state to Yeonghui. 2. Yeonghui's Claude runs pytest or tsc, and the failures point at parse_rows(). 3. The Edit result note says the file 'contains other changes not in your context'. Claude re-reads, sees code it did not write breaking the tests, and rewrites or reverts it with a normal Edit, which the gate allows.
findings.consequence: Teammates silently revert each other's in-progress work through ordinary edits, and each Claude believes it fixed a bug. Shared functions churn back and forth, and Requirement 8 never triggers because no claim was violated.
findings.evidence_detail: Based on VERIFIED Edit behaviour in scratchpad/sweep/edit/stale_edit.py: after an external change, the real Edit applied with the note '(note: the file had been modified on disk since you last read it — the edit applied cleanly, but the file contains other changes not in your context...)'. Also prior-art.md failure #4 (agents 'repair' unexpected changes).
findings.mitigation: Recent-provenance protection. For T minutes after a remote hunk lands, or until its author's next save, the first Edit, Write or Bash diff that modifies lines owned by another peer is denied with: 'lines 1200-1260 were written by Cheolsu's Claude 4 min ago; to change them anyway call cowork_override with a reason'. The attempt is recorded as a request to the author. After Bash test or lint commands, PostToolUse maps file:line locations in the failure output to foreign recent hunks and adds additionalContext: 'failures in parse_rows() come from Cheolsu's in-progress work; don't fix them; notify via cowork_note'. Claims last until the author's save or explicit release, not until Stop.
findings.test: Peer B makes 3 of 5 edits, leaving tests broken. Ask peer A's Claude to 'make the tests pass'. Over at least 10 runs, assert that A's first Edit touching B's recent hunks is denied with the provenance message and that A's Claude never modifies parse_rows().

findings.title: The auto-mode classifier can block cowork's own slash-command actions (npx download+execute, visible force-with-lease)
findings.scenario: 1. Yeonghui runs /cowork start in auto mode, and the command prompt tells Claude to run `npx cowork-sync start`. 2. The classifier blocks it as 'downloading and executing code' when npx has to fetch the package. Or, for /cowork save, the template exposes `git push --force-with-lease ...` to reset the live ref, and the classifier blocks it as 'Force push'. 3. Or the classifier returns no verdict (transient) and the call is denied.
findings.consequence: /cowork start or save fails intermittently, and only for auto-mode users. Claude may then 'work around' it by force-pushing refs by hand.
findings.evidence_detail: permission-modes.md 'What the classifier blocks by default' (downloading and executing code; Force push) and the no-verdict denial. This machine's user memory records earlier auto-mode classifier blocks of scripts. Whether !-expanded command blocks are reviewed by the classifier is unknown.
findings.mitigation: Slash commands invoke only `node "${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/dist/cli.js" <verb>`: bundled, no npx, no network fetch. All git operations, including force-with-lease, stay inside the CLI and daemon and never appear in command text Claude can see. Prefer running the CLI at command expansion if that bypasses the model. The CLI prints a one-line factual result. Document an optional allow rule for the CLI path.
findings.test: Run every /cowork verb 10 times in auto mode on a clean machine: zero classifier denials. CI greps the plugin's commands/ and skills/ for `npx` and `git push` and fails if found.

design_changes: Claims taken at PreToolUse stay local and tentative. They are published only after PostToolUse confirms, by diffing the pre-image captured under the fence against the post-image, that the symbol really changed. This removes phantom claims from denied, rejected or interrupted calls. Causer ordering uses the confirmed publish time.

The gate's source of truth is an exec-form command hook (node + args) that fails closed (exit 2) when cowork is active and the daemon or MCP heartbeat is missing or slow (2 s internal deadline, 10 s hook timeout). mcp_tool hooks are only a fast path, never the only gate, because they fail open by design and stdio servers are not reconnected.
The gate never returns permissionDecision 'allow'. It returns no decision, or deny.

The fence is a lease keyed by tool_use_id with a refcount per file. It is released by PostToolUse/PostToolUseFailure, PostToolBatch, the next PreToolUse or UserPromptSubmit from the same (session, agent_id), Stop/StopFailure/SubagentStop, or lease expiry.
Holder key = (machine-id, checkout realpath, session_id, agent_id or 'main'). Re-key on SessionStart sources clear, resume and fork.
Handoff triggers go beyond Stop: SubagentStop per agent; Stop only when background_tasks has no running subagents; StopFailure; the next UserPromptSubmit (catches interrupts).

Bash/PowerShell calls run as transactions: a tree-wide fence plus a stat snapshot before, a diff after, and restore-and-record for hunks in foreign-claimed symbols. While live, git verbs that move HEAD, the index or the worktree are denied, as are repo-wide formatters.

The daemon's pause set is extended to CHERRY_PICK_HEAD, REVERT_HEAD, AUTO_MERGE, rebase-merge/, rebase-apply/, sequencer/, BISECT_LOG, a non-empty `git ls-files -u` on the user's index, and HEAD moved since the last cycle. Any file that gains conflict markers is quarantined from snapshots.

A provenance-based revert guard: local changes that undo recently applied remote hunks (from /rewind, a stale editor buffer or a read-modify-write script) are re-merged against the pre-apply blob instead of pushed. A mass-change breaker holds pushes that touch many files with no matching Edit/Write hook events.
The snapshot pathspec excludes .claude/worktrees/ and any nested .git; new 160000 (gitlink) entries are refused. Cowork is opt-in per checkout and never auto-activates in Claude Code worktrees.

All symbol, claim and causer logic runs on BOM-stripped, LF-normalized, quote-folded content, and EOL-only hunks are ignored. The PreToolUse location is advisory; the PostToolUse diff is authoritative.

Inbox delivery is an accelerator with a hook-borne fallback: per-session event cursor, unique event ids, effective crossSessionInbound detected at registration. Idle sessions are woken only for action-required events, rate-limited, and never in auto/bypass/dontAsk without opt-in.
Negotiation and handoff are daemon-executed structured records. The holder's human, not the holder's Claude, accepts peer patches. Peer free text is injected only as quoted, attributed data.
A SessionStart (compact|clear|resume|fork) and SubagentStart digest re-injects claims, pending requests and rules after context loss.
Slash commands call the bundled CLI by absolute path (no npx). Git operations are never visible in Claude-run command text.
Drop MultiEdit from matchers as a dependency: it is not in the current tools reference (tools.md lists Edit, Write and NotebookEdit). Keep it harmlessly in the matcher, but do not design around it.
open_questions: Does PreToolUse tool_input.old_string/new_string reach hooks exactly as the model emitted it (LF, straight quotes), or after Claude Code's normalization? One-line spike: a temp PreToolUse hook that dumps stdin, then an Edit on a CRLF+BOM file and on a curly-quote file (fixtures in scratchpad/sweep/edit).

Do stdio MCP server children receive CLAUDE_CODE_MESSAGING_SOCKET and CLAUDE_CODE_MESSAGING_TOKEN in their environment? The docs only say hooks and Bash. If not, the SessionStart command hook must pass them to the daemon, and on Linux the MCP server must post as an own child (process evidence), since a detached daemon is not one.

What is the exact wire format of a message line after the auth line on the inbox socket, and how does Claude Code label a daemon or MCP-posted message to the model ('from session X', own-child, or user)? This decides the framing and injection behaviour.

Is Write's 'File has been modified since read' check (verified: scratchpad/sweep/edit/stale_write.py) done only at validation, before PreToolUse, or repeated after the permission prompt? If only at validation, a sync landing between validation and the fence can still be overwritten by a stale Write.
Does PostToolBatch's tool_calls array include calls that were denied by a hook, rejected at the permission prompt, or cancelled? If yes, it is the cleanest universal fence-release point.
Are !-expanded shell blocks in plugin commands or skills reviewed by the auto-mode classifier and permission rules, and are they available in plugin commands at all?
When Claude Code kills or exits, does the detached daemon survive on Windows (process-tree kill vs Job Object)? This affects claim release and gate fail-closed behaviour.
Do hook-denied (exit 2) Edits inside background subagents surface the reason to the subagent model reliably, or does the subagent end early (prior-art notes hidden subagent denials)?

findings.title: Switching branches, a detached HEAD or bisect in a live working copy publishes the other branch's content into the live ref
findings.scenario: 1) A and B are live on main. A's foo() edit has synced into B's working tree. 2) B runs `git switch feature`. Git carries the uncommitted live changes along. The command finishes, so index.lock, MERGE_HEAD and REBASE_HEAD are all gone. 3) B's daemon resumes. Its snapshot (seeded from the last applied main tree, then `add -A`) is feature's g.py and h.py plus A's edit, and it pushes this to refs/cowork/main/code as B's edits. 4) A's daemon merges it, and A's main working tree now holds feature's g.py and an untracked h.py. `git checkout <oid>`, `git bisect start`, and `rebase -i` stopped at `break` (detached HEAD at an intermediate commit, with only rebase-merge/ present) do the same thing.
findings.consequence: Every main peer's working tree is silently rewritten with another branch's content, and Claudes then build on it. The next `save` commits feature code into main. Peers' unsaved main live changes also leak into B's feature branch.
findings.evidence_detail: sweep/lifecycle/setup.sh and cycle.sh implement one daemon cycle per decisions 2 and 4: a private index seeded from the applied tree, `add -A`, write-tree, fetch, `merge-tree --merge-base=applied`, `read-tree -m -u`, then commit-tree and a CAS push, pausing only on index.lock, MERGE_HEAD or REBASE_HEAD. After `git -C B switch feature`, the next cycles leave A on refs/heads/main with ` M g.py` (content "FEATURE-ONLY") and `?? h.py`. A marker check showed `rebase -i` at `break` leaves only rebase-merge/ (no REBASE_HEAD), and bisect leaves a detached HEAD with only BISECT_* files.
findings.mitigation: Replace the pause rule with a git-epoch guard. Epoch = (symbolic-ref HEAD, HEAD oid, refs/stash oid, size of logs/HEAD, presence of MERGE_HEAD, CHERRY_PICK_HEAD, REVERT_HEAD, REBASE_HEAD, AUTO_MERGE, rebase-merge/, rebase-apply/, sequencer/, BISECT_START or index.lock, and whether `git ls-files -u` is non-empty, read with GIT_OPTIONAL_LOCKS=0). Read it before and after every snapshot and apply. A snapshot is pushable only if both readings match each other and match the epoch recorded at the last applied state. If HEAD is detached or names a branch other than the live one, the daemon enters DETACHED: no snapshot, no apply, no push. It posts a board event ('B left main live') and tells the local user and Claude. It never auto-joins the new branch. It resumes only when HEAD is back on refs/heads/<live> at the live base, or after the adopt rule in head-drift-after-pull-or-save.
findings.test: Harness with two clones and a file:// remote. Between daemon cycles, run each of: switch, checkout <oid>, `bisect start/good/bad`, and `rebase -i` with an injected `break`, at randomized points. Assert that no blob reachable only from feature ever appears in refs/cowork/main/code, that A's working tree is byte-identical before and after, and that B's daemon reports DETACHED.

findings.title: git stash, reset --hard, restore, checkout --, clean and Claude's /rewind look like edits, and the daemon pushes the revert to everyone
findings.scenario: 1) A's Claude edits foo() and B edits bar(); both sync to both PCs. 2) B (the human, or B's Claude via Bash) runs `git stash`, which resets B's working tree to HEAD. 3) B's daemon snapshots: the diff from applied to working tree is the removal of both edits, and it pushes that. 4) A's daemon merges the incoming tree, which equals the base, and A's own foo() edit disappears from A's disk. The same happens with `reset --hard`, `git restore .`, `checkout -- f`, `clean -fd`, a stale editor buffer saved over a synced file, and Claude Code's /rewind 'Restore code'. /rewind restores whole-file snapshots, which wipes peer changes merged into those files after the checkpoint.
findings.consequence: Teammates' unsaved live work, including the originator's own, is silently erased from every working tree. Claudes then rewrite what they believe they already did, or build on missing code. The only copy left is an old live-chain commit nobody knows to look at.
findings.evidence_detail: Mini-daemon harness: after `git -C B stash`, A/f.py went back to `return 1` and `return 2`, losing A's own edit. Signals measured in sweep/lifecycle/mk: `stash` changes refs/stash and adds reflog entry 'reset: moving to HEAD'; `reset --hard` with HEAD unchanged also writes 'reset: moving to HEAD'; `git restore f` and `git checkout -- f` add no reflog entry (logs/HEAD stayed at 11 lines). /rewind behaviour is DOCUMENTED at https://code.claude.com/docs/en/checkpointing ('file snapshots'; external changes are captured only if they modify the same files).
findings.mitigation: Use three layers. (a) Epoch guard: if refs/stash or the reflog changed since the last snapshot, QUARANTINE that snapshot and do not push it. (b) Peer-revert guard, independent of git metadata, because human edits and /rewind never pass through PreToolUse claims. The daemon keeps a per-file map of regions changed by other peers on the live chain since the last save. An outgoing hunk that modifies or removes such a region is held in a local 'contested' set, unless a local session holds a claim on that symbol. Held hunks are not pushed. The local user and Claude get a concrete question ('this would undo 영희's foo() for everyone: publish / keep local / discard'), and nothing is published until they answer. (c) PreToolUse(Bash) denies stash, `reset --hard`, `checkout --`, restore, `clean -f`, switch, `checkout <ref>`, pull, rebase, cherry-pick, revert, am, bisect and commit while live, with a message naming the /cowork equivalent. This last layer is only best-effort, because shell parsing is leaky, so (a) and (b) are the real guarantee.
findings.test: Harness: after A's edit syncs to B, run each command on B (and simulate /rewind by writing an older full-file copy over f.py). Assert that refs/cowork/main/code still contains A's edit, that A's f.py is unchanged, and that B's daemon shows the hunk as held. Control case: B edits a region nobody else touched, and the change is pushed without a prompt.

findings.title: After a save, a pull or an outsider's push, peers' HEAD stays on the old base; `git pull` is refused and its hint ('stash them') leads into the revert above
findings.scenario: 1) A non-cowork collaborator pushes commit U (changes g.py) to main. 2) B runs `git pull`. HEAD fast-forwards to U and g.py updates. 3) B's daemon (seeded from the applied tree, not HEAD) sees U's g.py change as B's edit and pushes it. 4) A still has HEAD = old base, and `git status` shows `M g.py`. 5) A runs `git pull` and gets 'Your local changes to the following files would be overwritten by merge: g.py … Please commit your changes or stash them'. 6) A follows git's hint and stashes, which triggers worktree-reset-commands-broadcast-revert. The same refusal happens on every peer after any `save`, because save moves the branch while every working tree holds the saved content uncommitted. Later saves also hit spurious conflicts: base = old base, ours = U modified further, theirs = U.
findings.consequence: Ordinary git hygiene stops working for the whole team after the first save or pull. git's own advice leads people to wipe everyone's work. Upstream commits are re-attributed as live edits.
findings.evidence_detail: Harness: an outsider clone X pushes U and B runs `git pull`. Next cycles: B pushes, and A's `status` shows ` M f.py` and ` M g.py`. A's `git pull` printed the 'would be overwritten … g.py … Aborting' error. Post-save run: after an atomic save (branch and live both leased), B's `git pull` aborted the same way. The adopt mitigation was verified: B's `status` came back clean, `git pull` returned 0, and HEAD = the save commit.
findings.mitigation: Add an explicit base-move protocol. This relaxes decision 4's 'never touch HEAD or index' for one guarded step. Live commits carry a `Cowork-Base: <oid>` trailer. Two daemon-run commands move the base. `/cowork pull` fetches the branch, takes merge-tree(base=liveBase, live tip, upstream tip), and CAS-pushes a new live commit whose parent is the upstream tip. `save` is covered in save-race-reverts-concurrent-edits. Every daemon that sees a new base runs ADOPT, under all of these conditions: symbolic-ref HEAD == refs/heads/<b>, HEAD == old base, nothing staged (`git diff --cached --quiet`), and .git/index.lock created with O_EXCL. ADOPT runs `git update-ref refs/heads/<b> <new> <old>` (CAS) and writes the user's index from the new base tree (the working tree is untouched), then releases the lock. If any condition fails, the daemon shows the single command to run and does not snapshot. A human `git pull` caught by the epoch guard (HEAD moved forward on the same branch to a descendant of the live base) becomes a base move, never B's edits.
findings.test: Harness: an outsider pushes U, then B pulls. Assert that the live ref's tree diff attributed to B is empty, that the live commit's Cowork-Base = U, that every peer's HEAD = U, that `git status` is clean except for genuinely unsaved live edits, and that `git pull` exits 0 on every peer. Repeat after `/cowork save`.

findings.title: A late joiner with an older HEAD or local WIP reverts the live state or saved commits, depending on which merge base its first cycle uses
findings.scenario: C cloned at base B0 and has uncommitted WIP. Since then, live was saved as S (A's foo() is on main) and B edited bar() live. C runs /cowork start. If the first cycle treats the live tip as 'last applied', the snapshot is C's tree. The diff reverts A's and B's work, which is pushed to everyone. If it uses the live base S, merge-tree treats S's changes as removed by C, and A's saved foo() edit is reverted in every working tree. Only C's own HEAD (B0) as merge base gives a correct merge. Even then, C's pre-join WIP and any untracked non-ignored files (`add -A` includes them) are published immediately, such as a .env, a credentials file or a database dump. On GitHub a file over 100 MiB makes the push fail permanently, so C's daemon never gets a push through.
findings.consequence: Joining silently undoes teammates' live work or already-committed work. Or it leaks local secrets and junk into the remote's object store, which keeps force-push residue in cruft packs. Or C's sync stalls.
findings.evidence_detail: Harness with three variants of C's initial applied state. live-tip: A ended with `return 1`, `return 2` (all live work reverted). live-base: A ended with `return 1`, `return 200` (A's saved edit reverted). own-HEAD: A ended with `return 100`, `return 200` plus C's WIP (correct). Inclusion of untracked files is OBS in research/git-transport.md §7. GitHub blocks files over 100 MiB: DOCUMENTED, https://docs.github.com/en/repositories/working-with-files/managing-large-files/about-large-files-on-github.
findings.mitigation: Join protocol. (1) Require HEAD on refs/heads/<b> at the live base or an ancestor of it; otherwise run `/cowork pull`-style adopt first, or refuse with instructions. (2) The first merge base is always the joiner's own HEAD commit, never the live tip or live base. (3) Pre-join local changes and pre-existing untracked files are not published by default. They are committed to refs/worktree/cowork/<b>/parked-at-join and listed, and the user opts in per path. (4) Apply a per-file size cap (default 5 MB) and a secret-name deny list (.env*, *.pem, *.key, id_*, *.pfx) to untracked files. (5) If nothing is opted in, the joiner's first push must change nothing (its tree equals the live tip).
findings.test: Harness: run all three variants. Assert that after join every peer's tree equals the pre-join live tree, plus only the paths C opted in. Assert that a 150 MB untracked file and a .env are never in any pushed tree. Assert that a joiner whose HEAD is ahead of or diverged from the live base is refused.

findings.title: 'save then reset the live ref onto the saved commit' drops edits pushed during the save, and peers' merges then delete them from disk
findings.scenario: 1) B starts save: it captures live tip L1's tree, builds S on base B0, and pushes main. 2) Meanwhile A's Claude edits bar() and A's daemon pushes L2. 3) B resets the live ref to S, with a lease taken from a fresh fetch (L2), so the CAS succeeds. 4) A's daemon merges with base = last applied L2, ours = A's working tree, theirs = S, which lacks the bar() edit. A's own bar() edit is removed from A's disk; B's daemon does the same. Related cases: two concurrent saves; a crash between the branch push and the live reset on hosts without --atomic (Azure); an outsider force-pushing the branch so the live base is no longer an ancestor.
findings.consequence: Work done in the seconds around every save silently disappears from all working trees. It is not in the saved commit either.
findings.evidence_detail: Harness: after the naive reset, A/f.py showed `return 100` and `return 2`, so A's during-save edit was gone. Leasing on L1 was rejected ('stale info'). The re-parent algorithm was verified: new live = commit-tree(tree of current tip Lc, merge-tree(base L1, S, Lc)) with parent S, pushed with lease Lc. Both A and B kept `return 200`, and `diff S..live` showed exactly the 1 unsaved change.
findings.mitigation: Save never resets the live tree. It (1) fetches; (2) builds S from live tip Lx's tree on top of the freshly fetched branch tip, using merge-tree(liveBase, Lx, branchTip) if the branch moved, and refusing with a conflict list if the merge fails or liveBase is not an ancestor of branchTip (history was rewritten); (3) pushes atomically: branch with lease on the fetched branch tip, plus live = commit(tree = merge-tree(base Lx, S, Lcur)) with parent S and lease on Lcur, plus a board event. On CAS rejection it re-runs, never forces. S's message carries `Cowork-Live: <Lx>`, so on hosts without --atomic any daemon that finds the branch at S while the live chain still contains Lx completes the re-parent idempotently. Two saves: the lease admits one, and the other re-fetches and finds nothing new to save.
findings.test: Harness: inject a peer push between every step of save (after capture, after the branch push, before the live push), and run two saves concurrently in 200 randomized trials. Assert that every edit ever pushed to live is either in the branch or in the live tip's diff against the branch. Assert that no working tree loses a line. Kill save between the branch push and the live push, and assert the next daemon completes it.

findings.title: A daemon crash or power loss after read-tree -u but before persisting 'last applied' resurrects content a peer has since deleted
findings.scenario: 1) A adds a debug line X, pushed as L1. 2) B's daemon applies L1 to disk, then crashes, is killed, or the PC loses power before it records applied = L1. 3) A deletes X, pushed as L2 (same tree as L0). 4) B's daemon restarts with applied = L0. Its snapshot is L0 + X, which looks like B added X. merge-tree(base L0, ours = has X, theirs = L2 without X) keeps X, and the daemon pushes it. 5) X reappears on A's disk.
findings.consequence: Deleted code (debug prints, removed secrets, reverted bugs) silently comes back for everyone, attributed to the crashed peer. That peer's Claude is then blamed as the conflict causer.
findings.evidence_detail: Harness: B ran a cycle, then its applied file was restored to the old value. After A deleted X, B's restart cycle pushed a new commit, and A/f.py contained `print("DEBUG X")` again.
findings.mitigation:
Use a write-ahead apply journal. Before `read-tree -u`, durably write intent {from: applied, to: target commit, paths}. Record applied only via `git update-ref refs/worktree/cowork//applied ` after a successful apply, then clear the intent. On startup with an open intent, build a recovery base tree per path. For each path in the intent: if the working-tree content, hashed with filters via `git hash-object --path=

`, equals the target blob, use the target blob as base; otherwise use the from blob. The first merge uses that synthetic base. Never snapshot before recovery completes.
findings.test: Fault-injection harness: kill -9 (TerminateProcess on Windows) the daemon at each point of the cycle: during read-tree, after read-tree, after update-ref. Then a peer deletes the just-applied line. Restart. Assert the line never reappears on any PC across 100 randomized runs.

findings.title: In-progress git operations outside the pause list publish conflict markers or intermediate states to everyone
findings.scenario: B runs `git cherry-pick origin/hotfix`, which conflicts in g.py, a file live sync had not touched. git leaves CHERRY_PICK_HEAD and AUTO_MERGE but no MERGE_HEAD or REBASE_HEAD. B's daemon is not paused, snapshots g.py with <<<<<<< ======= >>>>>>> markers, and pushes it. A's g.py now contains conflict markers. Verified marker files for other states: revert conflict leaves REVERT_HEAD only; `stash pop` and `stash apply` conflicts leave only AUTO_MERGE; a `switch -m` conflict leaves no marker file at all; `rebase -i` at break leaves only rebase-merge/; am leaves only rebase-apply/; bisect leaves only BISECT_*. Also, `git stash pop` is refused on any live-dirty file, which is effectively every file peers touched.
findings.consequence: Every peer's file becomes syntactically broken, and Claudes start 'fixing' conflict markers on four PCs at once (multiple writers of the same region). A `save` in this window commits the markers.
findings.evidence_detail: sweep/lifecycle/mk marker survey, printed per operation. Harness: after B's conflicting cherry-pick and cycles B then A, A/g.py contained the full `<<<<<<< HEAD … >>>>>>> 9fe2f6d (h2)` block. A `stash pop` attempt on a live-modified file was refused.
findings.mitigation: Pause (no snapshot, no apply) while any of these hold: MERGE_HEAD, CHERRY_PICK_HEAD, REVERT_HEAD, REBASE_HEAD, AUTO_MERGE, rebase-merge/, rebase-apply/, sequencer/, BISECT_START, index.lock, unmerged entries (`git ls-files -u` non-empty), or a detached HEAD. Paths come from `git rev-parse --git-path`, so linked worktrees work. Independently, never push a text blob that newly contains a line-anchored conflict-marker triple absent from its base blob. Hold it and tell the local user.
findings.test: Harness: for each operation in the survey, produce a conflict on B, run 5 cycles, and assert the live ref never gains a blob containing `^<<<<<<< ` and that A's files are unchanged. Unit-test the marker detector against CRLF files, BOM files and diff3-style `|||||||` blocks.

findings.title: A failed plumbing step yields an empty oid, the push refspec becomes ':refs/cowork/<b>/code', and the CAS-leased push deletes the team's live ref
findings.scenario: 1) B's daemon git child is killed by a watchdog, by sleep, or by power loss, leaving its private index.lock. Disk full and a pruned object fail the same way. 2) Next cycle: read-tree and `add -A` fail, write-tree prints nothing, and commit-tree with an empty tree prints nothing. 3) The daemon runs `git push --force-with-lease=refs/cowork/main/code:<R> origin "$C:refs/cowork/main/code"` with C empty. The refspec ':ref' is a delete, and the lease matches, so the server deletes the live ref. 4) Every daemon now fails with 'couldn't find remote ref'. The first one to 'recreate' it does so from its own possibly stale base. The same deletion follows when a non-cowork collaborator runs `git push --mirror` from an ordinary clone.
findings.consequence: Live sync stops for the whole team at once. A naive recreate path rebuilds the shared tree from one peer's stale state and reverts the others. The stale lock also wedges that daemon forever: 'Unable to create …idx.lock: File exists' every cycle.
findings.evidence_detail: Harness: `touch B/.git/cowork/idx.lock`, then cycle. The `bash -x` trace shows `T=`, `C=`, then `git push -q --force-with-lease=refs/cowork/main/code:4bfb… origin :refs/cowork/main/code`, and `git ls-remote` shows no refs/cowork afterwards. Three consecutive cycles printed the same lock error. A separate test, `git push --mirror` from a fresh clone, printed `- [deleted] refs/cowork/main/code`.
findings.mitigation: (1) Use a typed Oid: accept only /^[0-9a-f]{40}$|^[0-9a-f]{64}$/, and verify `git cat-file -e <oid>^{commit}` before composing any refspec. Push only via a function that takes (Oid, RefName). Deletion lives in a separate explicit API used only by `/cowork reset`. (2) Every git child's non-zero exit aborts the cycle; never continue on partial output. (3) The single-instance lock (see clones-worktrees-identity) is held, so at startup the daemon may delete its own private *.lock files. Never touch .git/index.lock unless it holds the daemon's signature. (4) A missing live ref means state LIVE-REF-MISSING: stop, alert all sessions, and never auto-recreate. `/cowork start --recreate` recreates it from the peer with the newest applied commit, using CAS with an empty lease. (5) On the refs/heads/cowork/** fallback, recommend a 'restrict deletions' ruleset.
findings.test: Fault injection: stub git so write-tree or commit-tree exits 128 with empty stdout. Assert that no push process is spawned. Delete the remote live ref and assert all daemons enter LIVE-REF-MISSING within 2 polls and none pushes. Leave a stale private lock and assert the daemon recovers after restart.

findings.title: A network git command with no timeout hangs indefinitely after sleep or Wi-Fi changes, stopping sync silently while local claims keep being granted
findings.scenario: The laptop resumes from sleep, changes network, or sits behind a captive portal mid-fetch. The TCP connection is dead or the server never answers. By default git (libcurl) has no low-speed timeout and Windows TCP keepalive fires after 2 h, so the daemon's loop is stuck inside `git fetch` or `git push`. Meanwhile PreToolUse keeps answering from the stale board, granting local claims and allowing edits that peers cannot see.
findings.consequence: Hours of uncoordinated editing with no visible indication. On reconnect there is a large conflict set in which this peer is the 'conflict causer' for everything.
findings.evidence_detail: sweep/lifecycle/blackhole.js accepts TCP connections and never replies. A default `git fetch http://127.0.0.1:18765/r.git` was still running when the 25 s watchdog killed it (rc 124, reproduced twice). With `-c http.lowSpeedLimit=1000 -c http.lowSpeedTime=5` it failed after 5 s with 'Operation too slow'.
findings.mitigation: Every network git call gets `-c http.lowSpeedLimit=1000 -c http.lowSpeedTime=10`. For SSH: `GIT_SSH_COMMAND='ssh -o BatchMode=yes -o ConnectTimeout=10 -o ServerAliveInterval=5 -o ServerAliveCountMax=3'`. Add a hard watchdog of 45 s that kills the process tree. Watchdogs apply only to network commands, never to local mutating plumbing (`read-tree -u`). Expose 'seconds since last successful fetch' in every PreToolUse answer. Above 30 s, edits on symbols that anyone else claimed at last fetch are denied, other edits are allowed with an 'OFFLINE: uncoordinated' note, and /cowork status shows it.
findings.test: Point the daemon's remote at the black-hole server. Assert the loop recovers within 60 s, that the status shows OFFLINE after 30 s, and that a PreToolUse for a symbol claimed by a peer at last fetch is denied while offline.

findings.title: Sleep, hibernate and offline periods leave stale claims for others and false claim ownership for the sleeper; the lease TTL competes with the 6-pushes/min budget
findings.scenario: 1) A holds claims on foo() and closes the lid for 3 h. Peers stay blocked on foo() until a lease expires. With a 6 pushes/min team budget, 30 s heartbeats for 4 peers would need 8 pushes/min, so the TTL must be long, which makes stale holds long. 2) If expiry is computed from wall-clock timestamps written by other PCs, clock skew (a laptop 10 min fast) expires claims early or never. 3) On Linux and macOS the monotonic clock does not advance during suspend, so A's own lease timer still thinks A holds foo(). Meanwhile 영희 took foo() after expiry. A's Claude resumes mid-task and keeps editing foo(). 4) If A was offline and kept working, its claims were never published, so on reconnect it is the 'later' claimant for every overlap. merge-tree conflicts, and the design does not say where A's conflicting version goes; read-tree cannot apply a conflicted tree, so sync for those files stalls.
findings.consequence: Hours-long stale holds block teammates. A woken peer overwrites a symbol it no longer owns. Offline work is either silently lost or stalls sync (prior-art failure #7, 'sync halts silently on conflict').
findings.evidence_detail: Budget arithmetic from decision 3. Node's monotonic clock uses CLOCK_MONOTONIC on Linux and mach_absolute_time on macOS, neither of which counts suspend. Prior-art top-15 #7 and #9 (research/prior-art.md).
findings.mitigation: (1) Leases expire per observer: each daemon measures monotonic time since it last saw a renewal commit for that claim. Wall-clock fields in the board are display-only. (2) Renewals piggyback on any push. A dedicated renewal goes out at most every TTL/2, default TTL 10 min, about 0.8 pushes/min for 4 peers. (3) Wake detection: wall-clock delta exceeds monotonic delta by more than 60 s, or no successful fetch for more than TTL. On wake, the daemon marks all its own claims SUSPECT, and PreToolUse on those symbols waits up to 5 s for a fresh fetch before deciding. A claim lost to someone else results in a deny plus a note. (4) On reconnect with conflicts, the daemon never stalls: the causer's conflicting version is committed to refs/cowork/<b>/parked/<peerId>/<n>, the winner's version is applied, and both Claudes are told. The parked patch becomes a queued request to the holder (decision 7).
findings.test: Suspend the daemon process (SIGSTOP, or NtSuspendProcess on Windows) beyond the TTL while a peer claims the same symbol. On resume, the sleeper's Edit is denied. Inject ±10 min wall-clock skew and assert no claim is taken over before TTL of observed silence. Run an offline-conflict scenario and assert no conflict markers on any disk, the parked ref holds the causer's text, and sync of other files continues.

findings.title: An MCP server crash silently disables claims and fences for the rest of the session; a fence whose PostToolUse never arrives freezes a file
findings.scenario: 1) The per-session MCP server crashes (OOM, a plugin update or /reload-plugins, a bug) while claude keeps running. mcp_tool hooks fail open on disconnect, so every Edit proceeds with no claim check and no fence, while the daemon keeps applying peer changes into the same files.
