A daemon write between the Edit tool's read and write is overwritten by the Edit, and the next snapshot pushes the revert of the peer's change. 2) Conversely, PreToolUse sets 'don't write X', then Claude is killed or the tool fails, so PostToolUse never comes. The file is never updated again and diverges silently. Only PostToolUseFailure or a disconnect could release it, and the design does not mention either.
findings.consequence: A lost update that nobody notices because the guard looks installed, or one file permanently frozen out of sync on one PC.
findings.evidence_detail: mcp_tool hooks give a non-blocking error (fail open) when the server is not connected or returns isError, per https://code.claude.com/docs/en/hooks as summarized in research/runtime-dist.md §3. PostToolUseFailure is a separate event (research/plugin-hooks.md event table). The lost-update interleaving is REASONED.
findings.mitigation: (1) The SessionStart command hook registers {session_id, claude PID, MCP connection id, CLAUDE_CODE_MESSAGING_SOCKET and token} with the daemon. (2) Each MCP server holds one persistent IPC connection; a disconnect while the claude PID is alive marks the session UNGUARDED. (3) Apply gate: the daemon does not write files that an UNGUARDED session edited in the last 10 min, holding those incoming changes, and delivers 'cowork guard down: run /mcp reconnect' through that session's inbox socket. (4) Fences are leases: released on PostToolUse, on PostToolUseFailure, on IPC disconnect, or after 60 s max. (5) The MCP server never returns isError; when the daemon is unreachable it respawns it and answers allow with an explicit warning.
findings.test: Kill the MCP process mid-session while a peer streams edits to the same file. Assert the daemon stops writing that file within one poll and the session receives the inbox alert. Fire PreToolUse without PostToolUse and assert the fence is released within 60 s or immediately on PostToolUseFailure.

findings.title: Peers on different plugin versions drop each other's board fields, map edits to different symbols, and older daemons lack newer safety guards
findings.scenario: 1) v0.2 adds a claim field, such as symbol kind or a range. A v0.1 peer read-modify-writes the board JSON and drops the unknown fields, so v0.2 claims silently lose their scope. 2) The two versions bundle different tree-sitter grammar versions, so the same edit maps to `Foo.bar` on one PC and `<toplevel after=Foo>` on another. Claims don't match, nothing is denied, and both edit. 3) v0.1 has no epoch guard. One teammate who hasn't updated can still run the branch-switch and stash scenarios against everyone, and newer peers cannot stop it.
findings.consequence: Claims vanish or stop overlapping without any error. The team's protection is only as strong as its oldest install.
findings.evidence_detail: Prior-art top-15 #15: mixed versions revert newer work (ruflo#3005, OBSERVED in research/prior-art.md).
findings.mitigation: (1) The board is a tree of per-peer files (board/peers/<peerId>/claims.json and so on). Each daemon writes only its own subtree, so merges are trivial and nobody rewrites another peer's data. Unknown JSON fields are preserved on any read-modify-write. (2) board/protocol.json holds {min, current}. From the very first release, every daemon reads it before every push and goes read-only with an alert if it is below min. (3) Every live commit carries a `Cowork-Version:` trailer. Newer daemons quarantine (do not apply) commits from peers below min and announce it. (4) Claims carry (path, base blob oid, byte range) as well as the symbol name, and overlap checks fall back to range intersection when the names come from different mapper versions.
findings.test: Run a mixed-version harness: board round-trips through the old version keep the new fields byte-identical. Raise min, and the old daemon stops pushing within one cycle. Map the same edit with two grammar versions that name the symbol differently, and assert a deny still happens via range overlap.

findings.title: Uninstalling or disabling the plugin mid-session deletes CLAUDE_PLUGIN_DATA while the detached daemon keeps running, unguarded or re-initialising
findings.scenario: 1) The user runs `/plugin uninstall cowork-sync`, removing it from its last scope. Claude Code deletes ~/.claude/plugins/data/<id>/, which holds the IPC token and any daemon state. 2) The detached daemon is still running. Hooks are gone or failing, so Claude edits are unguarded while the daemon keeps syncing. 3) If the daemon re-reads 'last applied' from the deleted directory, it takes the fresh-join path with base = live tip and pushes a revert of all live work (the live-tip variant verified in late-join-wrong-merge-base). The daemon also never releases this user's claims, and nothing remains on the PC to run `/cowork stop`.
findings.consequence: A mass revert pushed to the team, or a zombie daemon holding claims and pushing an unguarded working tree indefinitely.
findings.evidence_detail: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/plugins/cli-reference ('plugin uninstall'): uninstalling from the last scope deletes the data directory unless --keep-data is passed. The consequence chain reuses the VERIFIED live-tip join revert.
findings.mitigation: (1) Correctness state lives in the repository: refs/worktree/cowork/<b>/{applied,base,pending,parked/*} plus `git rev-parse --git-path cowork/` for the journal. CLAUDE_PLUGIN_DATA holds only tokens and caches. (2) A running daemon keeps state in memory and never re-initialises; if persisted state disappears, it stops and alerts. (3) The daemon runs a graceful stop (flush, release claims, return queue items, mark offline) when its entry script path no longer exists, when no session or CLI lease has been attached for N minutes, or when `npx cowork-sync stop` asks. (4) At startup it refuses to run if the plugin is not enabled.
findings.test: Start live, run `claude plugin uninstall` in another shell, and assert within one cycle: no push containing reverts, the board shows this peer offline with no claims, and the daemon process has exited. Reinstall and start again, and assert recovery from the refs/worktree state with no revert.

findings.title: Disk full or a locked file during read-tree -u leaves truncated or partially applied files, which the next snapshot publishes as edits
findings.scenario: 1) While checking out an entry, git unlinks the old file and recreates it with O_CREAT|O_EXCL before writing. 2) The disk fills (the daemon's loose objects add about a 1.3 MB blob per snapshot of the big .py file), so the write stops partway. The 1.3 MB file is left empty or truncated, and `read-tree` reports an error after some other files were already written. On Windows, a file held open by Visual Studio or Excel makes the unlink fail with the same partial outcome. 3) The design's retry ('not uptodate', re-snapshot) snapshots the damaged working tree as the user's edit and pushes the truncation.
findings.consequence: The team's largest file is truncated on every PC. If object writes fail during `add -A`, the empty-oid push path can also delete the live ref.
findings.evidence_detail: git entry.c: checkout_entry with force unlinks the old path, then write_entry/create_file opens with O_EXCL and writes, so the replacement is not atomic. research/git-transport.md §8 lists the Windows-lock partial apply as UNK. The empty-oid deletion is VERIFIED separately.
findings.mitigation: (1) Before applying, require free space of at least 2× the sum of the blob sizes being written plus 256 MB; otherwise defer and alert. (2) Any non-zero exit from `read-tree -u` puts the daemon in WORKTREE-SUSPECT. It re-hashes each target path with `git hash-object --path` against the intended merged tree and re-applies or restores from objects until every path matches the target or its pre-apply blob. No snapshot runs while SUSPECT. (3) Outgoing guard: a file that drops to 0 bytes or loses more than 50% of its lines without a local Claude tool event is held for confirmation, using the peer-revert guard path.
findings.test: On Linux CI, use a size-limited tmpfs or loop mount and fill it mid-apply. On Windows, hold f.py with FileShare.None from a PowerShell process during the apply. Assert that no pushed tree ever contains a truncated version, and that the daemon converges after space is freed or the lock is released.

findings.title: Daemon-only objects (pending local snapshot, base after a save reset, parked work) are pruned by `git gc`
findings.scenario: B works offline. Its pending snapshot commit is referenced only by the daemon's state file. B (or an IDE) runs `git gc --prune=now`, or B is away longer than gc.pruneExpire (2 weeks by default) while auto-gc runs. The pending commit, or the applied base that is unreachable after a save re-parent, disappears. The next merge fails with 'bad object', and a naive daemon falls back to the fresh-join path.
findings.consequence: Unpublished offline work is lost, or the fallback re-init reverts the team (late-join-wrong-merge-base).
findings.evidence_detail: Harness: the pending commit 97399c7… existed (`cat-file -t` gave commit). After `git gc -q --prune=now`, `cat-file` failed with 'could not get object info'. The gc.pruneExpire default of 2.weeks.ago is DOCUMENTED at https://git-scm.com/docs/git-gc.
findings.mitigation: Every object the daemon depends on is reachable from a per-worktree ref: refs/worktree/cowork/<b>/{applied,base,pending,parked/*,journal}. These are invisible to other worktrees (VERIFIED) and retained by gc, which scans all worktrees' refs. A missing object means STOP and alert, never re-init. Daemon fetches pass `--no-auto-gc` (or `-c gc.auto=0 -c maintenance.auto=false`), so the daemon never triggers gc in the user's repo mid-operation.
findings.test: Create offline pending work, run `git gc --prune=now` and `git maintenance run --task=gc`, reconnect, and assert the pending work is pushed intact with no revert.

findings.title: /clear starts a new session_id in the same process, so the old conversation's claims, fences and requests stay held while the new context has no idea it owns them
findings.scenario: 1) Claude holds claims on foo() and bar(), and 영희's handoff request for foo() is queued for it. 2) The user types /clear. Claude Code starts a new session id, but the MCP server process and its stdin stay open, so the design's 'release on stdin EOF' never fires. 3) The fresh context does not know it holds foo() and bar(). Peers stay blocked, and '영희 requests foo(); handle it?' is asked to a Claude with no memory of the work. With /compact the id is kept, but the summary may drop the claims. With `--resume` after a crash, the new MCP process must re-attach the old claims within the grace period or the resumed Claude is denied on its own work.
findings.consequence: Symbols stay blocked until the user quits Claude Code, and the handoff and ask flow (requirements 7 and 8) talks to an agent with no context about the work.
findings.evidence_detail: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/checkpointing: after /clear, the rewind menu offers '/resume <session-id> (previous session)', so /clear creates a new session id within the same process. SessionStart source values startup|resume|clear|compact|fork are in research/plugin-hooks.md and the hooks doc.
findings.mitigation: On SessionStart with source=clear, compact or resume, the daemon re-keys the previous session's claims, fences and inbound requests to the new session_id. It matches them by MCP connection, or by transcript directory on resume. It injects additionalContext listing them: 'You hold claims on foo(), bar() from before /clear; pending request from 영희 for foo(). Keep or release?'. Claims with no edits in the last 10 min are released automatically on clear. On resume, claims are held for a 5 min grace period keyed by (peerId, transcript path).
findings.test: Hook harness: claim, then simulate SessionStart(source=clear) with a new id. Assert claims are re-keyed and the context lists them. Claim, then kill claude and resume within grace, and assert no self-deny. Resume after grace, and assert claims were released and the board shows it.

findings.title: Two clones, linked worktrees, path spelling and nested .claude/worktrees break daemon identity and publish a bogus gitlink
findings.scenario: 1) If the daemon is keyed by remote URL, a second clone on the same PC attaches to the first clone's daemon, so its edits never sync and its fences block the wrong tree. 2) If it is keyed by a path string, `C:\Users\x\repo` and `c:/users/x/repo` start two daemons on one worktree, which race snapshots and applies. 3) Claims compared by user name let the same person's two clones edit the same symbol with no deny. 4) Shared refs such as refs/cowork-local/<b>/* or a hard-coded <top>/.git/... path collide across linked worktrees. 5) Claude Code's isolation worktree at .claude/worktrees/agent1 inside the repo is snapshotted by `add -A` as a 160000 gitlink and pushed. Peers get an empty directory, and a later save commits a dangling submodule. Subagent edits inside it are neither synced nor correctly claimed.
findings.consequence: Missed sync and claims, racing daemons on one tree, and a bogus submodule entry that can break clones and CI after save.
findings.evidence_detail: Harness: `git worktree add .claude/worktrees/agent1` inside A, then a cycle. The live tree contained `160000 commit 2a0e7b0… .claude/worktrees/agent1` and B got an empty agent1/ directory. In linked worktree A2, `--git-path cowork` resolved to A/.git/worktrees/A2/cowork, refs/worktree/cowork/applied set in A was invisible from A2, and refs/cowork-local/main/applied was visible from both.
findings.mitigation: (1) Use a single-instance lock file at `git rev-parse --git-path cowork/daemon.lock`. It is per worktree and independent of path spelling, and it is in addition to the pipe name. (2) Keep all per-worktree state in refs/worktree/cowork/* and in `--git-path` directories. (3) Peer identity is a random peerId stored per worktree; claims compare (peerId, session_id, agent_id), and the user name is display-only. (4) The snapshot excludes any directory containing a .git file or directory (no new gitlinks unless they are in the base) and always excludes .claude/worktrees/. (5) Resolve each Edit target to the worktree that contains the path, not the session cwd. Targets in a non-live worktree get a note, not a claim.
findings.test: Run two clones and two linked worktrees on one machine plus mixed-case path spellings. Assert exactly one daemon per worktree, cross-clone denies on the same symbol, no 160000 entries appearing in live, and no state shared between worktrees.

findings.title: '/cowork stop' has no defined effect on in-flight changes, claims, queues or the shared working tree
findings.scenario: 1) A runs /cowork stop while a debounced snapshot is waiting for the push governor. If stop just kills the daemon, A's last edits never reach peers, and nobody is told. 2) A's claims and fences are not released, and requests in A's queue are neither answered nor returned. 3) A's working tree still contains 영희's and 철수's unsaved live work. A later runs `git commit -am` and pushes, publishing their half-finished code under A's name, or runs `git stash`. When A starts again, that becomes the stash revert in worktree-reset-commands-broadcast-revert.
findings.consequence: Silently unpublished work, stuck claims, requests that vanish (contradicting 'nothing is ever lost'), and teammates' half-finished code committed by someone else.
findings.evidence_detail: Decisions 7, 10 and 11 define start, save and the queue but not stop. `git status` on a peer lists teammates' synced edits as its own modifications (VERIFIED in the head-drift run: A showed ` M f.py ` for B-side changes).
findings.mitigation: Stop runs as a state machine. (1) Freeze: no new claims. (2) Flush: a final snapshot and push, bypassing debounce but still CAS-leased, for up to 30 s. On failure, record 'unpublished since L_x' and print it. (3) Release claims and fences. Inbound queue items return to their requesters with reason 'holder left'; the user's own outbound requests stay, marked 'requester offline'. (4) Mark the peer offline in the same atomic push. (5) Leave the working tree intact, but print the files that contain other peers' unsaved work. `stop --park` commits the full live diff to refs/worktree/cowork/<b>/parked-at-stop and restores HEAD state. The next start goes through the join protocol with base = last applied, only if the epoch is unchanged.
findings.test: Stop during a pending debounce and assert the edit reaches peers or is reported as unpublished. Assert claims and queue items move as specified on the board. Stop, then run `git stash` and start, and assert the epoch guard quarantines it with nothing reverted on peers.

design_changes: Decision 4 ('never touch the user's index or HEAD') needs one guarded exception, ADOPT. After a save or base move, each daemon CAS-updates refs/heads/<b> from the old base to the new one and rewrites the user's index from the new base tree, holding .git/index.lock. It does this only when HEAD is on that branch at the old base and nothing is staged. Without this, every peer's `git pull` is refused after the first save or pull (VERIFIED), and git's own advice ('stash them') leads into the team-wide revert (VERIFIED).

'save' must not 'reset the live ref onto that commit'. It must re-parent the CURRENT live tip onto the saved commit: new live = commit(tree = merge-tree(base Lsaved, S, Lcur)) with parent S, leased on Lcur. The branch is leased on a freshly fetched tip and merged if it moved. Branch and live are pushed atomically, or ordered with a `Cowork-Live:` trailer for crash completion. The naive reset deleted concurrent edits from every disk (VERIFIED); re-parent preserved them (VERIFIED).

Replace the pause list (index.lock, MERGE_HEAD, REBASE_HEAD) with a git-epoch guard and QUARANTINE state. Inputs: HEAD symbolic-ref and oid, refs/stash, reflog size, the full marker set (CHERRY_PICK_HEAD, REVERT_HEAD, AUTO_MERGE, rebase-merge/, rebase-apply/, sequencer/, BISECT_START), unmerged index entries and detached HEAD. A changed epoch makes the snapshot non-pushable, rather than merely pausing and later resuming on the changed tree.

Add an outgoing peer-revert guard in the daemon. Human edits, git working-tree commands, /rewind and stale editor buffers never pass through PreToolUse claims, so any outgoing hunk that removes or changes a region authored by another peer since the last save is held for explicit local confirmation instead of being pushed.

Store daemon correctness state (applied, base, pending, parked, apply journal) in per-worktree git refs (refs/worktree/cowork/*) and `git rev-parse --git-path cowork/`, not in CLAUDE_PLUGIN_DATA. Uninstall deletes that directory (DOCUMENTED), and gc prunes unreferenced objects (VERIFIED).

Define a join protocol and a stop protocol as part of v1. Join: base = joiner's own HEAD, HEAD must be at or behind the live base, and pre-join WIP and untracked files are parked rather than published. Stop: flush, release, return queue items, mark offline, and park on request.

Ship the board as per-peer files plus a protocol.json min-version kill switch that every daemon checks before every push, starting with the very first release. Otherwise one outdated install can disable the team's guards.
open_questions: Should the daemon run, and sync human edits, when no Claude session is open, for example after a reboot before Claude is started? If yes, who starts it (login item, or the first `git` use)? If no, edits made before then sync late, and peers see stale claims until the lease expires.

When a human runs `git commit` (and maybe push) directly while live, should cowork forbid it (Bash deny plus an opt-in pre-commit hook) or adopt it as a save, moving the base for everyone? Today it sweeps teammates' unsaved work into one person's commit.

Is the team willing to accept the ADOPT step (cowork moves the local branch ref and index after save or pull under strict conditions), relaxing decision 4? The alternative is that every peer must run a cowork command after each save.
What should `stop` do to teammates' unsaved work still in the local working tree: keep it (default) or park it and restore HEAD?
Is switching branches while live forbidden (Bash deny plus DETACHED state) or supported as an automatic stop-and-park?
What lease TTL is acceptable? With a 6 pushes/min team budget, a crashed or sleeping peer's claims can block others for up to about 10 min unless the budget is raised.
Can /rewind 'Restore code' be intercepted by any hook? If not, the peer-revert guard (ask before publishing) is the only protection, and users must be told about it.

findings.title: 'Commit local changes on top' after a partial apply reverts teammates' work, and seeding the snapshot from the tip deletes their files
findings.scenario: 1) A pushes C1, which changes x.py:f. 2) B has its own edit in y.py. x.py cannot be applied on B: it is fenced (B's Claude is between PreToolUse and PostToolUse), or read-tree -m -u fails with 'not uptodate' because a human's editor autosaves the 1.3 MB file, or a Windows lock blocks the write. 3) B's daemon skips that apply, sets L:=C1, then does what decision 2 literally says: it snapshots W and commits it with parent C1. Variant: the temp index is seeded from the fetched tip instead of the applied tree, so every file the tip has and W lacks is recorded as a deletion.
findings.consequence: The pushed commit puts B's stale x.py back, and in the variant it deletes A's new files. Every peer applies that commit. A's work disappears from every working tree with no conflict and no warning. Two secondary problems: read-tree -u is all-or-nothing, so one hot file blocks every incoming change for that peer forever (it never converges). And a fence that leaks blocks that file forever, because PostToolUse fires only when the tool succeeds.
findings.evidence_detail: sweep/protocol/e1 (helpers in sweep/protocol/common.sh; file:// bare remote with clones A and B). The naive `commit-tree $SNAP -p $R`, then `git diff R C2`, showed x.py '-    return 100 / +    return 1' although B edited only y.py. `merge-tree --write-tree --merge-base=$L0 $SNAP $R` produced a diff touching only y.py. Variant: in the first run of e6, 4 concurrent peers seeded their snapshots from the tip without applying it, and the final tip tree kept only own_C.txt. own_A, own_B and own_D were deleted.
findings.mitigation: INV-BASE plus INV-DELTA. (1) A is a per-path base. After an apply, A[p]:=tip[p] only for paths actually written; fenced, failed or hot paths keep their old A[p]. (2) Seed the temp index from A, never from the fetched tip. (3) The pushed tree is always `merge-tree --write-tree --merge-base=<A> <snap(W)> <tip>`, never a snapshot committed on top of the tip. (4) Before every push, assert that every path with snap[p]==A[p] has C[p]==tip[p]. If not, abort the push and raise a doctor alert. (5) Apply in per-path groups. On 'not uptodate' for path p, drop p from this apply, keep A[p], and apply the rest. Retry p once its (size, mtime) has been stable for 2 or more polls. (6) Release a fence on PostToolUse, on PostToolUseFailure, when the MCP server's stdin closes, and after a hard timeout (e.g. 120 s). A held fence only excludes that path from the apply.
findings.test: Use the INV-NOLOSS property harness (see design_changes). 4-6 simulated peers share a file:// remote and run random interleavings of {edit carrying a unique marker string, fetch, push-ok, push-reject, push-ambiguous, apply-partial (fence or not-uptodate), stash, external commit to main, save/reset}. After every push, assert that the pushed diff touches only paths in diff(A, snap). Also assert that no marker ever leaves the tip unless a peer whose A contained it removed it, and that a removed marker is in the queue if it was withdrawn. Keep e1 as a deterministic regression test.

findings.title: A 'save' that commits the live tree on top of the branch reverts commits that reached the branch outside cowork
findings.scenario: 1) The live chain is based on branch commit B0. 2) A PR merge, a CI bot or a teammate not using cowork pushes B1 (adds hotfix.py) to main. 3) Someone runs /cowork save, which commits tree(live tip) with parent origin/main. Variants: (b) after the first save the board still records B0 as the chain base. A change saved in S1 and later undone in the chain then comes back on the next save, from the 'theirs' side. (c) Two peers save at once, and the loser re-pushes its stale save. (d) The reset commit uses the saved snapshot tree, which drops live commits that landed while the save ran.
findings.consequence: The save commit deletes hotfix.py on main. That is a silent revert of reviewed work on the real branch, and everyone who pulls gets it. Live peers also never receive B1's changes.
findings.evidence_detail: sweep/protocol/e9: the naive save diffed against main showed 'hotfix.py | 1 -' on top of the intended x.py change. `merge-tree --write-tree --merge-base=B0 <live tip> origin/main` changed only x.py.
findings.mitigation: Save = merge3(base = chain_base recorded on the board, ours = live tip, theirs = current branch head). Commit it with parent = branch head and push it fast-forward only, never forced. The reset commit's tree = the saved tree merged with any live commits that landed since the save point; its parent is the save commit, and it is CAS'd on the live tip it merged. The same atomic board commit sets chain_base := save commit. If the branch push is rejected as non-fast-forward, refetch and recompute; never re-push a stale save. Peers' own merges are unaffected because they use an explicit A (finding explicit-base-not-ancestry), and B1 reaches them through the reset commit.
findings.test: Keep e9 as a regression test. Add 'external commit to main' and 'two concurrent saves' to the INV-NOLOSS harness. After every save, assert that the branch head contains every external commit's change and every live hunk present at the save point, and that a second save after an undo-in-chain does not resurrect the undone hunk.

findings.title: A stale base after a push that timed out but landed, or after a crash between read-tree -u and persisting the base, undoes an undo
findings.scenario: (a) B pushes C (tree = L0+Δ). The response is lost or times out, so the daemon records a failure and keeps base L0. The user or Claude then removes Δ. Next round: base L0, ours = L0 content, theirs = tip C, so Δ is put back. (b) B applies A's R1 (adds a debug line) with read-tree -u and crashes before persisting base:=R1. A then reverts the debug line (R2). B restarts with base L0: ours has the line and theirs does not, so B pushes the line again.
findings.consequence: Undo and revert operations are silently reversed. The user's deletion reappears in their own file, or a teammate's revert is re-pushed to every peer. Both cases were reproduced.
findings.evidence_detail: sweep/protocol/e3: with stale base L0 the merged file was back to '    return 2  # DELTA by B'. Using `git merge-base --is-ancestor C tip` and then base:=tree(C), the undo survived. sweep/protocol/e3b: after the restart with base L0, the diff B would push re-added '# A temp debug'.
findings.mitigation: INV-BASE plus INV-OPID. (1) Treat every push without an explicit server ok or reject as UNKNOWN. Fetch; if `merge-base --is-ancestor <C> <tip>`, set A:=tree(C) and mark C's board ops as applied, otherwise handle it as rejected. (2) Keep a write-ahead apply journal {A, snap S, merged M, tip T, paths}, fsynced before read-tree -u. The A ref (refs/cowork-local/<branch>/applied, per worktree) is updated after the write. (3) On startup with a journal present, decide per path p: if clean(W[p])==M[p], set A[p]:=T[p]; if it equals S[p], leave A[p] unchanged; otherwise quarantine p and let a human decide. (4) Because A is a ref, `git gc --auto` cannot prune it. If A is missing anyway, refuse to auto-merge and enter rejoin mode, which shows the delta against HEAD and asks.
findings.test: Fault injection: kill the daemon at every step boundary (after snapshot, after merge, during read-tree, after read-tree but before updating A, after sending a push but before its response), and drop push responses. The INV-NOLOSS harness must pass. Keep e3 and e3b as regressions.

findings.title: A human's (or Claude's) git stash, restore, checkout or reset is synced to everyone as a revert
findings.scenario: 1) B's working tree contains A's synced work. B's HEAD is still B0, so git status shows that work as modified. 2) The human tidies up with `git stash`, `git restore .`, `git checkout -- .` or `reset --hard`, or switches branch. Claude can do the same through Bash. 3) index.lock exists for only milliseconds, and MERGE_HEAD or REBASE_HEAD never appear, so the pause rule does not trigger. 4) The daemon's next snapshot sees every synced path changed back to HEAD.
findings.consequence: Under the correct delta rule this looks like a legitimate local change. B's daemon pushes a revert of everyone's unsaved work to the live ref, and every peer's working tree loses it. A branch switch pushes the other branch's content into this branch's live ref.
findings.evidence_detail: sweep/protocol/e10: after `git stash` in B, the delta-only push diff was '-    return 100  # A work / +    return 1'. stash does not move HEAD and restore leaves no reflog entry, so watching HEAD alone misses both.
findings.mitigation: (1) Run a revert-to-HEAD detector before every push. If the new W[p] equals HEAD:p or index:p while A[p]≠HEAD:p, and no edit event touched p (PostToolUse, or a file-watcher write attributed to an editor), hold the delta and surface it in /cowork status instead of pushing. (2) Freeze sync when HEAD's symref or oid changes, or when refs/stash changes. (3) Add a mass-change breaker: hold deltas that have no edit events and touch more than N files, delete files, or change more than X% of a file. (4) While live, PreToolUse(Bash and PowerShell) denies stash, restore, checkout --, reset --hard, clean, and switching branch, with a note explaining why.
findings.test: Run each of stash, restore ., checkout -- ., reset --hard and switch while sync is running. Assert that no push carries their effect and that status shows the hold. Add a 'stash' action to the INV-NOLOSS harness.

findings.title: With code and board in two refs and no real atomic CAS, code lands in a region someone else holds
findings.scenario: The host lacks --atomic (Azure, according to a Q&A answer), or the implementation falls back to two sequential pushes or forgets --atomic. 1) C publishes a claim on x.py:f, so the board ref moves. 2) B, unaware, edits f and pushes code and board with a lease on each. 3) B's board lease is stale; its code lease is still valid.
findings.consequence: The code ref takes B's edit to f and the board push is rejected. The shared tree now holds a change to f by B while the board says C owns f and has no record of B. Nobody can attribute the change, and C's next merge conflicts with an edit the claim system says cannot exist. Even on hosts with atomic pushes, a board-only push cannot assert that the code ref is unchanged, because git cannot CAS a ref without updating it. Claim/code consistency therefore holds only if every code push also carries a board commit.
findings.evidence_detail: sweep/protocol/e4. Without --atomic: the code ref was accepted ('6415666..32521fc') and the board was '[rejected] (stale info)'. The remote code then matched B's edit while the board read 'C claims x.py:f'. With --atomic: 'atomic push failed', both refs rejected and the code ref stayed at L0. The board rejection was made client-side against the ref advertisement, and the client still sent the code update.
findings.mitigation: INV-FENCE. Every code push is one atomic update of {code commit, board commit whose parent is the board tip the delta's claims were validated against}. At /cowork start, read atomic support from the receive-pack capability advertisement (e.g. `GIT_TRACE_PACKET=1 git push --dry-run`); never infer it from a push that succeeded. If 'atomic' is not advertised, use SINGLE-REF mode: the board lives as a reserved '.cowork/' subtree inside the live commit and is stripped before merge, apply and save. Never fall back to two sequential pushes. Re-probe on any 'does not support --atomic' error.
findings.test: Host-matrix integration test: a file:// remote with receive.advertiseAtomic=false must select single-ref mode. Race harness with one board-only pusher and one code pusher: for every (code, board) pair fetched in one advertisement, assert that each region changed in code since the last save is covered by an active claim of its author in that board commit.

findings.title: The loser of a claim race still lands its edit, because the text merge is clean
findings.scenario: 1) A and B both start editing f inside the propagation window, which is tens of seconds when the push budget is busy. 2) A's push (claim and code) lands first. 3) B's push is rejected, so B refetches and merges. A changed line 2 of f and B changed line 5, so merge-tree exits 0. 4) B's daemon pushes the merged tree.
findings.consequence: B is the 'conflict causer' under decision 6, but its hunk is already in the shared f, combined with A's related logic change and never reviewed. The handoff and queue flow never starts because nothing was blocked. If B's daemon withholds the hunk but leaves it in B's working tree, B diverges from the tip permanently and conflicts every round. The same gap opens whenever mcp_tool hooks fail open, the MCP server dies while the session lives (decision 10 releases claims on stdin close while edits continue), or a human edits.
findings.evidence_detail: sweep/protocol/e8: a 5-line f(x). The winner edited line 2 and the loser edited line 5; merge-tree exited 0 and the result contained both edits.
findings.mitigation: Apply INV-FENCE to the delta, not to tool calls. This pre-push check is the real safety boundary; the PreToolUse deny is only an early warning. Before every push, map the hunks of diff(A, snap(W)) to regions and check each against the board tip. If an earlier active claim by another holder covers a region, withdraw the hunk: (a) the push tree takes the tip's version of that region; (b) the hunk is stored as a handoff record (a patch against the winner's version, with an op-id) in the same atomic board commit; (c) once the file's fence is free, B's working-tree region is set to the tip's version and B's Claude gets the conflict notice. Hunks with no claim (a hook failed open, or a human edit) get an implicit claim at push time under the same rule. Hunks a human made (no PostToolUse attribution) should be held, not withdrawn; see open_questions.
findings.test: Two-peer race harness with injected delays on claim publication. Assert that the tip never contains a hunk in region ρ written by a peer that did not hold the earliest active claim on ρ in the board commit pushed with it. Assert that every withdrawn hunk is in the queue (INV-NOLOSS).

findings.title: A merge base computed from commit history after a save-reset brings deleted code back
findings.scenario: 1) Chain commit k: A adds Y_NEW. 2) B applies k, so B's base is k, and B starts an unrelated edit. 3) Chain commit k+1: C deletes Y_NEW. 4) C saves and resets the live ref onto the save commit, whose parent is the old branch commit B0. 5) B fetches the new tip X and merges with `git merge-tree --write-tree <B local commit> X` without --merge-base, or computes the base with `git merge-base`.
findings.consequence: Commit history gives B0 as the base, because the old chain is not an ancestor of X. Y_NEW then looks 'added by B, untouched by theirs', so it survives. B pushes it back, and C's deletion is silently undone for everyone. Any add-then-remove inside the chain comes back at every reset.
findings.evidence_detail: sweep/protocol/e2: confirmed merge-base(Cb, X)==B0. The history-based merge kept 'Y_NEW = 1  # added by A'. With `--merge-base=<tree(k)>` the line was dropped and B's unrelated edit (return 222) was kept.
findings.mitigation: INV-BASE. The merge base is always the explicit persisted tree A (`--merge-base=<A tree oid>`) and is never derived from the commit graph. The daemon must not use merge-base, ancestry walks, or merge-tree without --merge-base on cowork refs; enforce this with a lint. Reset commits carry a 'Cowork-Prev-Tip:' trailer for diagnostics only.
findings.test: Keep e2 as a regression test. Add a CI grep requiring every merge-tree call in the daemon to pass --merge-base. Include reset events in the INV-NOLOSS harness.

findings.title: CAS retry storms burn the 6/min budget, and the busiest or fastest peer starves the others
findings.scenario: 4 peers edit continuously and retry immediately on reject. After a reject a peer must refetch, apply, re-snapshot and retry. That loop is longer than the winner's, whose tip already equals its own commit and needs no apply, so the winner reaches the next race first.
findings.consequence: Many attempts are wasted. If GitHub counts rejected pushes, a large share of the 6/min team budget goes to rejects. The starved peer's latency grows without bound, and its claims, which are published only on push, stay unpublished, widening the race window in race-loser-hunk-lands. A peer whose local config sets a larger budget takes everyone else's share.
findings.evidence_detail: sweep/protocol/e6c: 4 background pushers on a file:// remote with a correct per-peer base. Result: A 5 attempts/0 rejects, B 20/15, C 15/10, D 10/5, so 50 attempts for 20 landed commits (2.5x), and all four converged (snap==tip). In all three runs the first-started peer had 0 rejects. That 'winner keeps winning' mechanism is REASONED: it was measured only on local file:// with no network latency.
findings.mitigation: Derive the governor from the observed chain, not from clocks or config. (1) The team budget B is a board field; each daemon uses min(local, board). (2) Each daemon counts the chain commits it observed in its own last 60 s (local monotonic time of observation) plus its own attempts, rejects included. (3) N_active = peers with a presence op on the board in the last 10 min. (4) Right of way: after observing a tip written by peer P, each later peer in ring order (sorted peer ids) gets a window W, e.g. 3 s measured from when it observed the tip. P may not push again until those windows pass or the chain moves. A rejected peer gets the next window. (5) After a reject, back off with full jitter in [0, observed gap between pushes], and count rejects against the peer's own share. (6) Priority: conflict and withdraw records first, then claim publications, then code-only pushes.
findings.test: Simulate 4-6 peers with injected network latency of 200-800 ms and different apply costs (one peer holds the 1.3 MB file). Under saturation assert attempts/landed ≤ 1.3, each peer's share of landed pushes within ±15% of 1/N, and a bounded claim-publication delay.

findings.title: Lease renewal by push breaks the budget, wall-clock TTLs break under clock skew, and suspended holders become zombies
findings.scenario: (a) A heartbeat every 30 s per peer means 8 board pushes/min for 4 peers, above the 6/min budget before any code moves. (b) A holder writes 'expires_at 12:05' by its own clock. An observer whose clock runs 5 min fast sees every lease as expired and takes them over; a slow observer never expires dead claims. (c) A holder's laptop sleeps for 1 h with claims held. Others expire them and edit f. On wake, the holder's monotonic clock has not advanced during suspend, so its local lease still looks valid. Its Claude resumes editing f and PreToolUse allows it.
findings.consequence: (a) Nothing is left in the budget for code. (b) Spurious takeovers produce conflict-causer verdicts against sessions that did nothing wrong, or claims never expire and block the team. (c) Two peers both believe they own f, and the zombie's edits merge into the new holder's work.
findings.evidence_detail: https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man2/clock_gettime.2.html says CLOCK_MONOTONIC 'does not count time that the system is suspended'; libuv's uv_hrtime uses CLOCK_MONOTONIC on Linux. The budget arithmetic comes from git-transport.md §3. The rest is REASONED.
findings.mitigation: INV-CLOCK. A lease = (holder peer, epoch, seq, ttl ≥ 10 min). No timestamp written by one machine is compared with another machine's clock. (1) Observer expiry: each observer starts its own monotonic timer when it first sees (holder, epoch, seq). (2) Takeover is a CAS'd board op that names that exact (holder, epoch, seq). If a renewal lands first, the takeover push fails and is re-evaluated. (3) The holder's own validity ends at its push-success time + ttl − margin, with margin ≥ poll interval + maximum push latency, so the holder always expires before any observer does. (4) Renewals ride on pushes that happen anyway. A dedicated renewal push is allowed only when less than 25% of the ttl remains and the session is active. (5) Gap detection: if the wall-clock delta exceeds the monotonic delta by more than 5 s, or the loop stalled for more than 3 polls, mark all own claims UNKNOWN and deny edits under them until a fresh board fetch revalidates them. (6) INV-FENCE makes a zombie's code push fail regardless.
findings.test: Deterministic simulator with per-peer wall clocks skewed up to ±10 min, a monotonic clock with a 1 h suspend gap, and network delays. Assert: (i) two peers never both hold ρ for longer than poll + push latency; (ii) the zombie's hunk in ρ is withdrawn, not pushed; (iii) renewals use at most 1 push per peer per 5 min.

findings.title: Claims on different symbols still give merge-tree conflicts, and the design has no conflict policy
findings.scenario: Both claims are valid, yet the second pusher's merge-tree exits 1. Cases: A edits the last line of f while B changes g's signature on the very next line; both add an import; or both append a different new function at end of file.
findings.consequence: Decision 2 says 'merge incoming into the local working tree' but not what to do on exit 1. An implementation will fall into one of three outcomes. It writes conflict markers, which sync to everyone and which a Claude will 'fix', possibly deleting the teammate's code. It halts sync, and the copies drift silently (prior-art #7). Or it prefers 'ours', which is a revert.
findings.evidence_detail: sweep/protocol/e7 and e7b. Clean: f's body and g's body separated by one unchanged line. CONFLICT (exit 1): the last line of f against the signature of g on the next line; both appending an import; both appending a different function at end of file.
findings.mitigation: Make the conflict policy deterministic and marker-free, a pure function of (base, ours, theirs, board tip). (1) Never write markers into the working tree or into a pushed tree. (2) Splice by region: parse the three versions and take each region from the side that changed it; with disjoint claims the splice is well defined. (3) For '<imports>' and for insertions at end of file or '<toplevel after=X>', use a union merge ordered by board position, theirs first. (4) If the splice fails, the tip's version stays in the shared tree and ours goes to the queue through the path in race-loser-hunk-lands, with a conflict event.
findings.test: Corpus test of the e7 cases plus generated adjacent-edit cases. Assert no '<<<<<<<' anywhere, both changes present in the import and append cases, and every hunk that cannot be spliced in the queue.

findings.title: The daemon's 2-3 s poll overwrites FETCH_HEAD and can make the user's git pull merge the live chain
findings.scenario: 1) The user runs `git pull`, which is a fetch of origin main followed by a merge of FETCH_HEAD. 2) Between those two steps, the daemon's poll fetch (explicit refspec, default flags) rewrites FETCH_HEAD to point at refs/cowork/main/code. 3) Separately, every poll fetch starts `git maintenance run --auto --detach`, which can repack while the user's own git commands run.
findings.consequence: The user's real branch fast-forwards onto the live WIP chain of unattributed snapshot commits instead of origin/main. The user's next normal push publishes it, and the upstream commit is never merged. Each pull has a small chance of hitting the race, but polling never stops.
findings.evidence_detail: sweep/protocol/e5: after `git fetch origin main`, FETCH_HEAD pointed at main. The daemon-style fetch rewrote it to ''refs/cowork/main/code'', and `git merge FETCH_HEAD` moved HEAD to 'live WIP'. GIT_TRACE showed 'run_command: git maintenance run --auto --quiet --detach' after the poll fetch. With -c maintenance.auto=false and --no-auto-maintenance, no maintenance ran.
findings.mitigation: Every daemon fetch runs as `git -c gc.auto=0 -c maintenance.auto=false fetch --no-write-fetch-head --no-auto-maintenance --no-tags origin +refs/cowork/<b>/*:refs/cowork-remote/<b>/*`. The daemon never writes refs/heads, refs/remotes, FETCH_HEAD or ORIG_HEAD, and sets GIT_OPTIONAL_LOCKS=0. /cowork doctor asserts that FETCH_HEAD's mtime does not change across 10 polls.
findings.test: Keep e5 as a regression test. Run the poll loop while a script repeatedly runs `git pull`, and assert that HEAD never reaches a refs/cowork commit.

findings.title: 'Byte-identical' convergence cannot be achieved as stated, and a path that does not round-trip livelocks the team
findings.scenario: On peer i, checking out the tip tree T and cleaning it again does not return T for some path p. Causes: a clean/smudge filter that is not idempotent (git-bash sed strips CR), a detached daemon environment missing a variable the filter needs, a filter driver configured on only one peer, a per-peer watcher that reformats files on change, or a different formatter version in a PostToolUse hook. Peer i snapshots a 'change' to p that it never made and pushes it. Peer j's own normalization flips p back, and the cycle repeats.
findings.consequence: The cycle never ends. Every round pushes p, using the whole team's budget; the 1.3 MB file is rewritten in every editor; Claude keeps getting 'file modified' notices. Under INV-DELTA these look like legitimate edits, so nothing flags them. Separately, byte-identical working trees across Windows (CRLF) and macOS (LF) are impossible, so a naive byte-equality check would never pass.
findings.evidence_detail: The round-trip requirement for filters is documented at https://git-scm.com/docs/gitattributes. CR stripping by git-bash sed was observed in git-transport.md §7. The cycle itself was not reproduced. e6c showed convergence (snap==tip on all 4 peers) when every path round-trips.
findings.mitigation: INV-CONVERGE defines convergence as equality of git tree OIDs of the normalized trees: snap_i(W_i) == A_i == tree(tip) for every peer i. Working-tree bytes may differ by each peer's checkout conversion. (1) At /cowork start, check out the tip into a temp directory using the daemon's own environment and config, snapshot it, and compare with the tip. On a mismatch, refuse to start or exclude the listed paths. (2) After every apply, re-snapshot the written paths and quarantine any that do not match. (3) Ping-pong breaker: if a path's blob alternates between two values written by different peers 3 or more times with no edit event, stop syncing that path and alert. (4) Each peer publishes a config fingerprint on the board (filter driver hash, autocrlf, eol attributes, git version).
findings.test: Give two peers deliberately different clean filters for one path. Assert the breaker trips within 3 cycles and pushes stop, and that the start-time round-trip check catches a filter that strips CR. Convergence test: random edits, then quiescence; assert every peer reports snap==A==tip within a bounded number of rounds.

findings.title: Board events keyed by commit position get duplicated or lost, and a board merged as text gives one symbol two holders
findings.scenario: (a) Each session's cursor is the last board commit OID it saw. A save-reset or a board compaction rewrites history, so the cursor is no longer an ancestor of the tip, and `git log cursor..tip` errors or returns everything. (b) After an ambiguous push, board ops that had already landed (claim f, event 'conflict #7') are retried by content. The claim is now duplicated; a later release removes only one copy, leaving a phantom claim forever. (c) Board files are merged with merge-tree, for example per-holder files claims/f@A.json and claims/f@B.json. They merge cleanly, leaving two active claims on f.
findings.consequence: Duplicated events make each Claude receive the same conflict warning again; it apologizes again, asks 'may I go first?' again, and creates duplicate handoffs. A skipped event means a warning is lost and the causer never learns. Phantom or double claims block edits wrongly or allow them wrongly.
findings.evidence_detail: Follows from git semantics: history rewrite plus OID-based cursors, and clean merges of distinct files. Prior art (agent_mail #274) shows the re-announcement problem in practice.
findings.mitigation: INV-OPID. (1) Every board op has an id (peer_id, epoch, seq). epoch is a random id created whenever the daemon's local state is (re)initialized, so a reinstall never reuses a seq. (2) Board state is a deterministic fold of the ops in board order; applying an op that is already folded does nothing. (3) After a CAS reject, pending ops are re-validated against the new tip, never merged as text; a claim that now loses becomes a 'lost' event. (4) Layout: one append-only file per peer, ops/<peer_id>/<epoch>.jsonl, written only by its owner, plus a state/ snapshot. (5) A session's cursor is a vector {peer_id/epoch → highest seq delivered}. It advances only on confirmed delivery; an inbox message without an ack is re-included in the next hook under the same short id (e.g. [cw#A3-17]), with a standing instruction to ignore ids already seen.
findings.test: Inject duplicate ops, retries after ambiguous pushes, and compaction and reset mid-stream. Assert that each session receives each op id addressed to it exactly once (no duplicates, no gaps), and that the folded state is identical on all peers for the same board tip.

findings.title: An offline peer keeps editing under stale claims, then reconnects into a mass conflict, or its old claims block others for hours
findings.scenario: 1) C's network drops (VPN, a flight) for 2 h. Its daemon cannot fetch, and PreToolUse keeps allowing edits based on the last board it saw. 2) C's Claude edits f, g and h, taking local claims that cannot be published. 3) Meanwhile A and B claim and edit g and h, and someone saves, which resets the live ref. 4) C's claims published before the drop stay on the board the whole time.
findings.consequence: On reconnect, every C claim loses to anything published meanwhile. If C's daemon pushes before evaluating, a large merged delta nobody reviewed lands. If it withdraws, 2 h of Claude work goes to the queue in one burst. Meanwhile C's pre-drop claims block A and B for the full TTL.
findings.evidence_detail: Follows from the optimistic claim rule (decision 6) and an unpublished local claim; offline behaviour is not covered by the approved design.
findings.mitigation: (1) Enter offline mode after K consecutive failed fetches or more than 30 s since the last successful fetch. PreToolUse still allows edits but adds additionalContext 'OFFLINE: edits are provisional and may be withdrawn', and claims taken offline are flagged provisional. (2) On reconnect, run a reconcile phase before any push. Fold the board and classify every delta hunk as clean, losing to an earlier claim, or a text conflict. Push only clean hunks automatically. If the lost hunks exceed a threshold (e.g. more than 3 regions or more than 200 lines), hold them and ask the user. (3) Other peers expire C's stale claims by the observer-local lease rule (lease-expiry-clocks-heartbeats), so the block lasts at most ttl + margin.
findings.test: Partition simulation: cut one peer off for N rounds while the others edit overlapping regions and save. On heal, assert that no auto-pushed hunk violates INV-FENCE, that every lost hunk is in the queue (INV-NOLOSS), and that others were blocked for at most ttl + margin.

findings.title: Taken literally, requirement 8 produces N-1 warnings written by Claudes, each costing a push and an idle-session wake
findings.scenario: 1) B becomes the conflict causer on f. 2) The daemons of A, C and D each detect it from the board and each wakes its Claude, which writes a warning to B: 3 board pushes. 3) B's Claude is woken 3 times and answers each, possibly asking 'may I go first?' three times. 4) C and D, with stale board views, may name different causers; for example C has not yet seen A's claim.
findings.consequence: One conflict costs 3-6 pushes from the budget and 3-6 extra paid turns. The inbox drops only identical repeats, so differently worded warnings all get through. Contradictory verdicts make the agents argue, and a busy hour can hit the 50-message inbox cap.
findings.evidence_detail: Inbox rate limits and the per-message usage cost come from realtime-push.md and the cross-session-messaging docs.
findings.mitigation: (1) Verdicts are a pure function of board order: the causer owns the later claim op in board order. They are computed only from a fetched board tip and keyed by conflict_id = H(winner op id, loser op id). (2) Exactly one active message per conflict goes to the causer. The causer's own daemon generates it as soon as a refetch or CAS reject reveals the earlier claim, which needs no propagation, and words it as coming from the holder. (3) The holder gets one notice, and only when a request needs its answer. (4) Other daemons add a passive line to their sessions' next hook context and never wake them. (5) 'May I go first?' is a board op addressed to one holder, with at most one open request per (conflict_id, requester). (6) Each session has a wake budget, e.g. at most 1 wake per 2 min, with events coalesced.
findings.test: Scenario test with 4 simulated sessions. One conflict must produce exactly 1 wake for the causer, at most 1 for the holder and 0 for the others, with at most 1 board push attributable to the conflict. With a stale view on C, no session may receive a verdict naming a different causer.

findings.title: Events can arrive before the code they describe
findings.scenario: 1) B fetches A's commit C (which changes f) together with the event 'A changed f, don't revert'. 2) The apply of f.py is blocked by a fence, by 'not uptodate', or because the file is busy, but the event is delivered at once. 3) B's Claude reads f.py, does not see the change, and concludes it is not there.
findings.consequence: Claude implements the change a second time, or re-edits code that then conflicts with A's change when the apply finally lands. Claude learns to trust neither the notices nor the files.
findings.evidence_detail: Follows from the event channel being separate from the per-path apply, which can be blocked (see naive-push-reverts-unapplied-paths).
findings.mitigation: INV-CAUSAL. Deliver an event that references code commit C only once A covers C on the referenced paths. Otherwise deliver it with an explicit marker ('not in your files yet; do not re-implement; wait') and re-deliver it under the same id once the code is applied. Claim and release events are delivered only after the board state containing them has been folded locally.
findings.test: Block the apply of one path while events are delivered. Assert that no event referencing that path arrives without the pending marker, and that the follow-up arrives after the apply.

findings.title: The board and the live chain grow without bound, and naive compaction races and loses queue items
findings.scenario: At about 6 commits/min the board gains about 8,600 commits in 24 h. If events are appended to one JSON blob, every push rewrites a file that grows with the whole history. A compaction (a new root commit) by one peer races with other peers' pending ops and with another peer compacting at the same time. OID-based cursors break (op-identity-cursors-board-merge). A compaction that drops events older than X also drops handoff-queue items still waiting for an answer. Without saves, the live chain gains thousands of snapshot commits of the 1.3 MB file per day.
findings.consequence: Push and fetch slow down over the day. In a double compaction, the loser loses its pending ops if it re-pushes them by content. A queue item compacted away breaks 'nothing is ever lost'. Force-push residue keeps growing on the host.
findings.evidence_detail: GitHub keeps data overwritten by force-pushes in cruft packs before deleting it (DOCUMENTED, git-transport.md §5). The commit rate is 6/min × 1440 min.
findings.mitigation: (1) Use the board layout from op-identity-cursors-board-merge: append-only per-peer op files plus a state snapshot. (2) Compaction is itself an op. Only the active peer with the lowest peer_id compacts, and only when ops since the last compaction exceed K (e.g. 2,000). It is a CAS'd commit that rewrites state/ and drops event ops older than a horizon H. Claims, leases and queue items are state and are never dropped. (3) A peer whose vector cursor predates the horizon gets one 'resync summary'. (4) Squash the live chain the same way when the team is idle (CAS). This is safe because merges use an explicit A.
findings.test: Run 50k random ops while two peers attempt to compact concurrently. Assert the folded state is the same before and after compaction, every unanswered queue item survives, and the board data written per push stays proportional to ops since the last compaction.

findings.title: Two daemons on one clone corrupt each other's temp index and bases
findings.scenario: Two Claude sessions start in the same clone at the same moment. Both SessionStart hooks find no daemon running and each spawns one; alternatively, an old-version daemon survives a plugin update. Both daemons use .git/cowork-index and refs/cowork-local/<branch>/applied.
findings.consequence: One daemon's read-tree reseeds the shared temp index while the other is running add -A and write-tree. The result is a snapshot of a half-seeded index: a pushed tree with missing files, which become deletions for everyone. With two different A values the bases go wrong (see the base findings above), and pushes and events are doubled.
findings.evidence_detail: Follows from two processes sharing one temp index file and one A ref with no lock between them.
findings.mitigation: (1) Allow one daemon per (clone gitdir, worktree). Creating the daemon's IPC endpoint is the lock: on Windows a named pipe with FILE_FLAG_FIRST_PIPE_INSTANCE (Node listen returns EADDRINUSE); on Unix an O_EXCL lock file plus a PID liveness check and a socket probe. Processes that lose this race connect as clients. (2) Include the daemon instance id in the temp index file name. (3) If the board's protocol version is newer than the daemon's own, the daemon goes read-only, and it exits when a newer local daemon takes over.
findings.test: Start 5 SessionStart hooks concurrently and assert exactly one daemon process. Kill it with SIGKILL, restart concurrently, and assert exactly one again. Version-skew test: the old daemon goes read-only.

design_changes: INV-LINEAR: the live ref advances only by a compare-and-swap (CAS) push from an OID the daemon observed. Every live commit has exactly one parent, the previous tip. The only exception is a reset commit, whose parent is the save commit and which carries a 'Cowork-Prev-Tip: <oid>' trailer for diagnostics. Reason: this gives one total order, which everything below depends on.

INV-BASE: each peer persists A, the per-path applied base, as a local ref (refs/cowork-local/<branch>/applied, per worktree). A[p] changes only after the working-tree write it describes, with a write-ahead journal for crash recovery. The merge base is always `--merge-base=<A>` and is never computed from commit ancestry. The temp index is seeded from A, never from the fetched tip. Reason: findings naive-push-reverts-unapplied-paths, explicit-base-not-ancestry and ambiguous-push-and-crash-stale-base (VERIFIED reverts and resurrections).

INV-DELTA: the pushed tree is merge-tree --write-tree --merge-base=A snap(W) tip, never 'snapshot on top of the tip'. Before every push, assert that every path with snap[p]==A[p] has C[p]==tip[p]; a violation aborts the push and raises a doctor alert. In words: a peer never pushes a change to a path it did not change locally.

INV-FENCE: a code commit may change region ρ only if it is pushed in the same atomic CAS as a board commit whose parent is the validated board tip and in which the pusher holds the earliest active claim on ρ. This is checked on the delta before the push, not only at PreToolUse, so it also covers hooks that fail open, a dead MCP server and human edits. Hunks that lose are withdrawn to the queue.

Fallback for hosts without atomic push: SINGLE-REF mode. The board is a reserved '.cowork/' subtree inside the live commit and is stripped before merge, apply and save. Never use sequential two-ref pushes. Atomic support is detected from the receive-pack capability advertisement at /cowork start. Reason: finding non-atomic-pair-and-fence (VERIFIED partial update). This hardens the approved fallback rather than replacing decision 2.

INV-OPID: the board is an op log, not text that git merges. Op ids are (peer_id, epoch, seq), with an append-only file per peer plus a state snapshot. State is a deterministic fold of the ops in board order, applying an op twice does nothing, and pending ops are re-validated after a CAS reject. A session's cursor is a vector {peer/epoch → seq}.

INV-CLOCK: no timestamp from one machine is ever compared with another machine's clock. Leases are (holder, epoch, seq, ttl ≥ 10 min). Each observer expires a lease by its own monotonic timer started when it first saw that seq. The holder's validity runs from its push success minus a margin, so the holder always expires first. A takeover is a CAS op naming the exact (holder, epoch, seq). After a detected suspend or stall, the holder revalidates against a fresh board before allowing edits. Renewals ride on pushes that happen anyway.

INV-CAUSAL: an event about code commit C is delivered only once A covers C on the referenced paths; otherwise it carries a 'not applied yet' marker and is re-delivered once applied. Conflict verdicts are a pure function of board order and keyed by conflict_id. Exactly one active message goes to the causer, generated by its own daemon. The holder is notified only for requests, and everyone else gets passive context without a wake.

INV-NOLOSS (acceptance gate): every hunk a peer produced is, at all times, either in the tip or in the handoff queue, unless a later commit by a peer whose A contained the hunk changed it. Build one property-test harness: N simulated peers on a file:// remote, a unique marker string per edit, and random interleavings of {edit, fetch, push-ok, push-reject, push-ambiguous (landed but reported failed), apply-partial (fence or not-uptodate), crash at each step, stash/restore, external commit to main, concurrent save/reset, partition}. This one test is the shared test for most findings above.

INV-CONVERGE (definition): convergence means equal git tree OIDs of the normalized trees, snap_i(W_i) == A_i == tree(tip) for every peer i. It does not mean byte-identical working trees, which legitimately differ by CRLF/LF and smudge output. Proof sketch: INV-LINEAR gives a total order. INV-DELTA means each successful push adds only that peer's local delta D_i, after which D_i is empty and A_i equals the pushed tree. After edits stop, each peer with a nonempty D_i lands it in one successful push (assumes bounded fairness). A peer with an empty D_i and A_i≠tip applies merge3(A,A,T)=T (assumes paths can eventually be applied) and re-snapshots to T (assumes round-trip). No delta is then left, so no further push happens, the tip is fixed and every peer equals it. Each assumption maps to a finding: bounded fairness to cas-storm-starvation-governor, eventual apply to naive-push-reverts-unapplied-paths (hot files and fence leaks), round-trip to phantom-delta-pingpong-convergence. Convergence is NOT correctness: without INV-DELTA and INV-BASE the peers still converge, but to a tree with a teammate's work reverted (e1). Correctness is INV-NOLOSS.

Save semantics: save = merge3(base = the board's chain_base, ours = live tip, theirs = current branch head), committed with the branch head as parent and pushed fast-forward only. The reset commit's tree includes any live commits that landed during the save, and the same atomic board commit sets chain_base := save commit. Reason: finding save-reverts-external-commits (VERIFIED revert of an external PR commit).

Push governor derived from the chain: the budget lives on the board (each daemon uses min(local, board)); N_active comes from presence ops on the board; rate is measured by counting observed chain commits on the observer's own monotonic clock; peers take turns by ring order of peer id after each observed tip; rejected attempts count against the peer's share; priority classes are conflict, then claim, then code. Reason: e6c measured 2.5x attempts per landed commit with one peer never rejected.

Daemon git hygiene: every fetch uses --no-write-fetch-head, --no-auto-maintenance, -c gc.auto=0 and -c maintenance.auto=false. The daemon never writes refs/heads, refs/remotes, FETCH_HEAD or ORIG_HEAD. One daemon per clone/worktree, with the IPC endpoint as the lock. A revert-to-HEAD and mass-change breaker runs before every push, and a PreToolUse(Bash) deny list covers stash, restore, checkout --, reset --hard, clean and branch switching while live. Reason: findings fetch-head-hijack-and-auto-maintenance and local-git-ops-propagate-as-reverts (VERIFIED).
open_questions: Does GitHub (and do GitLab, Bitbucket and Gitea) advertise the 'atomic' capability on receive-pack? git-transport.md lists this as unknown. If GitHub does not, single-ref mode becomes the main path rather than a fallback. Test: GIT_TRACE_PACKET=1 git push --dry-run against a throwaway repo.
Does a push that is rejected for a stale lease, where the client sends no pack, count toward GitHub's 6 pushes/min? This decides how expensive CAS retry storms are.

When a hunk that a human typed in an editor (with no PostToolUse attribution) loses a claim race, should it be held, meaning kept local, not pushed, and shown in status, or withdrawn? Withdrawing makes the editor's unsaved buffer fight the daemon. This is a user decision.

Requirement 8 says 'ALL other Claudes ... warn the causer's Claude'. Is one message, generated deterministically and attributed to the holder, plus passive awareness in every other session acceptable? Taken literally, the requirement costs N-1 pushes and N-1 paid wakes per conflict.

On Windows, does Node's monotonic clock (QueryPerformanceCounter through uv_hrtime) advance during sleep or hibernate? The wall-clock versus monotonic gap detector is specified either way, but the lease margins depend on the answer.

Does Claude Code's Edit/Write replace the file atomically (rename) or truncate and rewrite it in place? If in place, a snapshot can capture a half-written file. The fence would then also have to exclude the path from snapshots, and human-edited files would need a stability check before snapshot.
Is squashing the live chain while the team is idle acceptable, given that intermediate snapshots are then lost? Only 'save' commits are durable history.

findings.title: (f) A 'save' from a lagging working tree, followed by the live-ref reset, erases a teammate's in-progress work. A save from a current tree commits half-done code to the branch.
findings.scenario: VERIFIED. B edits gamma (half-done) and publishes L1. A runs /cowork save. A's fetch shows tip L1, but A's working tree has not applied L1 yet (poll lag or a 'not uptodate' retry). save commits A's snapshot S, whose tree is still L0, pushes it to master, then resets the live ref to S with --force-with-lease=live:L1, and the push is ACCEPTED. B's daemon merges with base=L1 and incoming=S, which reverts B's lines. Second case (REASONED): if A's tree is current, B's syntax-broken half-done function is committed and pushed to master under B's attribution without B's consent.
findings.consequence: In the first case, a teammate's in-progress work is lost silently: it disappears from B's own disk and master never had it. In the second, unreviewed broken code lands on the real branch, CI breaks, and B's name is on it.
findings.evidence_detail: Two clones over a file:// bare remote, git 2.55.0.windows.3, core.autocrlf=true. Script: <scratchpad>/sweep/social/harness_e5_e6.sh e6 printed 'lease on L1 accepted' and 'RESULT e6: B-HALF-DONE in B's own tree = 0', and master lacked the line. The half-done-commit case is REASONED.
findings.mitigation: Detector: the saver's daemon checks before it pushes. Rules: (1) The save tree is derived from tree(T), where T is the fetched live tip, never from the saver's working tree. Assert this before pushing; if it fails, abort with no push. (2) Exclude in-progress work by splicing those symbols back to their last-saved text in the commit tree S'. This covers symbols with an ACTIVE claim (edited in the last N minutes, or the holder is mid-turn) and any file that fails to parse. Exclusion is the default; the holder's human can use /cowork ready to include. (3) Never reset the live tree. The new live head is commit(tree=tree(T), parent=S'), pushed with --force-with-lease=live:T and atomically with the branch update where the host supports it. If the lease fails, restart from the new tip. Peers then see a live head with zero diff. (4) Canonical event: one 'save' event listing included and excluded symbols per author. Holders get it pull-only; nobody is woken. (5) A daemon treats an incoming live head whose tree equals its last-applied tree as a no-op rebase onto the new parent.
findings.test: Run harness_e5_e6.sh e6 with rules 1 and 3: assert grep -c B-HALF-DONE B/m.py == 1 after save, and live-head^{tree} == L1^{tree}. With B's claim ACTIVE: master's gamma equals the base text. Fault injection: save computes a tree different from the one derived from T -> the process exits non-zero and git ls-remote shows master and live unchanged.

findings.title: (b) Bypass paths (git checkout --/stash/restore, Bash scripts, an editor's stale-buffer 'Overwrite') silently erase a teammate's work from the teammate's own disk. Finished-but-unsaved work has no claim protecting it.
findings.scenario: VERIFIED. B edits beta and publishes L1. A's daemon applies it, and A's 'git status --porcelain' now shows ' M m.py', so the teammate's change looks like A's own modification. A's Claude tidies the 'unexpected change' with 'git checkout -- m.py'. A's next snapshot lacks B's line and is pushed as an ordinary change. B's daemon applies it, and B's own working tree loses the line. The same path exists for git stash/restore/reset --hard, 'python fix.py' through Bash, and VS Code 'file is newer -> Overwrite'. A foreign-held-symbol gate would catch this only while B's claim is ACTIVE. Once B has finished (claim released) and nothing has been saved yet, which can be hours because commits happen only at save, nothing catches it.
findings.consequence: Completed teammate work disappears across the whole team with no warning. B's Claude may later report work as done that no longer exists.
findings.evidence_detail: harness_e5_e6.sh e5 (same scratch folder) printed ' M m.py' in A's status and then 'RESULT e5: B-WORK in B's own tree = 0'. The finished-but-unsaved gap is REASONED from the claim-lifetime rules.
findings.mitigation: Detector: the pre-push gate of the PC whose local diff contains the change. Check (i): if changed lines fall inside a symbol held, ACTIVE or DORMANT, by someone else, quarantine the hunk: splice the published symbol text into the outgoing blob. Check (ii), a REVERT DETECTOR that runs whatever the claim state is: keep per-symbol content hashes for the live commits since the last save. If a local change makes a symbol equal an older version while the newer version came from a peer, or deletes lines a peer added since the save, classify it as 'revert-of-peer' and quarantine it. Attribution: if the file changed inside session S's PreToolUse..PostToolUse(Bash|PowerShell) window, or appears in bashEditDiff.changedFiles, it is S's Claude, which gets one inbox message mid-turn. If there was no tool window, it is the human, who gets an OS toast, the status line and next-prompt context. Never auto-revert human work: pin that symbol to the human's version locally until /cowork resolve. Canonical event id = sha1('revert'|symbolKey|peerVersionHash). The peer author gets a pull-only FYI. Prevention: while live, PreToolUse(Bash|PowerShell) denies git stash, checkout --/<path>, restore, reset --hard, clean, commit and add, with the reason 'teammates' synced changes are in your working tree; use /cowork save'. SessionStart (startup, compact and resume) states that modified files include teammates' work.
findings.test: Run harness_e5_e6.sh e5 with the gate: A's pushed tree still contains B-WORK and grep -c B-WORK B/m.py == 1. Repeat with B's claim released: still caught by the revert detector. Exactly one 'revert' event appears on the board. Hook unit test: tool_input.command='git checkout -- m.py' returns permissionDecision=deny.

findings.title: (a) Race-window overlap: the loser's edits leak into the winner's held function unless the integrating daemon gates its own push. Only that daemon should create the conflict event.
findings.scenario: With 6 pushes/min shared by 4 daemons, a claim can sit unpublished for up to ~40 s. 10:00:00 영희's Claude edits handle_upload; the claim is local only. 10:00:12 철수's Claude edits handle_upload; PreToolUse sees no published claim and allows it. 10:00:20 영희's daemon pushes code and claim and wins the CAS. By 10:00:45 철수's Claude has made 3 more edits. At 10:00:48 철수's daemon gets a CAS reject, refetches and runs merge-tree. The edits are on different lines of the function, so the merge is clean, and the design as written pushes 철수's code together with an overlapping claim.
findings.consequence: 영희's working tree receives foreign half-done logic inside a function she is still editing, so 'earlier claim wins' has no effect on code. Both claims sit on the board, every daemon can raise its own warning, and 철수's Claude is told it made a 'mistake' it could not have avoided.
findings.evidence_detail: Derived from approved decisions 2, 3 and 6. Edit applies against current content (https://code.claude.com/docs/en/tools-reference), and CAS ordering was observed in research/git-transport.md §2. Key structural fact: the CAS chain forces the later publisher to merge published state before it publishes, so the winner never sees an unpublished conflicting claim. The integrator is therefore the only possible detector.
findings.mitigation: Principle: the integrating daemon, the one holding unpublished changes while it merges published state, is the SOLE detector. Rules: (1) The detector is the loser's daemon during its rebase step. It compares its local claims with the fetched board, including ancestor and descendant symbols. (2) The loser publishes ONE event in the same atomic push, id = sha1('race'|symbolKey|winnerClaimId|loserClaimId). An overlapping claim is never published on its own. In the non-atomic fallback, push the board BEFORE the code so code never lands without its event. (3) Push gate: splice the published text of every foreign-held symbol into the outgoing blob; if the splice fails, take the whole file from base. The loser's hunks stay local (quarantined). (4) Notification: the causer gets one inbox message mid-turn (it is active by definition). The holder gets a pull-only FYI at its next hook on that file. Bystanders get nothing pushed. (5) Label the event 'race' when the winning claim was not yet fetched at the causer's edit time (the daemon knows its own fetch timestamps), and 'violation' otherwise. (6) The causer's options, through cowork_resolve(event, action), are: handoff (default; the patch goes to the holder's queue), go-first (patch-bound, see the go-first finding), withdraw, or wait (handoff plus notify-on-release). Proceeding anyway is human-only. (7) Anything unresolved at the causer's Stop is converted to a handoff, the shared version is restored in the causer's tree, and the hunk is kept in .git/cowork/quarantine/<id>.patch. (8) Shrink the window: a first claim on a symbol goes out as a priority push ahead of code-only pushes. PreToolUse also does a synchronous fetch (~0.45 s) when the target symbol has no known claim.
findings.test: Two-clone harness with a board: A and B claim the same symbol, A publishes first, and B edits other lines of the same function. Run B's cycle. Assert the function in B's pushed tree is byte-identical to A's version. Assert exactly one event with the deterministic id and label=='race'. Run all 4 daemons for 10 cycles and assert no further events. Mock inboxes: B's received 1 message, A's received 0.

findings.title: (e) Whole-file paths: a repo-wide formatter rewrites teammates' held functions. Write on a busy file livelocks on 'modified since read', which pushes Claude toward Bash writes.
findings.scenario: (1) Claude runs 'black .', 'prettier --write .' or 'dotnet format' through Bash. Symbols held by 3 people get whitespace-only changes, and no hook can attribute them per symbol. Prior art: a repo-wide ruff --fix rewrote other agents' code (agent_mail #272). (2) VERIFIED on CC 2.1.270: after the file changed on disk since Read, Write was refused with 'File has been modified since read, either by the user or by a linter', while Edit applied with a note. On a file teammates touch every 10–40 s, Claude re-Reads and then spends 30–120 s generating a full-file Write. Another sync lands in that time, so the Write is refused again, and the cycle repeats. A common agent fallback is 'cat > file' or a Python write through Bash, which skips both the stale check and our Edit/Write hooks. (3) A Write past the threshold claims the whole file and blocks everyone from it.
findings.consequence: Formatting churn turns into a storm of quarantines and notices. Teammates' changes are reverted through Bash writes, output tokens are burned on retries, and whole files are blocked.
findings.evidence_detail: In this session: Read w.py, changed it externally with sed, then Write was refused with the quoted error, and Edit then applied with '(note: the file had been modified on disk since you last read it...)'. File: scratchpad/sweep/social/w.py, CC 2.1.270. The livelock and Bash fallback are REASONED. The Write refusal is observed behaviour, not a documented guarantee, so the design must not depend on it.
findings.mitigation: (1) While live, PreToolUse(Bash|PowerShell) denies formatter and fixer runs without explicit paths: black, ruff --fix, prettier --write, eslint --fix, dotnet format, clang-format -i on globs, gofmt -w on a directory. With explicit paths it allows only files whose changed symbols the caller holds or that are unclaimed. (2) Push gate: whitespace- or format-only hunks inside foreign-held symbols are dropped from the outgoing tree.
