Assert: (i) no live commit removes a hunk introduced by another peer without an explicit human-confirm event on the board; (ii) main's live tree never contains a path that exists only on another branch; (iii) after save with fastForwardLocal, `git status --porcelain` is empty on every peer; (iv) pause, three teammate edits, then resume converges with no reverts.

findings.title: A peer whose local git config differs (filter not configured, or core.autocrlf=false) pushes the real secret, or CRLF blobs, into the shared ref
findings.scenario: 1) A new teammate clones. .gitattributes marks secret.py with filter=sec, but filter.sec.clean and smudge live in .git/config, which a clone does not copy. 2) He pastes the real secret into secret.py, as the onboarding notes tell him to. 3) His daemon snapshots with `git add -A`. With no clean filter configured, git stores the content verbatim. 4) The commit is pushed to refs/cowork/main/code. The object stays on the host after save resets the ref, as unreachable cruft whose GC timing is outside our control. When the repo is made public later as planned, anyone with an old fetch of refs/cowork/* has it. Variant: a Windows peer with core.autocrlf=false stores CRLF blobs, so every line differs from the other peers' LF blobs. Second leak path: debug logs, handoff 'proposed patch' text or a doctor bundle that contains working-tree content of secret.py.
findings.consequence: The secret is exfiltrated into remote history outside branch protection. With the autocrlf variant, edits to two different functions of the 1.3 MB file become a whole-file conflict on every merge, which shows up as endless conflict records and wrong 'causer' accusations.
findings.evidence_detail: sweep/e2: peer B cloned without the filter config. Its snapshot blob for secret.py was KEY = "REAL_SECRET". With autocrlf=false and CRLF on disk, B's m.py blob had 6 CR lines. merge-tree of A (edited a()) and B (edited b()) gave exit 1 with 'CONFLICT (content)'. The control with B on autocrlf=true gave exit 0, clean. The log and bundle leak path is REASONED.
findings.mitigation: (a) `cowork start` and doctor compute a normalization fingerprint. For every filter driver named in .gitattributes, require clean and smudge to be configured and filter.<x>.required=true in the daemon's effective config. Clean must be idempotent: run it twice on the smudged file and compare. For a sample of unchanged tracked files, a private-index `git add` must reproduce HEAD's blob oids exactly. On any mismatch the peer may only join read-only, and doctor prints the exact fix command. The fingerprint is published on the board, and daemons refuse merges from a peer whose fingerprint differs. (b) Snapshot `add` runs with `-c core.autocrlf=input` while checkout keeps the user's own config. The round-trip fixture must include explicit eol=crlf paths (.bat, .sln) to prove their blobs are unchanged. (c) Pre-push secret guard: the config lists protected paths. Before any push, the blob for each protected path must equal clean(working file) and must not contain the smudged bytes. Optional regex denylist scan over changed blobs. (d) Logs, events and doctor bundles never contain file content, only oids, paths and line ranges. The bundle generator scans its own output for every protected path's smudged content and aborts on a hit.
findings.test: Fixture repo with a filter and the canary secret 'COWORK_CANARY_SECRET'. A peer joins without the filter config: assert start refuses. A peer with autocrlf=false: assert pushed text blobs contain no CR, a different-function edit merges clean, and eol=crlf paths are byte-identical to HEAD. After a 30-minute simulated session with handoffs and conflicts on secret.py, `git cat-file --batch-all-objects` on the bare remote, all logs and the doctor bundle contain zero occurrences of the canary.

findings.title: Claim enforcement through mcp_tool hooks fails open silently whenever the per-session MCP server is down or returns isError
findings.scenario: 1) A session starts, but its stdio MCP server fails to launch: node is missing from PATH in a GUI-launched VS Code session, an nvm or volta shim breaks, or antivirus quarantines the bundle. Or the server crashes later, or the daemon IPC times out and the server returns isError. 2) The PreToolUse mcp_tool hook yields the documented non-blocking error, and the Edit proceeds. 3) PostToolUse is also mcp_tool, so the daemon never learns this was a Claude edit. No claim, no fence. 4) Teammates' published claims are ignored for the rest of the session, and the human sees nothing because nothing failed loudly.
findings.consequence: The core promise (block edits to claimed symbols, fence files) silently disappears for a whole session. Conflicts and last-writer-wins happen while everyone believes they are protected. This is the top failure mode in the prior-art survey.
findings.evidence_detail: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/hooks says an mcp_tool hook whose result has isError, or whose server is not connected, produces a non-blocking error (runtime-dist report §3). Supporting VERIFIED data, sweep/e11 on this PC: an exec-form node hook that connects to a named-pipe daemon measured p50 30.8 ms and p95 42.8 ms (n=40), against a 30.3 ms node baseline with no IPC. With the daemon down it exits 2 in 32 ms. Windows pitfall: waiting for the pipe 'end' event raised p50 to 91.9 ms; exiting on the first complete reply line avoids it.
findings.mitigation: The deny path is an exec-form command hook, `node <data>/runtime/hook.js`, on PreToolUse Edit|Write|MultiEdit|NotebookEdit plus Bash|PowerShell write detection. It is fail-CLOSED while cowork is active for this repo (marker file <gitdir>/cowork/active). If the daemon is unreachable, takes more than 400 ms, or returns a malformed reply, the hook exits 2 with 'cowork-sync is not running for this repo: run /cowork doctor or /cowork pause'. When cowork is inactive the hook exits 0 at once without IPC. mcp_tool hooks remain for context, claims and notifications only. The hook client exits on the first complete reply line. `/cowork doctor` runs a live canary: the daemon plants a claim held by a synthetic peer on a temp file, the real hook binary is invoked for an Edit there, and doctor asserts exit 2 and an unchanged file.
findings.test: Integration tests on the real hook binary: (i) daemon killed: exit 2 and the file is unchanged; (ii) daemon hung and never replies: exit 2 within 450 ms; (iii) CI perf gate on windows-latest: p95 at or below 60 ms over 200 invocations; (iv) doctor's canary passes on ubuntu, macOS and Windows runners.

findings.title: merge-tree's conflicted result tree contains conflict markers; if it is applied or pushed, every peer's file stops parsing, and there is no conflict viewer
findings.scenario: Two peers edit the same function inside the propagation window, before either claim is published. merge-tree exits 1 but still returns a tree whose blob holds <<<<<<< / ======= / >>>>>>>. The design says '3-way merge incoming into local working tree' and does not define the exit-1 path. If the daemon applies that tree and then 'commits local changes on top', the markers go to every peer. hub.py no longer imports. Tree-sitter maps the 1.3 MB file to ERROR nodes, so claims fall back to the wrong pseudo-symbols. Every Claude sees a SyntaxError and starts 'fixing' it, each fix being another claimed edit.
findings.consequence: A team-wide broken build, plus several agents racing to repair the same markers: the worst case of agents behaving badly.
findings.evidence_detail: sweep/e10, extra check: on exit 1 the result tree's m.py blob contains the marker lines, and ast.parse of that blob raises SyntaxError.
findings.mitigation: Rule: a merge result with conflict stages is never applied or pushed. On exit 1, each conflicted path takes the version backed by the earlier published claim (board order). Without claims it takes the version already in the live ref, because that was published first. The other side becomes a conflict record on the board, {id, path, symbol, base/ours/theirs oids, causer, holder}, and the losing blob stays reachable (a board-tree file or refs/cowork/<b>/conflicts). Product surface: `/cowork conflicts` lists them. `/cowork conflicts show <id>` renders a 3-way view from the oids (git merge-file -p --object-id / diff3). `/cowork conflicts resolve <id> --take mine|theirs|edit` produces a normal live edit under a claim. The losing Claude receives the record and its patch through additionalContext.
findings.test: Property test over random concurrent edits to the same symbol. Assert that no live commit tree contains a line matching ^(<<<<<<<|>>>>>>>)( |$) or ^=======$ that its parent lacks. Assert that every exit-1 merge has a board record whose losing blob `cowork conflicts show` can retrieve.

findings.title: read-tree -m -u is not all-or-nothing on Windows: a share-locked file (Excel, antivirus, IDE indexer) gives exit 128 after other files have already been written
findings.scenario: 1) 영희 has book.xlsx open in Excel, which opens it with FILE_SHARE_READ and no delete sharing. The same happens briefly when an antivirus scanner or indexer holds a .py. 2) An incoming merge changes a.py, book.xlsx and z.py. 3) read-tree -m -u writes a.py and z.py, fails with 'unable to unlink old book.xlsx', and exits 128. 4) The design treats exit 128 as 'not uptodate: re-snapshot and retry'. The re-snapshot, seeded from BASE, sees the teammate's a.py and z.py as local edits, credited to 영희. The retry fails every 2-3 s for as long as Excel is open. Any logic that advances the base to MERGED because most of the merge applied makes the next snapshot push the old book.xlsx, reverting the teammate's change.
findings.consequence: Several failures together: a silent stall (the teammate's change never lands and nobody is told why), a retry storm, wrong attribution, and a revert whenever the base is advanced.
findings.evidence_detail: sweep/e6: PowerShell held book.xlsx with FileShare.Read. `read-tree -m -u BASE THEIRS` printed "error: unable to unlink old 'book.xlsx': Invalid argument" and exited 128. On disk afterwards, a.py and z.py held 'v2 teammate' and book.xlsx still held 'sheet v1'. The temp index's entry for book.xlsx still pointed at the BASE blob; the other entries were not inspected before the re-snapshot. A snapshot taken on the assumption that THEIRS was applied showed book.xlsx changed, which would be pushed as a revert.
findings.mitigation: (a) Any nonzero apply exit means the disk state is unknown. Hash each target path (hash-object --path, so filters apply) and classify it as BASE, MERGED or other. Track applied state per path, and advance a path's base only when its disk content hashes to MERGED. (b) For locked paths, build MERGED' (MERGED with the locked paths set back to their BASE entries), apply MERGED', and mark the locked paths 'pending-apply: locked by another program' in status and on the board. Retry them only after a cheap open-for-delete probe succeeds, with backoff up to once a minute. (c) Attribution comes from live-chain commit trailers, never from which snapshot first contained the bytes. (d) Office binaries (*.xlsx, *.docx, *.pptx) default to whole-file claims with no 3-way merge.
findings.test: Windows-runner fault injection: open a target file with FileShare.Read during apply. Assert that the other files applied, the locked file appears in `cowork status --json` within one cycle, no later live commit contains the old version of the locked file, and the file converges within two retries after the handle closes. Repeat with a 200 ms transient lock, like an antivirus scan.

findings.title: A crash between a successful push and persisting the new base makes the restarted daemon merge against a stale base, causing false conflicts and possible reverts
findings.scenario: 1) Daemon A pushes commit C (its change to f) on top of R, and the push succeeds. 2) A is killed before writing last_applied=C: laptop sleep, BSOD, taskkill or Windows Update. 3) B refines the same lines on top of C, producing D. 4) A restarts with base R and merges (base R, ours = A's working tree with the same content as C, theirs D). That conflicts on lines that should simply fast-forward to D. If resolution keeps the local side, or claim order favours A (its claim was earlier), A pushes the old value over D.
findings.consequence: A teammate's later refinement is reverted, or spurious conflict records and handoffs appear after every crash. Neither is reproducible by hand.
findings.evidence_detail: sweep/e10: `merge-tree --merge-base=R OURS D` gave three conflict stages for m.py. With `--merge-base=C` it was clean, and the result was D's 'return 3'.
findings.mitigation: Keep write-ahead state in <gitdir>/cowork/state.json, written to a temp file, fsynced, then renamed. Before pushing, record {intent: push, commit: C, parentTip, tree}; after the push succeeds, record base=C. On startup with an intent present: fetch. If C is reachable from the remote tip, base=C. Otherwise base=parentTip, and C's changes are re-derived from the working tree. Always validate that the base is an ancestor of, or equal to, the fetched tip. If the working-tree snapshot equals the tree of a recent live commit, use that commit as the base. Also keep refs/cowork-local/<b>/base as a reflogged ref so the base survives a corrupted state file.
findings.test: Crash-injection harness: SIGKILL the daemon at every step boundary (after fetch, merge-tree, read-tree, commit-tree and push, and before and after the state write) across 1000 seeded runs with 3 peers. Properties after quiescence: all working trees equal the live tip tree, and every peer edit is present unless a later edit to the same lines overwrote it. The oracle replays the operation log against a reference model.

findings.title: Sync scope is implicit ('git add -A' of everything not ignored) and excludes can change mid-session: untracked junk and secrets get broadcast, and an excludes change can delete files on every peer
findings.scenario: A) A peer has untracked files that are not gitignored: test_runs outputs, .xlsx fixtures, a local .env.local, a 200 MB built server .exe, and generated docs (docs/generated) that each machine regenerates. `git add -A` includes them, so they are pushed to all peers, run through the LFS pre-push hook, and exposed. Generated files regenerated on two machines differ by timestamps and ping-pong between them, using up the push budget. B) This assumes excludes are implemented by dropping paths from the snapshot, since the design does not specify. 영희 adds docs/generated/** to the cowork config while those files exist in the live tree. Her next snapshot omits them, so the commit deletes them, and every peer's read-tree -m -u removes them from disk because clean files are deleted.
findings.consequence: A: data leak, repo bloat and wasted push budget. B: real files silently deleted on every PC.
findings.evidence_detail: The git-transport report (OBS) found that untracked, non-ignored files were included by the private-index `add -A`. B depends on how excludes are implemented, which the design does not yet say.
findings.mitigation: (a) Default scope: files tracked in the branch's HEAD, plus new files under configured include globs (default: source extensions), each new file text-only and at most 1 MB. Everything else stays local and is listed in `cowork status` as 'not shared (reason)'. (b) Excludes are carry-through. On snapshot, an excluded path keeps its BASE entry and is never added or removed. On apply, excluded paths are never written or deleted. (c) The committed config (.cowork/config.json) is versioned on the board, and changes made during a live session take effect only at the next save, when all daemons switch together. (d) Presets for the pilot team: generated (never synced; regenerate locally), union (CHANGELOG.md and patch-note .txt files; see the attribute finding), binary-lock (*.xlsx: whole-file claim, no merge).
findings.test: Simulation: one peer creates 50 untracked files, including a 5 MB binary and a .env. Assert that none of them appear among the remote's objects. Add an exclude for an existing tracked directory mid-session. Assert that no peer's disk loses a file and the live tree keeps those files until save. Two peers regenerate the same generated file: assert zero live commits touch it.

findings.title: Peers update at different times; an older daemon read-modify-writes the board and drops fields or records added by the newer schema (for example handoff queue items)
findings.scenario: 1) Version 1.3 adds handoff.priority and a new event type, request.goFirst. 영희 updates. 철수's long-running daemon is still 1.2, running from the old plugin root. 2) 영희's Claude asks 'may I go first?' and the request goes on the board. 3) 철수's 1.2 daemon updates the board for its own claim. It parses into its typed model, serializes without the unknown fields and records, and pushes with a valid CAS. 4) The request and the priority are gone, and 영희's Claude waits forever. Related: a bad release reaches all four peers within hours and takes the whole team's live session down at once.
findings.consequence: Silent loss of coordination state, waits that look like deadlock, or a team-wide outage caused by a single release.
findings.evidence_detail: The analogous observed failure is prior-art #15 (ruflo#3005, mixed versions reverting newer content). The runtime-dist report notes that CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT changes on every version and old roots are swept 14 days after they are orphaned.
findings.mitigation: (a) Board format: append-only event logs, one file per peer per day that no other peer ever rewrites, plus derived state. Any rewrite must preserve unknown keys and records. (b) Board header {protocol, minReader, minWriter}. A daemon whose protocol is below minWriter goes read-only and shows 'update cowork-sync to keep editing'. minWriter is raised only for incompatible changes. (c) The daemon compares versions with each MCP server on handshake. When a newer version connects, the daemon drains and re-executes from a runtime copied into <data>/runtime/<version>/, never from CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT. (d) Release process: protocol semver kept separate from the plugin version; a 'next' marketplace channel for canary (team lead first), promoted to stable after 72 h; plugin.json pins the version so updates are explicit; the changelog calls out protocol changes; rollback means republishing the previous code under a higher version.
findings.test: Mixed-version CI simulation: build bundles N-1 and N and run peers on both over 1000 random board operations. Assert that no record written by N disappears, that N-1 never writes while minWriter is above its protocol, and that every request reaches a terminal state (granted, declined or returned).

findings.title: Claims and asks are tied to process lifetime, not activity: a session left open over lunch or overnight holds symbols indefinitely and never answers 'may I go first?'
findings.scenario: 1) 철수's Claude claims Pipeline.run at 11:50, finishes its turn, and 철수 leaves for lunch with the terminal open. The MCP server's stdin stays open, so the claim stays. 2) 영희's Claude is denied on Pipeline.run, records the change, carries on, and at Stop hands it off to 철수's queue. The protocol asks the holder 'when its own work finishes', but that work is finished and nobody is there. 3) 영희's Claude re-asks or waits, and 영희's session ends with the request still sitting there. At 4 PM she is still blocked and does not know why.
findings.consequence: Team throughput falls to the pace of the most absent person. Agents either spin (re-asking costs usage) or give up. Humans start overriding, and prior art shows bypass then becomes the norm (agent_mail #238).
findings.evidence_detail: Derived from decision 10 (claims are released when the MCP server's stdin closes) and decision 7 (the holder is asked when its work finishes). Neither covers a session that is open but idle.
findings.mitigation: (a) Claims are leases renewed by activity. Any PreToolUse or PostToolUse in the holding session renews them. 15 minutes after the session's last tool call the claim turns 'dormant': still visible, no longer blocking. A request against a dormant claim is granted automatically after a 2-minute notice to the holder, delivered through the inbox and an OSC 9 desktop notification (terminalSequence) on the holder's next hook. (b) Every request carries a TTL, default 30 minutes. On expiry, or when the holder session ends, it returns to the requester as 'returned: holder unavailable'. (c) `/cowork away` makes your claims dormant at once. `/cowork status` shows each claim's age and the holder's idle time. (d) Only the holder's human may decline a request. A Claude may only 'defer with an ETA'.
findings.test: Virtual-clock simulation. The holder session sits idle for 20 minutes holding a claim, and a requester asks: assert the grant happens within the notice period and the holder's next activity receives the change as context. A crashed holder session's claim goes dormant within one heartbeat. No request is non-terminal after its TTL.

findings.title: When sync stalls (auth expired, lock loop, daemon crash, host throttling) while a human edits outside Claude, nothing on screen shows it, and plugins cannot set the main status line
findings.scenario: On day 12 the GCM token expires. With GCM_INTERACTIVE=never, every fetch fails. Or the daemon dies at 03:00. Next morning 철수 edits in VS Code for two hours with no Claude turn running, so no hook fires and no additionalContext is shown. His changes pile up locally and teammates' work is not applied. When Claude next runs, it plans against a stale tree. The planned status-line indicator cannot be installed by the plugin at all.
findings.consequence: Hours of drift, then large divergent merges and conflicts on recovery. Users find the tool has quietly stopped (prior-art #7) and lose trust in it.
findings.evidence_detail: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/plugins/manifest-reference: plugin settings apply only 'agent' and 'subagentStatusLine'; other keys are dropped at load. https://code.claude.com/docs/en/hooks: terminalSequence is limited to OSC 0/1/2/9/99/777 and BEL, and is written only in interactive sessions while the UI is on screen. GCM_INTERACTIVE=never fails instead of prompting (git-transport report §6).
findings.mitigation: (a) Each cycle the daemon writes <gitdir>/cowork/status.json: heartbeat timestamp, state (ok|degraded|stalled|paused), lag in seconds, pending pushes, locked paths, conflicts, auth state. (b) The first `/cowork start` offers to install a chaining status line: a small script that runs the user's existing statusLine command and appends 'cowork 3 peers / 4s' read from status.json, with no IPC. A heartbeat older than three cycles shows 'cowork: DOWN'. A status line locked by managed settings is detected and skipped with a note. (c) Every UserPromptSubmit and PreToolUse hook checks status.json. When degraded, it sends a systemMessage to the human and additionalContext to Claude, for example 'your tree is 47 min behind'. (d) Human notification without Claude: on a transition to stalled, the daemon raises a dependency-free OS notification (Windows WinRT toast through PowerShell, macOS osascript, Linux notify-send when present) at most once per 30 minutes. (e) Messages are actionable and per class: auth, ref rejected by host, file lock, push budget throttled.
findings.test: Chaos tests: revoke credentials, kill the daemon, cut the network (rename the remote directory or point at an unroutable proxy), hold a file lock. For each, assert status.json changes state within two cycles, the status-line script output changes, the next hook emits a systemMessage, and the mocked OS notifier is called exactly once. The state must never stay 'ok'.

findings.title: Uninstalling or disabling the plugin deletes CLAUDE_PLUGIN_DATA (journal, unflushed handoffs, token) while the detached daemon keeps rewriting the working tree; stale live refs stay on the remote
findings.scenario: 1) A user runs /plugin uninstall cowork-sync, or disables it, while the detached daemon is running; by design it outlives sessions. 2) Claude Code deletes ${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_DATA} by default, taking the journal of denied changes, the unflushed handoffs and the IPC token with it. 3) The daemon keeps polling and applying teammates' changes with no hooks, no claims and no UI, or it crashes on missing files partway through a cycle. 4) refs/cowork/<b>/{code,board} stay on GitHub indefinitely. Months later, after 'feature' was cowork-live and then deleted, starting cowork on a new branch 'feature/code' fails with 'refname conflict'.
findings.consequence: An invisible process keeps modifying files after the user believes the tool is gone, which is the worst possible trust failure for an open-source plugin. Handoffs are lost, and push failures appear later with no obvious cause.
findings.evidence_detail: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/plugins/manifest-reference: 'By default, Claude Code deletes the ${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_DATA} directory when you uninstall the plugin from the last place it's installed.' VERIFIED in sweep/e4: with refs/cowork/main/{code,board} on the remote, pushing refs/cowork/main/board/code was rejected with '(refname conflict)'. The orphan daemon's behaviour is REASONED.
findings.mitigation: (a) Durable state (journal, handoff outbox, base, conflict records) lives in <gitdir>/cowork/. It survives uninstall and is removed only by `cowork uninstall --purge`. CLAUDE_PLUGIN_DATA holds only caches and the runtime copy. (b) Daemon lifetime contract: flush, then exit, when the plugin is no longer enabled or its runtime is gone (checked every 30 s), or when no session has connected for idleExit (default 30 minutes) and nothing is unpushed. Syncing human-only edits with no Claude session requires an explicit `cowork start --headless`, which shows an OS notification when it starts. (c) `npx cowork-sync uninstall` and `/cowork uninstall` flush the outbox, release claims on the board, stop the daemons for every repo listed in a registry file, and optionally delete remote refs/cowork/* for branches that have no other live peer. (d) `/cowork gc` archives locally, then deletes remote live refs whose branch is gone or that have had no peer heartbeat for 14 days.
findings.test: Start the daemon, create a handoff, then uninstall through the CLI. Assert the handoff survives in <gitdir>/cowork/outbox (or was pushed), the daemon process is gone within 60 s, and no working-tree file has an mtime after the uninstall. gc test: refs for a deleted branch are removed, and a new 'feature/code' branch then starts cleanly.

findings.title: 'Nothing is ever lost' cannot be demonstrated: the live chain has no local reflog, save resets it, and the host garbage-collects the old chain, so there is no 'who changed this line' and no undo of a teammate's change
findings.scenario: 1) A teammate's change is reverted through one of the other paths (mass revert, file lock, stale base). 2) Someone runs /cowork save, and the live ref is force-reset onto the saved commit. 3) The person whose work vanished asks where their function went. Locally, refs/cowork-remote/* has no reflog, so the pre-save chain is unreachable. On GitHub it is cruft waiting for GC. Recovery needs an expert running git fsck --lost-found within about two weeks.
findings.consequence: Lost work cannot be found or restored by ordinary users, and the first incident destroys trust. Lines produced during a session cannot be attributed for review or blame.
findings.evidence_detail: sweep/e7: after a forced update of refs/cowork-remote/main/code under the default core.logAllRefUpdates=true, `git reflog show` printed nothing, and .git/logs/refs contained only heads/. With `-c core.logAllRefUpdates=always` the reflog recorded 'storing ref' and 'fast-forward'. A ref under refs/remotes/cowork/ (a namespace logged by default) recorded 'forced-update'.
findings.mitigation: (a) Every daemon ref update runs with -c core.logAllRefUpdates=always. (b) Before save resets the live ref, archive it locally as refs/cowork-archive/<b>/<save-seq>, kept for 30 days. The save commit carries Co-authored-by trailers, and a note in refs/notes/cowork maps line ranges to live commit, peer and session. (c) Live commits carry the trailers Cowork-Peer, Cowork-Session and Cowork-Claim. (d) User-facing commands: `/cowork log [path[:symbol]]` (live-chain history by peer and Claude session), `/cowork blame <path>`, and `/cowork undo <live-commit|hunk>`, which reverse-applies the change as a new live edit under a claim and notifies the original author.
findings.test: Peer A's change is reverted by peer B, then save runs, then `git gc --prune=now` runs on the peer. Assert `cowork log` still lists A's commit, `cowork undo` restores a diff identical to A's original, and `cowork blame` attributes the restored lines to A.

findings.title: A simulation that mocks git, or runs each OS in isolation, passes while real mixed-OS teams break (case collisions, eol, file locks, attribute source, partial apply)
findings.scenario: The CI matrix runs the 3-peer simulation separately on ubuntu, macOS and Windows, and all pass. In production a Linux peer adds Utils.py next to utils.py. The Windows peer's read-tree -m -u returns 0 with no warning. Only one file exists on disk, holding the second file's content, so the Windows human and Claude never see Utils.py while it stays in the tree, and their runtime imports differ from the Linux peers'. None of the behaviours in e1 to e13 would show up with a mocked git runner.
findings.consequence: Ship-blocking bugs reach a pilot team, and 'no sync issues' cannot be demonstrated before rollout.
findings.evidence_detail: sweep/e13: a tree with Utils.py ('# by linux peer A') and utils.py ('# by linux peer B') was applied on Windows (core.ignorecase=true). Exit 0; `ls` showed only utils.py, with B's content. After the Windows user edited it, the snapshot still held Utils.py with A's content and utils.py with the Windows edit. How deletes and renames propagate from this state was not tested.
findings.mitigation: (1) The daemon core is a deterministic state machine with an injectable clock, scheduler, fs watcher and process runner, but the runner executes REAL git against a local file:// bare remote. Only the network and Claude are faked. A transport shim simulates a network drop (rename the remote), latency (delayed fetch), and a CAS race or host rejection (a pre-receive hook rejects). Scripted fake sessions call the real hook binary. (2) At least 10k seeded interleavings per CI run, each reproducible from its seed. Properties: convergence after quiescence; no lost update (operation-log oracle); no conflict markers; the user's index and HEAD byte-identical before and after; at most one holder per symbol once the board settles; every request reaches a terminal state. (3) Faults injected: a kill at every step, Windows file locks, a present index.lock, clock skew of ±2 minutes, disk full, auth failure. (4) Mixed-OS federated job: ubuntu, macOS and Windows runners in one workflow join the same throwaway GitHub repo under a per-run ref prefix (refs/cowork-ci/<run>/...) with a deploy key, and make scripted edits including case-colliding names, the executable bit, symlinks and CRLF. A final job compares trees per OS. The same job runs a 30-60 minute push-budget soak. (5) A preflight rejects trees with paths that differ only by case before applying on a case-insensitive peer, and the board flags whoever created them.
findings.test: Mutation-test the harness: reintroduce each verified defect (re-seeded index, applying a conflicted tree, stale base, missing attr.tree, quoted paths) and require the suite to fail. A release is blocked if any mutant survives.

findings.title: Re-seeding the private index from the last applied tree every cycle wipes stat data, so git re-reads and re-filters every tracked file every 2-3 s
findings.scenario: Decision 4 seeds the private GIT_INDEX_FILE from the last applied tree, and read-tree writes index entries without stat data. Each poll cycle then runs read-tree, add -A and write-tree. With 4k+ files and several 1.3 MB copies (the pilot workspace has a folder per version), git re-hashes all content every cycle, re-runs the clean filter process for filtered files, and Defender scans every read.
findings.consequence: About 1 s of CPU per cycle even on a 32-core machine, so a 4-core laptop burns a constant share of a core, with fan noise and battery drain. Slower cycles stretch propagation, and the filter spawns every cycle. Users uninstall because 'it makes my PC slow'.
findings.evidence_detail: sweep/e1, 32-core PC. With 4002 files, a re-seeded cycle took 859-868 ms against 57-105 ms for a persistent private index (after one initial add -A). With six 1.3 MB BOM+CRLF files added, re-seeded cycles took 1000-1264 ms against 60-122 ms persistent. The counting clean filter ran on every re-seeded cycle and 0 times with the persistent index. Every cycle also printed 'LF will be replaced by CRLF' warnings to stderr.
findings.mitigation: Keep one persistent private index per (repo, branch) in <gitdir>/cowork/index. After a successful apply, carry the temp index forward (read-tree -m -u records stat data for the files it writes) instead of re-seeding. Skip the snapshot when nothing changed, using built-in fsmonitor (Windows and macOS; Linux from git 2.55) or an fs.watch hint. Whether core.fsmonitor and untrackedCache work with a non-default GIT_INDEX_FILE must be confirmed by the perf test, not assumed. Silence the eol warnings for the snapshot. Budgets, gated in CI on windows-latest with a generated 5k-file, 15 MB repo: an idle cycle at most 100 ms wall and at most 2% average of one core over 10 minutes; a snapshot with one changed file at most 200 ms; daemon RSS at most 250 MB.
findings.test: Benchmark job: generate the fixture (5k files, six 1.3 MB BOM+CRLF files, one file with a counting clean filter) and run the daemon idle for 10 minutes. Assert the clean-filter count stays 0 while idle and the budgets hold, including on the first cycle after an apply, where stat data is most likely to go missing again. The release fails if any budget is exceeded.

findings.title: Parsing the 1.3 MB file on the daemon's main thread stalls its event loop for about 350 ms, and PreToolUse requests queue behind it
findings.scenario: An incoming change to hub.py, or to all six version copies, lands. The daemon reparses with web-tree-sitter on the same Node thread that serves the hook pipe. Meanwhile Claude issues a MultiEdit on that file and the hook request waits. With a 400 ms hook-client timeout, a fail-closed hook issues a spurious 'daemon unreachable' deny; with mcp_tool, the edit goes through unenforced. A claim computed from a tree older than the file maps offsets to the wrong symbol.
findings.consequence: Random denies, or unenforced edits, at exactly the busiest moments. Wrong-symbol claims lead to false 'conflict causer' accusations between Claudes.
findings.evidence_detail: sweep/e12, web-tree-sitter 0.25.10 with tree-sitter-python 0.25.0 on a synthetic 1.3 MB BOM+CRLF file. Full parse 230-248 ms; incremental reparse after one insert 104-114 ms; maximum event-loop gap 337-368 ms (the number that sets the hook budget); RSS 163 MB.
findings.mitigation: Parse in a worker_threads pool and cache trees by blob oid in an LRU capped at 300 MB. The main thread answers hooks from the cached tree whose blob matches the current file bytes. If that tree is not ready, it takes a conservative fallback claim (the line range of old_string widened to the enclosing indentation block or top-level def found by a regex scan) and upgrades the claim asynchronously. Budgets: daemon-side handling at most 15 ms p95, end-to-end at most 60 ms p95 on Windows. The event loop must never block longer than 20 ms; perf_hooks.monitorEventLoopDelay watches this and puts a warning in status when it is exceeded.
findings.test: CI load test: while a stream of changes is applied to six 1.3 MB files, fire 500 hook requests. Assert p95 at or below 60 ms, zero timeouts, and claims that match a ground-truth symbol map computed offline for each request.

findings.title: Synchronized polling turns one burst of changes into N(N+1)/2 push attempts; a governor that counts successful pushes, or infers team usage from the remote chain, undercounts real push operations by about 2.5x
findings.scenario: Four daemons poll every 2.5 s and see the same new tip at the same moment. Each merges and pushes with a lease: one wins, three are rejected, refetch and retry, and so on. Landing 4 commits takes 10 receive-pack operations. Rejected pushes leave nothing in remote history, so a team governor that estimates the others' usage from board or live commit timestamps cannot see them.
findings.consequence: The team exceeds GitHub's 6 pushes/min guidance while believing it is at 2-3/min. The likely result is throttling or slow pushes (exact behaviour UNKNOWN), latency spikes during busy periods, and 'push failed' noise.
findings.evidence_detail: sweep/e5: in 3 rounds of 4 simultaneous peers on a file:// remote, each round landed 4 changes in exactly 10 push attempts (1+2+3+4).
findings.mitigation: The governor budgets attempts, not successes. Pushes are slot-scheduled: each window of W = 60 s / budget is divided into N slots, and peer i pushes only in slot (hash(peerId) + k) mod N. Window boundaries are derived from the committer time of the current live tip, a shared reference that tolerates ±5 s of skew. After a CAS reject, the loser merges and waits for its next slot rather than retrying at once. Each daemon publishes its attempts per minute on the board (piggybacked on its push), so the team rate includes rejected attempts. Code and board go in one atomic push.
findings.test: Virtual-clock simulation with 4 peers and random edit bursts for an hour. Assert push attempts per sliding 60 s never exceed the budget and median propagation stays within the bound the budget implies. The GitHub soak (see open questions) records attempts, 4xx/5xx responses and push latency.

findings.title: merge-tree reads .gitattributes (merge=union and others) from the local working tree, not from the trees being merged, so peers merge identical inputs differently and a CHANGELOG union only works by accident
findings.scenario: 1) The team wants merge=union on CHANGELOG.md. 영희 adds it to .gitattributes in the live tree, but 철수's daemon has not applied that yet (or .gitattributes is locked, or only partly applied). 2) Concurrent CHANGELOG appends arrive from both. 영희's daemon merges cleanly as a union; 철수's daemon gets a CONFLICT for the same base, ours and theirs. 3) One peer pushes the union while the other records a conflict and a handoff, which causes ping-pong and a 'causer' accusation that is purely an artifact.
findings.consequence: Merges are non-deterministic across peers, which violates convergence. Spurious conflicts hit every CHANGELOG and patch-note edit, the most co-edited files at release time.
findings.evidence_detail: sweep/e9, same O and T commits each time. No attribute anywhere: CONFLICT. Attribute only in the uncommitted working-tree file: clean. Attribute committed in both merged trees but absent from the working tree: CONFLICT. With `-c attr.tree=<ours>`: clean union containing both entries. Attribute only staged in the index with the working-tree file deleted: CONFLICT.
findings.mitigation: Every merge-tree call passes `-c attr.tree=<oid>` pointing at a synthetic tree, built with mktree and cached by content hash, whose .gitattributes is the merge-base's .gitattributes plus the cowork config's union list. Merge attributes then depend only on the merge inputs. Do not pass it to add or checkout, which must keep the user's own eol and filter attributes. Doctor enforces the minimum git version that honours attr.tree; take that version from git's release notes and confirm it with this determinism test.
findings.test: Determinism test: run the same (base, ours, theirs) merge in two clones whose working-tree .gitattributes differ (present, absent, stale) and assert identical result-tree oids. Union fixture: 4 peers append to CHANGELOG concurrently for 10 minutes; assert zero conflict records and every entry present.

findings.title: Delivering requirement 8 by pushing inbox messages starts new turns in idle sessions, burning usage and producing unattended edits
findings.scenario: 1) Three daemons detect the same conflict. Each posts to its own sessions, and the causer receives three near-identical warnings relayed from three peers. 2) Idle sessions, whose humans are away, get a message, and an IDLE session starts a NEW TURN. In acceptEdits or auto mode, Claude may act on it: re-reading files, 'helping' with edits, or posting board replies that trigger further messages. 3) Each delivered message counts toward usage like a prompt. Once the 50-message queue fills and burst refusal starts, later critical messages are dropped.
findings.consequence: Usage is spent without a human present, unattended agents edit in response to teammates' notices, important messages are lost to rate limits, and Claudes ping-pong with each other.
findings.evidence_detail: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/cross-session-messaging: an idle receiving session starts a new turn; each delivered message counts toward usage; at most 50 are queued; identical repeats are dropped; bursts are refused (realtime-push and prior-art reports).
findings.mitigation: Meet requirement 8 with a delivery policy. (i) Every peer's Claude learns of a conflict at its next hook through additionalContext, which is real time for anyone working, and the board records each peer's observation. (ii) The causer receives one consolidated warning that carries every peer's observation; the event is deduplicated by id, and only the causer's own daemon sends it. (iii) An idle session is woken only for an event addressed to it that needs a decision (a request to it, or 'you are the causer'). Wakes are coalesced into a digest and capped at 1 per 10 minutes and 6 per hour per session. Purely informational events never start a turn. (iv) A wake message is labelled informational and says 'do not edit files in response; summarize for your human and wait'. (v) Humans are told through terminalSequence OSC 9/777 and the status line, not by waking Claude.
findings.test: Harness with a fake inbox socket that implements the auth line and counts deliveries. Run a 3-peer conflict storm for 30 minutes with every session idle. Assert at most 6 deliveries per hour per session, zero deliveries for informational events, exactly one consolidated warning per conflict to the causer, and every peer's additionalContext containing the conflict at its next hook.

findings.title: Parsing git's human-readable output breaks on non-ASCII paths (octal-quoted) and on localized git messages, so paths are silently skipped or errors misclassified
findings.scenario: A Korean-named file such as '패치노트.txt' changes (the same applies to NFD, space or emoji paths). The daemon parses `git diff --name-only` without -z and gets "\355\214\250...txt" in quotes. Claim keys, exclude matches and status entries then refer to a path that does not exist, and the hook cannot map the edit. On Linux or macOS peers with LANG=de_DE.UTF-8 or ko_KR.UTF-8 and a git build that ships translations, errors such as "Entry 'x' not uptodate. Cannot merge." are localized. Detection by message text fails, so a routine race is treated as fatal and sync stops, or the reverse.
findings.consequence: Files with non-English names are silently left unsynced and unclaimed, and users of localized git anywhere end up with stuck daemons.
findings.evidence_detail: VERIFIED in sweep/e8: `git diff --name-only` printed "\355\214\250\354\271\230\353\205\270\355\212\270.txt", while -z gave raw UTF-8. The locale half is REASONED: Git for Windows 2.55 on this PC ships no locale directory, so messages stayed English under LANG=de, ko and fr. Upstream git ships gettext translations (po/ includes de, fr, ko, zh_CN), which Linux distro packages install, but this was not reproduced here.
findings.mitigation: Every git invocation uses `-c core.quotepath=off`, -z for every path list and porcelain formats, and runs with LC_ALL=C and LANGUAGE unset (filters inherit this, so document it). Classify outcomes by exit code plus structured output; for example, detect 'not uptodate' by re-hashing the target paths, never by matching message text. Claim keys are normalized to NFC and compared case-insensitively on case-insensitive peers. User-facing i18n: the board stores message codes and parameters only, each viewer renders them from its own catalog (6 languages, English fallback), and text sent to Claude is English with a hint of the human's locale.
findings.test: Fixture repo with Korean, NFD 'café', space, emoji, leading-dash and 200-character paths. Run the full simulation on Linux with LANG=de_DE.UTF-8 and ko_KR.UTF-8, with git translations installed. Assert every file syncs, claims resolve, and retry classification behaves exactly as under LANG=C.

design_changes: Decision 4 (apply via read-tree -m -u treated as all-or-nothing): FALSIFIED by sweep/e6. Under a Windows FileShare.Read lock it exits 128 after 2 of 3 files have already been written. Change: treat any nonzero apply exit as 'disk state unknown', verify each path by hash against BASE and MERGED, advance the base per path only, defer locked paths (MERGED' = MERGED with locked paths kept at BASE), and show them in status.

Decision 4 (private index seeded from the last applied tree every cycle): measured at about 1.0 s per cycle against about 60 ms with a persistent index (sweep/e1), because seeding wipes stat data and every file is re-hashed and re-filtered each cycle. Change: one persistent private index per (repo, branch) in <gitdir>/cowork/, carried forward after each apply, with fsmonitor-gated snapshot skipping. The fsmonitor part must be confirmed by the perf test.

Decision 10 (enforcement through mcp_tool hooks): these fail open by documentation. Change: the deny path is an exec-form `node` command hook that is fail-closed while cowork is active. It costs about 31 ms p50 and 43 ms p95 on this PC (sweep/e11), and the client must exit on the first reply line, because waiting for pipe 'end' costs about 92 ms. mcp_tool stays for context, claims and notifications only. Doctor runs a live deny canary.

Decision 2 (3-way merge into the working tree): define the merge-tree exit-1 path. A conflicted result tree contains markers (sweep/e10) and must never be applied or pushed. The earlier claim's version, or the version already live, stays in the tree; the losing side goes to a board conflict record with a reachable blob; add a /cowork conflicts viewer and resolver.

Decision 2/4 (merge-tree): always pass `-c attr.tree=<synthetic tree: merge-base .gitattributes + cowork union list>` so merges are deterministic across peers and CHANGELOG union works. Without it, merge-tree reads the local working tree's .gitattributes (sweep/e9).

Decision 2 (snapshot = git add -A): replace with an explicit sync scope: files tracked in HEAD plus configured include globs, new files limited in size and to text. Excludes are carry-through (taken from BASE, never written on apply), and config changes take effect only at the next save.

Decision 4 (never touch user index/HEAD): keep it as the default, and add (1) HEAD, branch and stash change detection that holds the snapshot and rebaselines, (2) a blast-radius breaker that quarantines snapshots reverting peers' hunks or touching many files, and (3) an opt-in guarded fast-forward of HEAD and the index to the save commit, only when HEAD == S^ and index == HEAD. Without these, the save flow pushes humans into stash, checkout or switch, which become team-wide reverts (sweep/e3).

Decisions 6/7/10 (claims released on MCP stdin close; holder asked when its work finishes): add activity-based lease TTLs (dormant after 15 minutes idle) and request TTLs that return the request to the requester. Process lifetime alone lets idle-but-open sessions block the team.

Decision 9 (inbox delivery): adopt a wake policy. Never start a turn for informational events; wake only for decisions addressed to that session; at most 6 wakes per hour per session; one consolidated warning to the causer, deduplicated by event id. Everyone else learns through additionalContext at their next hook, which still satisfies requirement 8 for anyone actively working.

Decision 3 (team push governor): budget push attempts rather than successful pushes, use slot-scheduled pushes keyed to the live tip's commit time, never retry immediately after a CAS reject, and publish per-peer attempt counts on the board. 4 synchronized peers used 10 attempts to land 4 changes (sweep/e5).

Decision 10 (state in CLAUDE_PLUGIN_DATA): move durable state (journal, outbox, base, conflict records) to <gitdir>/cowork/, because uninstall deletes the plugin data dir by default. Run the daemon from a runtime copied into <data>/runtime/<version>/; give it an idle exit and an exit when the plugin is disabled; add `cowork uninstall` and `cowork gc`.

Crash safety: write-ahead push intent log plus a reflogged base ref (refs/cowork-local/<b>/base). Run all daemon ref updates with -c core.logAllRefUpdates=always, and archive the live chain locally before each save reset, because the custom namespace has no reflog by default (sweep/e7).

Join gate: a per-peer normalization fingerprint (filter configured and required, clean idempotent, HEAD blobs round-trip) with read-only fallback on mismatch. Snapshot add runs with -c core.autocrlf=input. A pre-push secret guard covers protected paths, and logs and bundles never contain content (sweep/e2).
open_questions: Do rejected CAS pushes count toward GitHub's '6 pushes per minute per repository' guidance, and what does throttling look like in practice (latency, HTTP 429/5xx, error text)? Only a soak test on a throwaway GitHub repo can show this, with 4 clients for 30-60 minutes, counting attempts as well as successes.

Do GitHub Actions `on: push` workflows, or repository webhooks such as the pilot team's issue-tracker or bot integrations, fire for pushes to refs/cowork/*? If they do, every live push triggers CI runs or integration traffic. Test on a throwaway repo with a catch-all workflow and a webhook.

Is an exec-form command-hook deny (exit 2 or permissionDecision=deny) honoured for MultiEdit and NotebookEdit and inside subagents? Issue #76726 reports the parent seeing permission_denials: [] after a subagent was denied. Doctor's canary should be validated against a real `claude` build in CI before relying on it.

Can a turn started in an idle session by an inbox message run edits automatically under acceptEdits or auto mode? The docs say such a message 'can't approve anything'. Confirm whether that covers tool calls, since it decides how strict the wake policy must be.

Headless mode: should human-only edits sync while no Claude session is open? This decides the daemon's lifetime, the uninstall and orphan behaviour, and which visibility surfaces are needed (OS notifications, status file).
Which git version first honours `-c attr.tree` for merge-tree? It sets the minimum git version doctor must enforce, which may be higher than the 2.38 floor implied by merge-tree --write-tree.
Office files: the pilot team uses Excel heavily. Should *.xlsx be excluded by default, or synced as whole-file-claim-only? sweep/e6 shows Excel's locks are exactly what breaks apply.

INCIDENT NOTE for the user: the environment reported <workspace>/<pilot-repo> as 'not a git repository', but it is one. In my extra e10 check a `cd` failed, so git plumbing ran in that directory. It wrote a few unreferenced loose objects into <pilot-repo>/.git/objects (2 blobs, 2 trees, 2 commits whose parent is the repo's root commit, plus merge-tree output; known oids include commits 7910e62d..., a1b53884... and result tree 079e98bf...). It also created <workspace>/m_conf.py, which I confirmed was mine (141 bytes, conflict-marker content, created 14:02) and deleted. No refs, index, HEAD or working-tree files changed: HEAD is still the same commit from 13:17, and the only untracked file is a pre-existing design note. I deliberately did not delete the loose objects, to avoid further writes in that repo; git gc will prune them.

gaps.area: Region identity and the 'splice' operator (symbol keys across peers and versions)
gaps.why_missing: No lens owned region detection, even though research/region-detect.md exists. Many proposed safety rules assume a hunk maps to the same symbol key on every peer and at every version: INV-FENCE's pre-push hunk-to-region check; the push gate's 'splice the published symbol text into the outgoing blob'; distributed-protocol's per-symbol conflict splice; editor-fs's format-only hunk classification; negotiation's patch-bound grants keyed by symbol hash. That assumption is never tested. If two peers disagree about a key, or a splice is wrong, the result is a silent bypass (the claim no longer matches) or silent corruption (duplicated or truncated code pushed to everyone). There is also an unexamined interaction: claude-code puts all symbol logic on BOM-stripped, LF-normalized, quote-folded text, but the splice must write into a raw blob whose stored form may be BOM+CRLF (hub.py, 1.3 MB). Offsets computed on the normalized view are shifted by one byte per preceding line in the raw bytes.
gaps.finder_prompt: You are the REGION-IDENTITY lens for cowork-sync. Read <scratchpad>/research/region-detect.md first (key = path+kind+qualname+#n; C# overload groups; <imports>, const:NAME, <toplevel after=X>; rename = re-resolve by offset then publish alias; sub-block claims for symbols over 300 lines). In the scratchpad sweep dir, build a small harness with py-tree-sitter 0.26 (or Python ast for .py) and git merge-file. Fixtures must include a UTF-8 BOM + CRLF Python file of at least 5k lines, a JS file with IIFE and arrow-function members, and a C# file with overloads, properties and partial classes. For each scenario below, compute the claim key and region on BOTH peers' versions (base, holder's, requester's). Then run the 'splice published symbol text into outgoing blob' operation and report whether the output is byte-correct, parses, and has no duplicated or lost lines. Scenarios: (1) the holder renames the claimed function while a peer edits it under the old name, with the alias still inside the propagation window; (2) the holder moves the function to another place in the file, or to another file; (3) a peer inserts a same-named def above, so the '#2' ordinal shifts and the claim now points at the wrong function; (4) the X in <toplevel after=X> is deleted or renamed; (5) decorators, docstrings and leading comments: which symbol owns them, and does a decorator-only edit escape the claim?; (6) a C# overload added or removed while another overload is claimed; (7) the local file has an ERROR node from a half-typed edit, so peers compute different boundaries; (8) splice offsets computed on the LF/no-BOM normalized text but applied to the raw BOM+CRLF blob (measure the byte drift); (9) sub-block (blank-line block) claims inside a 3,000-line function after a peer adds or removes blank lines; (10) the push gate splices the holder's symbol into a local blob where the local side also added a new adjacent symbol, or deleted the following symbol. Label each result VERIFIED (harness output), DOCUMENTED (URL) or REASONED. For each failure, give one design rule (for example: claims carry (blob oid, byte range in the STORED form, a content hash of the symbol's first line); splice only when the region's base text hash matches on both sides, otherwise take the whole file from the tip and queue the local version; all offsets are computed on stored-form bytes; the grammar version is pinned and published on the board; a disagreement on a key means a whole-file claim) and a test that would prove it. Never touch <workspace> and never push to a real remote.

gaps.area: Lifecycle of held, quarantined, pinned and parked local hunks (interaction between revert guards, the push gate, the conflict policy and claims)
gaps.why_missing: At least seven local holding stores are proposed by different lenses: refs/cowork-held/* (product-ux-ops); refs/worktree/cowork/<b>/parked* (human-git-lifecycle); .git/cowork/quarantine/<id>.patch (negotiation); .git/cowork/conflicts/<path>@<peer> (editor-fs); refs/cowork-local/<b>/conflicts/<id> (git-integrity); board conflict and handoff records; the 14-day write ring. No lens defined what happens to a held hunk afterwards. Concrete holes: (a) A held hunk normally stays on disk, so every later snapshot re-derives it in diff(A, snap). If the hold is identified by content or position and the file shifts (a peer's apply, or a later local Edit), the matcher misses and the held revert is published. (b) human-git-lifecycle's contested-set rule exempts a hunk 'if a local session holds a claim on that symbol'. A human's held revert of a peer's foo() is therefore laundered the moment the local Claude claims foo() for an unrelated Edit. (c) An incoming change to the same region meets the held local bytes. The verifying writer then 3-way merges them, so the held content becomes part of the merged result, and the provenance-based detectors no longer recognise it. (d) Local-only stores die on re-clone, worktree removal, `stop --park` restore, or uninstall --purge. 'Nothing is ever lost' (decision 7) then depends on one PC's disk. (e) A peer with a permanently held hunk never satisfies INV-CONVERGE, and its pinned version silently differs from the team's for that region indefinitely.
gaps.finder_prompt: You are the HOLD-LIFECYCLE lens for cowork-sync. From the round-1 digest the orchestrator holds, list every mechanism that keeps a local change unpublished: the revert detector, mass-change breaker, contested set, push-gate withdrawal, quarantine pinned until /cowork resolve, conflict stage-2 blob, parked-at-join and parked-at-stop, pending locked paths, unreadable paths, the portability gate, and EOL/BOM normalisation. For each, specify the hold's identity and state machine: what keys it, where it lives, whether it stays on disk, what releases it, and what happens when (1) the file shifts because of a peer apply, (2) a local Claude later claims and edits the same symbol, (3) an incoming peer change touches the same region, (4) save happens, (5) the user re-clones, uninstalls or runs `/cowork stop`, (6) the same hunk is caught by two different guards. Build a small model in the scratchpad sweep dir (<scratchpad>/sweep/) with 2-3 peers on a file:// bare remote, using real git merge-tree and merge-file. Reproduce at least the following: (a) a held human revert of peer B's foo() is published after the local Claude claims foo() for an unrelated edit, under the 'local claim exempts contested hunk' rule; (b) a hold keyed by line range misses after a peer inserts 40 lines above it; (c) a held hunk is absorbed into a 3-way merge with an incoming change and then passes the revert detector. Label each result VERIFIED, DOCUMENTED or REASONED. Output concrete failure scenarios, and design rules such as: one hold registry keyed by (path, base blob oid, pre-image hash, post-image hash) stored in a ref; held regions are re-masked from EVERY outgoing tree regardless of claims, until resolved by a human command; claims never exempt hunks flagged revert-of-peer; holds are mirrored to the board as handoff records, so nothing depends on one disk; each hold has a visible age and escalates. Also give the INV-NOLOSS property-test extensions that include hold states.

gaps.area: Publication units versus logical change units (cross-file and cross-symbol atomicity)
gaps.why_missing: Each lens made its own part finer-grained, and no lens examined how those parts combine. The pieces are: decision 3's debounce or coalesce, which publishes whatever is on disk at push time; the push gate's per-hunk withdrawal of hunks inside foreign claims (negotiation, distributed-protocol INV-FENCE); the per-path deferred apply for locked, fenced or hot paths (editor-fs, git-integrity, product-ux-ops); claude-code's PostToolUse restore of hunks in foreign symbols; and negotiation's save, which splices ACTIVE symbols out of the saved commit. Each of these can publish a shared tree, materialize a receiver tree, or commit a branch tree that never existed on any PC. Examples: a signature change is published while its call-site update in a claimed function is withdrawn; file A's new import lands while file B is deferred because Excel or an IDE holds it; Claude's Edit 1 (A.py) is pushed and Edit 2 (B.py) arrives 40 s later. The consequences are that every peer's running server or dev reloader picks up broken code, tests fail on every PC, and Claudes 'fix' code that is not broken in anyone's intent. The recent-provenance rule only partly limits this, and it does not cover a tree created by withdrawal. A saved branch commit may never have been run anywhere. INV-NOLOSS and INV-CONVERGE both pass in these cases, because no hunk is lost; the build is broken anyway.
gaps.finder_prompt: You are the CHANGE-SET ATOMICITY lens for cowork-sync. Define what a 'logical change' is: one tool_use, one MultiEdit, one Claude turn, or one Bash transaction. Find every mechanism in the round-1 digest that can split one logical change across pushes, applies or saves: debounce, per-hunk push-gate withdrawal, per-path deferred apply, PostToolUse restore, save exclusion of ACTIVE symbols, the governor delaying the 2nd half, and CAS reject followed by a re-merge. Build a harness in the sweep dir (<scratchpad>/sweep/) with real git and a file:// remote, and Python+C# fixtures where a function signature and its callers live in different symbols and files. Show (VERIFIED) a published or applied tree that fails `python -m py_compile` or a simple import or test, even though every individual hunk merged cleanly. Then analyse the agent-side consequence: what a peer's Claude sees after running tests, and whether the existing 'recent-provenance don't fix' rule fires when the broken state is caused by a withdrawal rather than a peer's WIP. Also check whether a peer's running dev server (Python reloader, `dotnet watch`) restarts on each apply, and whether a crash loop results. Propose concrete rules and tests, for example: hunks are tagged with a change-set id (session, tool_use_id or turn); withdrawal and deferral are all-or-nothing per change-set, so that if any hunk of a change-set is withdrawn, the whole change-set is held and queued as a unit; receivers apply a change-set atomically across paths, or not at all, with deferral per change-set rather than per path; debounce waits for the turn's Stop or for a quiet period before publishing a multi-file change-set, with a cap; a save excludes whole change-sets, not individual symbols, and runs a configurable smoke check (compile or import) before pushing the branch. Measure the latency cost of each rule against the 6 pushes/min budget. Label each finding VERIFIED, DOCUMENTED or REASONED.

gaps.area: Claude Code host-behavior assumptions that the mitigations depend on, and the aggregate usage/cost model
gaps.why_missing: Several 'critical' mitigations assume host behaviour that no lens checked. (1) The 'fail-closed exec-form node command hook' (claude-code, product-ux-ops) is fail-closed only when the process exits 2. Per the hooks docs, any other non-zero exit is a non-blocking error, and a PreToolUse timeout does not block (region-detect.md cites this). So a missing node on the hook's PATH (runtime-dist.md: nvm/Homebrew PATH issues; the native Claude Code install needs no Node), an uncaught exception, a module-load error after a plugin update, or a slow Windows cold start all fail OPEN. Every lens's gate claims are therefore overstated. (2) runtime-dist.md marks it UNKNOWN whether a detached daemon survives `claude` exiting on Windows. Combined with fail-closed gating keyed on a marker file, that means either every Edit is denied, or the gate is silently open. (3) After every daemon write to a file a session has Read, Claude Code injects a 'file was modified by the user or a linter; this change was intentional' reminder containing changed content. No lens measured its frequency × size for 4 peers churning a 26k-line file, and editor-fs rated it [low]. Its framing tells the agent that a teammate's WIP is its own user's intent, so the agent may adapt to it, extend it or 'finish' it. (4) Write freshness is content-based (plugin-hooks.md §5), so a Write to a file peers keep changing may loop on re-Read of 1.3 MB files. (5) There are additionalContext size caps and truncation for hook output, plus Stop-hook block behaviour. (6) The cumulative billed cost of hook-injected context, reminders, wakes and Stop blocks per session-hour was never estimated. Each of these can cause runaway cost or agent misbehaviour, and the round-1 rules assume answers that may not hold.
gaps.finder_prompt: You are the HOST-ASSUMPTIONS and COST lens for cowork-sync. First check the documentation (code.claude.com/docs/en/hooks, tools-reference, plugins-reference) and the research files plugin-hooks.md, runtime-dist.md and realtime-push.md under <scratchpad>/research/. Then run the smallest possible local experiments in <scratchpad>/sweep/. Use a throwaway project with a project-level .claude/settings.json; never modify the user's real settings or <workspace>. Each `claude -p` run consumes the user's usage, so keep runs few and tiny, and prefer the docs where they are decisive. Determine and label VERIFIED, DOCUMENTED or REASONED: (1) the outcome of a PreToolUse command hook whose executable is missing (ENOENT), which exits 1 from an uncaught exception, or which exceeds its timeout; whether the Edit proceeds, and what Claude and the user see; (2) on Windows, whether a process spawned detached (stdio ignore, windowsHide) from a SessionStart hook survives `claude` exiting and survives /exit (check with tasklist); (3) when an external process modifies a file Claude has Read, run a background writer that changes a 5k-line BOM+CRLF file every 5 s during a short session. Measure what the injected reminder contains, its size, and how often it appears, and quote its exact framing (whether it says 'the user' or 'intentional'); (4) whether Write refuses or forces a re-Read when content changed since Read, and whether Edit's re-match ever applies at a moved location; (5) the maximum additionalContext or hook output size before truncation or a file redirect. Then build a cost model: tokens per session-hour for 4 peers on the 1.3 MB file, at 1 push per 10 s, counting hook additionalContext, change reminders, inbox wakes and Stop blocks. Mark which round-1 mitigations break if each assumption is false. Output failure scenarios and design rules, for example: the gate script is a self-contained file with a top-level try/catch that maps every failure to exit 2; a node-presence preflight at SessionStart that disables live mode loudly; the push gate is stated to be the only hard boundary; per-session coalescing of daemon writes into Read files; a context and token budget per session with a measured ceiling; attribution text that counters the 'intentional user change' framing. Each rule comes with a test.

contradictions: Live-ref shape after save. distributed-protocol INV-LINEAR, human-git-lifecycle and negotiation: the post-save live commit has a single parent (the save commit), which is a non-fast-forward update. security-hosts: live refs are fast-forward only (parents = save commit + old tip), and any incoming tip that does not descend from last-applied is a 'rewrite incident'. git-integrity: `merge-base --is-ancestor LAST_APPLIED TIP` must hold before every merge, otherwise run the join procedure. As written, every save triggers a rewrite incident or a join on every peer. distributed-protocol's INV-BASE ('never use ancestry') also contradicts both ancestry-based rewind checks.

Save content. negotiation splices ACTIVE-claim symbols and unparseable files out of the saved commit S' (live tree = tree(T)). distributed-protocol and human-git-lifecycle save the full live tip merged with the branch head. A partial save violates git-integrity's ADOPT precondition (worktree equals C's tree for the saved paths), so ADOPT never runs for the files with exclusions, and peers stay in the HEAD-drift state that leads to stash and revert.

Daemon git storage. git-integrity uses a private bare GIT_DIR with alternates pointing at the user's objects, and its own refs. human-git-lifecycle uses refs/worktree/cowork/* in the user's repo; distributed-protocol and product-ux-ops use refs/cowork-local/<b>/* plus <gitdir>/cowork/state.json. The private GIT_DIR also breaks ADOPT: fetched save/live objects live only in the daemon's store, so updating the user's refs/heads/<b> to C points at an object the user's repo lacks. Separately, the user's gc can prune objects in its own store that are reachable only from the borrower's refs.

Conflict policy. git-integrity: never union, ours or theirs; the incoming version goes on disk; the local version is handed off. editor-fs: keep LOCAL bytes on disk, save the incoming version to .git/cowork/conflicts, and pause the path. negotiation and distributed-protocol: union for pure insertions (imports, end of file), per-symbol splice. product-ux-ops: a synthetic attr.tree union list for CHANGELOG and patch notes; the earlier claim's version stays. Union is forbidden by one lens and required by three, and the disk-side choice is opposite.

attr.tree. security-hosts pins `-c attr.tree=<base commit>` on EVERY converting command (add, hash-object, read-tree -u, merge-tree, checkout-index). product-ux-ops passes attr.tree only to merge-tree (a synthetic tree with the union list), and says add and checkout must keep the user's own eol and filter attributes.

EOL/BOM handling. editor-fs: per-path autocrlf chosen to reproduce the base blob's stored form (CRLF-stored means autocrlf=false). product-ux-ops: always `-c core.autocrlf=input` on snapshot add. distributed-protocol: team-pinned autocrlf/eol from the board. git-integrity: refuse to join on an autocrlf mismatch, `-X renormalize` on every merge, and rewrite the blob to the base style. claude-code: drop EOL-only hunks. These yield different blobs for the same file.

fsmonitor. editor-fs and product-ux-ops enable core.fsmonitor=true and untrackedCache on the private index for performance. security-hosts forces `-c core.fsmonitor=false` on every daemon git call, to avoid running a configured hook. The safe rule is builtin-or-false, never a hook path, but as written the two lenses contradict each other.

Gate failure semantics. claude-code and product-ux-ops: fail closed (exit 2) and never return 'allow'. human-git-lifecycle: the MCP server never returns isError; when the daemon is unreachable it respawns it and 'answers allow with an explicit warning'. security-hosts: after 30 s offline, PreToolUse returns 'ask'. claude-code: 'ask' only in the override flow. Deadlines: product-ux-ops 400 ms, claude-code 2 s with a 10 s hook timeout, and editor-fs's PreToolUse wait of up to 2 s for in-flight writes, which cannot fit a 400 ms deadline. 'No fence, no apply' for the whole repo (security-hosts) versus UNGUARDED holding only that session's recent paths (human-git-lifecycle).

Hosts without --atomic. distributed-protocol: SINGLE-REF mode (board as a .cowork/ subtree of the live commit), never sequential two-ref pushes. negotiation: push the board ref BEFORE the code ref sequentially. Approved decision 2 assumes two refs plus a refs/heads fallback.

Push governor and clocks. product-ux-ops slot-schedules pushes from the committer time of the live tip (cross-machine wall clock, '±5 s tolerated'), which violates distributed-protocol's INV-CLOCK (no cross-machine timestamp comparison). Renewal cadence also differs: TTL/2 with a 10-minute TTL (human-git-lifecycle), an 'alive' push every 3 minutes (negotiation), under 25% of TTL remaining (distributed-protocol), and 30 s heartbeats with 3-minute expiry (prior-art implications).

Claim lifecycle. negotiation: DORMANT claims still block (auto-grant after 2 minutes). product-ux-ops: dormant after 15 minutes is 'no longer blocking'. claude-code: claims last until save or explicit release, not until Stop, and are never released on stdin EOF while hooks continue. negotiation and decision 10: release at MCP stdin EOF. Auto-grants against a dormant holder (negotiation, product-ux-ops) and negotiation's turn-origin lock (a wake-started turn cannot edit) both contradict approved decision 7, under which the holder is ASKED 'handle it?' and then does the work.

Board content. negotiation stores intendedSymbolText and newSymbolText (patch text) inline in board request records. security-hosts says code appears on the board only as blob or tree ids produced through the pinned clean path. This is a leak path for the filtered secret file.

Messaging token. human-git-lifecycle has SessionStart register CLAUDE_CODE_MESSAGING_SOCKET and the token with the daemon, which then delivers through that socket. security-hosts says the token never crosses daemon IPC and stays in the per-session MCP server (approved decision 9 routes delivery through the MCP child).

Message voice. distributed-protocol has the causer's daemon generate the warning 'worded as coming from the holder'. negotiation forbids writing '영희 says' unless 영희's human typed it, and requires 'cowork-sync on behalf of 영희's session'.

Attribution of Bash edits. claude-code attributes Bash/PowerShell diffs to the session, then restores the hunks that fall in foreign symbols and records them. editor-fs classes Claude's Bash edits as 'human', taking a soft claim with a 10-minute TTL and never auto-reverting them. negotiation attributes them to the session if they fall inside the tool window. The result differs between deny/restore and claim-and-publish.

Sync scope and caps. product-ux-ops auto-includes new files matching include globs (source extensions). git-integrity, security-hosts and editor-fs allow only tracked files, files created by a Write hook, and explicit /cowork add. The size cap is 5 MB (git-integrity) versus 1 MB (security-hosts, editor-fs, product-ux-ops). Fence TTLs are 20 s (claude-code), 60 s (editor-fs, human-git-lifecycle), 120 s (distributed-protocol) and 180 s for Read→Write (negotiation).

Approved-decision changes that need explicit user sign-off. Requirement 8 literally says ALL other Claudes notice and warn the causer; every lens replaces this with one daemon-generated message and pull-only bystanders. Decision 4 says never touch the user's index or HEAD; git-integrity and human-git-lifecycle make ADOPT automatic, while product-ux-ops makes it opt-in. Decision 4's read-tree -m -u apply is replaced by a per-path verifying writer (editor-fs) but kept with tree surgery (git-integrity, product-ux-ops), and 'git add -A' is replaced by an explicit list. Decision 10 says claims are released at stdin close; claude-code overrides this.

gapResults.lens: gap:Region identity and the 'splice' operator (symbol keys across peers and versions)

findings.title: Splice/claim offsets computed in the wrong coordinate system (UTF-16 units, BOM-stripped, LF-normalized or quote-folded text) applied to stored or raw bytes corrupt the pushed blob
findings.scenario: Hooks and claim logic work on Claude Code's view of the file: BOM stripped, CRLF folded to LF, curly quotes folded. The daemon parses with web-tree-sitter (decision 10), whose node.startIndex/endIndex are UTF-16 code units of the JS string. The push gate then applies [start,end) to the outgoing blob, which is in stored form: BOM+LF under autocrlf=true, or BOM+CRLF if the blob was committed with CRLF (e6/F7). Fixture: 5,958-line BOM+CRLF Python file with Hangul strings and curly quotes; claimed function at line 5,332. Each offset system was applied to the raw and to the stored form.
findings.consequence: Every wrong-form splice is corrupt. Region start drift against the stored BOM+LF blob: 14,467 (web-tree-sitter UTF-16 units), 9,135 (Node string of the BOM+CRLF file), 1,527 (quote-folded UTF-8), 3 (BOM-stripped UTF-8). Against the raw working-tree bytes: 19,798 / 14,466 / 6,858 / 5,334. Even the 3-byte (BOM only) drift produced invalid UTF-8 plus 2 duplicated and 3 lost lines, while tree-sitter still reported parses_clean=true. The pushed blob is cut mid-Hangul and mid-line, and every peer applies it. With correct offsets, inserting LF text into a CRLF blob left 7 lone-LF lines (mixed endings, then whole-file renormalization churn).
findings.evidence_detail: sweep/region/results_all.json S8_offset_drift (drift_bytes_vs_raw, drift_bytes_vs_stored, splice_results; 'stored_BOM_LF <- utf8_bytes_noBOM_LF': valid_utf8=false, parses_clean=true; '<- resolved in same form': byte_equal=true for both forms; correct_offsets_LF_text_into_CRLF_blob lone_LF_lines=7). web-tree-sitter 0.27.0 + tree-sitter-python 0.25.0 wasm (wts/units.mjs): startIndex == String.indexOf, not the byte index (alpha 29 vs byte 49); readFileSync keeps BOM -> root.startIndex=1. Cross-implementation (wts/dump.mjs vs py-tree-sitter 0.26): node types and ROWS identical for 435/9/8 nodes (py/cs/js) in both LF and BOM+CRLF forms, indices differ (EOF 103,400 vs 119,464). Rows are therefore form- and implementation-invariant; offsets are not. Scenarios S1-S7, S9 and S10 ran on the LF form for readability; this row-invariance is why their results carry over to BOM+CRLF. Stored-form flip: sibling e6/F7.
findings.mitigation: Rule: the only coordinates stored, published or exchanged between components (hook <-> daemon <-> board <-> gate) are (stored-form blob OID, 1-based inclusive line range). No byte, char or UTF-16 offset crosses a component boundary. Region computation reads the stored blob (`git cat-file blob`) and uses only node.startPosition.row/endPosition.row. Byte offsets, when needed, are derived inside one function from a line-start table of the same blob Buffer. Hook-side normalization (BOM, CRLF, quote folding) is allowed only for locating old_string and is converted to a line number immediately; none of these normalizations changes the '\n' line count. Splitting is on '\n' only (U+2028/2029, research). Any text written into a blob must come from another stored-form blob of the same path.
findings.test: Property test over fixtures with BOM, CRLF, LF, Hangul, astral emoji and curly quotes, both blob forms (LF blob and CRLF blob via the has_crlf_in_index guard): for 200 random claimed symbols and random requester edits, run the gate pipeline. Assert: output is valid UTF-8; bytes outside the claimed lines are byte-identical to the merge result; each line's ending matches the TIP blob's; output equals the oracle built by line-level replacement. Include a regression that runs the daemon's real WASM parser and asserts that no API returning startIndex/endIndex is used outside the line-table helper (lint rule).

findings.title: Building the spliced blob from working-tree text, or writing it with `git hash-object --stdin` without --path, bypasses the clean filter and eol conversion
findings.scenario: The repo has a clean/smudge filter that hides a secret in one file, and core.autocrlf=true.
