findings.title: Built-in cross-session rules and prompt-injection defences work against the 'politely ask to go first' and 'warn the causer' behaviours
findings.evidence_detail: cross-session-messaging.md says Claude 'is instructed never to ask another session for an action that was denied or blocked in its own session ... and to route that work back to you instead'. A received message is labelled as coming 'from another session, not from you', 'can't approve anything', and is never to change configuration. hooks.md#add-context-for-claude says text framed as out-of-band system commands 'can trigger Claude's prompt-injection defenses', and Claude then surfaces it to the user instead.
findings.scenario: 1. Bob's Edit is denied, and the design expects his Claude to ask the holder 'quick job, may I go first?'. Built-in policy pushes it to hand the matter back to Bob. 2. On the holder side, a hook injects 'STOP. Chulsoo caused a conflict. You must warn him now.' and Claude treats it as a possible injection and shows it to the user. 3. Handoffs that touch CLAUDE.md or .claude/settings are refused by the receiving Claude.
findings.consequence: The human-like negotiation of requirement 4 happens inconsistently. Agents oscillate between ignoring cowork notices and alarming their users, and handoffs on config files stall.
findings.mitigation: (a) Negotiation actions are taken by the DAEMON under the user's standing opt-in, recorded at /cowork start and restated in SessionStart context as the user's chosen workflow. Claude only calls cowork_request or cowork_respond MCP tools whose descriptions say they file a record in the shared board, not a message to another session. (b) All injected text is factual third-person status with no imperatives, capitals or 'system' framing. (c) Handoffs that touch config paths always go to the human holder, never to Claude.
findings.test: 20 runs each: (a) a denied edit, then measure how often Claude calls cowork_request versus refusing or deferring; (b) inject the status text, then measure how often Claude flags it as suspicious. Compare imperative and factual wordings, and require the factual one to be flagged in ≤1/20.

findings.title: Stop-based handoff silently never happens on Esc, API error or hook failure; Stop-based asks re-fire every turn
findings.evidence_detail: DOCUMENTED (hooks.md#stop): Stop doesn't run on user interrupt, API errors fire StopFailure, and the 8-consecutive cap applies only to consecutive continuations. VERIFIED from the 2.1.284 binary: the UI renders null for hook_non_blocking_error when hookEvent is Stop or SubagentStop, so a failing Stop hook is invisible to the user, and to the model (()=>[]).
findings.scenario: 1. Bob's blocked leftover is meant to be handed off at Stop. Bob presses Esc, or the turn ends with an overload error, or the Stop mcp_tool hook fails because the MCP server is disconnected. Nothing is handed off, and nobody sees an error. 2. On the holder side, the Stop hook blocks with 'Bob requests X: handle it?' at every turn end while the request is pending. The cap resets after each user prompt, so the request is asked at every Stop for hours, and each block is one more full-context request (≈0.5M tokens at this PC's median).
findings.consequence: The promise that nothing is ever lost breaks quietly, and nagging loops cost about 7.7M tokens/h at 15 Stops/h.
findings.mitigation: (a) The handoff record is created durably by the daemon at DENY time (PreToolUse) with status pending-leftover. Stop, SessionEnd, MCP EOF, and a 10-min idle timer are all just promoters, and none is required. (b) Ask each holder at most once per request through a Stop block, and record asked_at. The answer must arrive through cowork_respond(R, accept|decline|later). Later reminders are digest lines only. (c) Never block Stop when stop_hook_active is true, or when the turn was started by a wake.
findings.test: Inject Esc, StopFailure and a dead MCP server at turn end. Assert the request appears in the holder's queue within 10 min in all three cases. Run the holder for 10 turns with the request pending, and assert exactly 1 Stop block for that request id.

findings.title: Edit re-matches against current content, so after a peer moves code the edit lands in the new location and is reported as clean
findings.evidence_detail: In-session test (2.1.284, sweep/host/inses/moved.py). Claude read alpha() containing 'total = compute(1)'. An external writer moved those lines into beta(). The Edit was applied inside beta() with the note '(note: the file had been modified on disk since you last read it — the edit applied cleanly, but the file contains other changes not in your context...)'. CRLF was preserved.
findings.scenario: 1. Bob's Claude reads alpha() and plans a fix to the 'total = compute(1)' lines. 2. Younghee's refactor moves those lines into beta() and is applied to Bob's tree. 3. Bob's Edit matches uniquely in beta(). The gate maps the edit by current content to beta(), which is unclaimed, and allows it.
findings.consequence: The fix silently lands in code Bob's Claude never read, which is now Younghee's new function. alpha() stays unfixed. Claude reports success.
findings.mitigation: The gate resolves old_string twice: against the seat's last-read snapshot of the file (content hash and base tree recorded by the PostToolUse(Read) hook) and against current disk. If the enclosing symbol differs (moved or renamed), deny with the reason 'the code you are editing moved from alpha to beta (Younghee, 10:42); re-read and confirm the target'.
findings.test: Unit test: a read snapshot with the snippet in alpha and current content with it in beta gives a deny with a 'moved' reason. Same symbol in both gives allow. Integration test: replay the moved.py scenario through the gate.

findings.title: SessionStart re-fires with new sessions on /clear, resume and fork while the MCP server process persists; session_id-keyed claims orphan or self-conflict
findings.evidence_detail: DOCUMENTED: SessionStart sources are startup, resume, clear, compact and fork. /clear and in-session /resume rerun the hooks, and their results are discarded if the user switches again mid-hook. VERIFIED: the MCP server is one process per claude process and gets EOF only at process exit. Whether /clear changes session_id in every version is unverified.
findings.scenario: 1. Bob holds a claim on parse_row under session S1. 2. Bob runs /clear, which gives session S2 in the same process. 3. Bob's next Edit to parse_row is checked under S2, and the claim belongs to S1, which is live because the MCP stdin is still open. The edit is denied as conflicting with 'Bob (S1)'. Alternatively, fences opened under S1 are never closed. 4. A forked session in a second process also believes it holds S1's claims.
findings.consequence: The user is blocked by their own claims, fences get stuck so the daemon never writes a file, or two processes double-hold a claim.
findings.mitigation: Key claims and fences by SEAT, a random id created when the MCP server starts and passed into every mcp_tool hook input. Keep a map from session_id to seat. SessionStart with source clear, compact or resume rebinds the session to the seat; fork creates a new seat. On SessionStart(compact|clear|resume), re-inject a fresh board snapshot of at most 1.5k chars marked as superseding earlier notes.
findings.test: Claim, /clear, edit the same symbol: allowed. /compact: the board snapshot is re-injected. Fork: the second seat sees the first seat's claims as foreign and conflicts are resolved by board order. No fence older than its tool_use survives.

findings.title: mcp_tool and command hooks default to a 600 s timeout, so a stalled daemon freezes Claude's Edit for minutes and then lets it through
findings.evidence_detail: hooks.md#common-fields: the default timeout is 600 for command, http and mcp_tool. While a server is connecting, a blocking event waits up to MCP_TIMEOUT. A timed-out PreToolUse does not block (VERIFIED in run1 at 3 s).
findings.scenario: 1. The daemon is merging the 1.3 MB file, or blocked on a slow fetch or push retry, or Defender is scanning. 2. The MCP gate tool forwards the claim check to the daemon over IPC and waits. 3. Claude's Edit spins for up to 10 minutes, then proceeds ungated.
findings.consequence: The UI hangs (the user thinks Claude is frozen), followed by an ungated edit.
findings.mitigation: Set `timeout: 10` on every gate hook. The MCP server answers from an in-memory claim and symbol cache that the daemon pushes to it, so the answer never waits on git or the network. An internal 1 s deadline returns an explicit decision: deny when the cache shows a conflict; otherwise allow-and-record-as-unverified, so the publish gate re-checks it.
findings.test: Inject a 30 s stall in the daemon's IPC handler. Assert the gate decision arrives in ≤1.5 s, the edit is marked unverified in the ledger, and a publish-gate re-check runs.

findings.title: Hook text over 10,000 chars is replaced by a file path plus a 2,000-char preview, and Claude is not asked to read the file
findings.evidence_detail: hooks.md#json-output: additionalContext, systemMessage and plain stdout are each capped at 10,000 chars. Over the cap, the text is saved to a file and replaced by its path plus a preview of up to 2,000 chars, and 'Claude Code doesn't ask Claude to read the file'. The cap has no setting.
findings.scenario: 1. The board has 4 peers, 40 claims and a queue of 12 requests. 2. The digest grows to 14k chars. 3. The line 'your pending edit conflicts with Younghee's claim' sits at char 6,000. Claude sees only the first 2,000 chars.
findings.consequence: The critical notice is invisible, and Claude keeps working on the conflicted symbol.
findings.mitigation: The digest builder hard-caps at 1,500 chars, sorted by priority: this seat's conflicts, then requests addressed to it, then its claims, then a count of others. Everything else is available through the cowork_status tool.
findings.test: Unit test: 200 claims and 50 requests give a digest of ≤1,500 chars whose first line is this seat's conflict.

findings.title: Cost model: an unbudgeted design adds about 65% to a median active session-hour, and spends it even while the human is away
findings.evidence_detail: Parameters MEASURED on this PC (460 active main-thread hours from local transcripts): R = 60 requests/h median (p90 154); C = 511k context tokens/request median (p10 148k, p90 899k); baseline input 29.5M tokens per active hour (p90 88.5M); reminders 1.7k tokens (5.8k chars) each. Rates for the cowork scenario are REASONED. Price ratios ASSUMED: cache read 0.1x input, output 5x input, 1 h cache write 2x.
findings.scenario: Model: extra tokens per seat-hour ≈ wakes·k·C + Σ_reminders g·(R−i) + digests·g_d·R/2 + stopBlocks·C + writeLoops·(F·R/2 + 5·F_out). Setting: 4 peers, team pushes 1/10 s, 6 conflicts/h. NAIVE: wakes 8/h × 2 × 511k ≈ 8.2M; reminders 50 × 1.7k × 30 ≈ 2.5M in hour 1, plus about 5M each later hour; a 200-token digest on every hook ≈ 0.7M; Stop re-ask 15 × 511k ≈ 7.7M; 2 write loops ≈ 0.3M input-equivalent. Total ≈ 19M+ per seat-hour, about +65% of the median 29.5M, rising each hour. BUDGETED (rules in the other findings): wakes ≤2/h ≈ 2M, reminders ≤15/h ≈ 0.8M, delta-only digests ≈ 0.05M, ask-once ≤0.5M. Total ≈ 3.4M, about +11%, and 0 for idle seats. Second row for a 200k-window teammate at C ≈ 150k: naive ≈ 2.4M (wakes) + 2.3M (Stop) + 2.5M (reminders, same g) + 0.7M ≈ 8M/h, about +90% of a C-scaled baseline (60 × 150k = 9M). The relative overhead is HIGHER for small-context users because reminder and digest costs do not shrink with C. Reminders also force a compaction every 1-2 h, each a 150k-input plus 10-20k-output request. Budgeted at C=150k: about 0.6M + 0.15M + 0.8M + 0.05M ≈ 1.6M, about +18%.
findings.consequence: The wake and Stop share (about 16M/h) is spent while the session sits idle. A seat left open overnight at 8 wakes/h burns about 8M × 14 h ≈ 115M tokens, roughly 4 median active hours of that teammate's plan quota. Each wake after the cache TTL costs 12-20x more. Users hit plan limits and blame the plugin.
findings.mitigation: A per-seat token budget, enforced in the daemon. It counts every byte it causes to be injected (digests, attributions, inbox messages) and estimates reminder volume (applied diff chars into files in the seat's read set) and wakes multiplied by the last observed context size. The context_tokens field from SessionStart(resume), or the transcript usage, gives C. Defaults: ≤20k injected chars/h, ≤4 wakes/h, 0 wakes when the human has been idle more than 10 min or the cache is cold. Over budget, the seat degrades to digest-on-next-prompt. /cowork status shows the budget and usage.
findings.test: 1-hour soak, 4 seats, scripted churn and conflicts. Parse each seat's transcript usage. Assert extra input per seat-hour ≤15% over a no-cowork control run of the same script. Assert zero requests start in seats whose human has been idle more than 10 min.

design_changes: The authoritative claim boundary moves from the PreToolUse gate to a daemon-side PUBLISH GATE. Every changed hunk must be covered by a claim held before the change; conflicting hunks go to a local-only quarantine ref and are never pushed. The PreToolUse gate is advisory, because every hook failure mode fails open (verified).

The apply step must support per-path HOLDS (MERGED' = MERGED with held paths taken from the local tree, incoming kept pending) for read leases and busy-seat throttling. Today's all-or-nothing read-tree -m -u of the full MERGED tree cannot express this.
Add a PostToolUse(Read) hook that reports the seat's read set (path, range, content hash). The read lease, moved-code detection, attribution notes and reminder budgeting all need it.
Key claims and fences by SEAT (MCP-server instance id), not session_id; rebind sessions on SessionStart(clear|compact|resume|fork).

Daemon lifetime is lease-based (MCP heartbeats or an explicit human lease) with a version handshake, an env allowlist at spawn, and runtime assets copied into CLAUDE_PLUGIN_DATA. An orphan daemon is otherwise invisible and immortal (verified: it escapes the job object and survives claude exit).

Real-time delivery becomes a doorbell with a wake budget. The causer's own daemon issues the conflict warning (O(1) wakes per conflict, not O(N)); other seats get digest lines; no wakes to seats whose human is idle more than 10 min or whose cache is cold; wake-originated turns cannot cause wakes.
Handoff records are created at deny time. Stop, SessionEnd, MCP EOF and an idle timer are interchangeable promoters. Each holder is asked once per request via the explicit cowork_respond tool.
Each seat gets a token and context budget enforced by the daemon, with telemetry in /cowork status.

Corrections to round-1 assumptions. (1) The file fence closes the read-modify-write window for Edit only. For Write, the staleness check runs BEFORE PreToolUse, so the fence never engages (verified); it needs the read lease. (2) editor-fs F18 rated the 'modified-file notices' low; they should be HIGH: 560 reminders in local VS Code transcripts, 77% mid-turn, framed 'usually deliberate ... take it as the current state ... no need to call it out'. (3) 'Release claims when MCP stdin closes' works on normal exit (EOF observed), but needs a grace period plus a mark-unarmed step, because an MCP crash mid-session also closes the pipe while Claude keeps editing ungated. (4) A test plan that measures reminders with claude -p will report zero (2 runs). Use an interactive harness. (5) MultiEdit is no longer in the tools reference, so it can be dropped from the matcher; Edit|Write|NotebookEdit plus advisory Bash|PowerShell is enough.
open_questions: Why did claude -p (2.1.270) emit zero edited_text_file reminders (2 runs, including a 4-turn stream-json session) while VS Code sessions on this PC emit them mid-turn? Measuring reminder rates for the terminal CLI needs an interactive ConPTY harness.

Does /clear change session_id in current versions while the stdio MCP server persists? And what sender name and framing does the model see for a message that the session's own MCP server posts to its inbox (own-child)?

Does Node/libuv's detached spawn use CREATE_BREAKAWAY_FROM_JOB? If so, does it fail with access denied inside job objects that forbid breakaway (some EDR or terminal hosts)? The daemon would then never start.
Survival on interactive /exit, terminal-window close and VS Code window close was not exercised. It is inferred from the verified absence of a job object and from survival after the -p exit.

The price ratios used in the cost model (cache read 0.1x, output 5x, 1 h cache write 2x) should be confirmed against current Opus 5.x pricing. Plan-quota accounting for wakes on subscription plans is also not documented.
